# Course setup — tools for the MailGuard path

**Why this matters.** Security labs fail for boring reasons: wrong Python, no `venv`, Git missing, or tools installed too late. Without a repeatable machine baseline, every later module becomes “debug the laptop” instead of learning identity, email auth, and cloud access. On the job, the same hygiene — isolate deps, verify versions, defer heavy tooling until needed — keeps shared environments and CI honest.

**How it works.**

1. Install a small **core** set now: Git, Python 3.11+ (or current stable 3.x), `venv`/`pip`, `pytest`, and an editor.
2. Confirm each with a version check (`git --version`, `python3 --version`, `pytest --version`).
3. Create a Challenge Gym `.venv`, install `requirements.txt`, and run `pytest -q` so the toolchain is proven (failing kata tests are expected).
4. Defer Node, Go, Docker, Terraform, kubectl/kind, and cloud CLIs until the module that needs them.
5. Mark Module 00 complete only after the checklist below passes.

That staged path mirrors how teams onboard: unblock day-one work first, then add platform tooling when the workload appears.

### Worked example

```bash
git --version
python3 --version          # Windows: py -3 --version
cd 01-challenge-gym && python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest --version
```

You should see version strings for Git/Python/pytest. Kata failures are fine; an import or `venv` error means fix setup before Module 01.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Install every cloud/K8s tool on day one.”** Unused Docker/Terraform/kubectl stacks rot and fight each other; defer until the module that needs them so core Python labs stay unblocked.
- **“System Python is fine — skip venv.”** Global packages diverge from classmates and CI; a project `.venv` keeps `pyotp`/`cryptography`/pytest on a known graph.
- **“pytest red means setup failed.”** Early red tests prove the runner works; only interpreter/venv/import errors mean the machine baseline is wrong.

This module prepares your machine for the full course: identity / MFA katas, email authentication, Python APIs, TypeScript/Vue admin, Go workers, AWS/CI, Terraform, and local Kubernetes. You do **not** need every tool on day one — install **core** tools now, and the **later** tools when the matching module arrives.

Work through the installs below, then mark Module 00 complete on the site. This module has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What the course uses (audit)

| Area | Tools / libraries | First needed |
|------|-------------------|--------------|
| Editor + VCS | Code editor; **Git** | 00 / whole course |
| Python path | **Python 3.11+**, `pip`, `venv`, **pytest**, **pyotp**, **cryptography**; later **FastAPI** | 01, 05, 07, 10 |
| Frontend | **Node.js** + npm/pnpm; **TypeScript**; **Vue 3**; optional **Svelte / SvelteKit** | 08, 17 (also to preview the course site: `cd site && npm start`) |
| Go path | **Go** toolchain (`go test`, modules) | 09 |
| Containers | **Docker** + **Docker Compose** | 12 (image CI step), 13, 14 |
| Cloud / CI | **GitHub** account; **GitHub Actions**; **AWS** account (free tier) or local stand-ins; **AWS CLI** (optional early) | 12+ |
| IaC | **Terraform** | 13 |
| Kubernetes | **kubectl**; **kind** or **minikube**; YAML / Helm or Kustomize; **Argo CD** for GitOps in 16 | 14–16 |
| Course site | Modern browser; Node.js to preview the site locally (`cd site && npm start`); later modules use fillable quiz PDFs | 00 / whole course |
| Sample data | Module fixtures and stubs in-repo (no separate dataset download) | per module |

Official docs linked below. Prefer current stable releases unless a module README pins a version.

---

## Core installs (do these now)

### 1. Git

Why: every module is a git-tracked lab; without Git you cannot pull fixes or keep `my-work/` history separate from course stubs.

- Windows: [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win)
- macOS: [Git downloads](https://git-scm.com/download/mac) or `xcode-select --install`
- Linux: distro packages — e.g. `sudo apt install git` (Debian/Ubuntu)

**Check:** `git --version`

### 2. Python 3.11+ (or current stable 3.x)

Why: Challenge Gym and most identity/email katas are Python-first; an old or Store-alias interpreter breaks `venv` and pytest.

- Windows / macOS / source: [python.org downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/)
- macOS (Homebrew): `brew install python`
- Linux: distro `python3` / `python3-venv` / `python3-pip`

On Windows installer, enable **Add python.exe to PATH**.

**Check:**

```bash
python3 --version   # Windows: py -3 --version  (or python --version)
python3 -m pip --version
```

On Windows use `py -3` (or `python`) instead of `python3`; `python3` may open the Microsoft Store alias.

### 3. Virtualenv + Challenge Gym deps

Why: a project `.venv` keeps course packages (`pyotp`, `cryptography`, pytest) off the system Python so CI and classmates get the same import graph.

From the course repo:

```bash
cd 01-challenge-gym
python3 -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell: py -3 -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
#   If activation is blocked: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
# Windows cmd.exe: .venv\Scripts\activate.bat
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
pytest -q
```

(Expect failing tests until you implement katas — the important part is that `pytest` runs. Why run it now: proves the toolchain, not that solutions exist yet.)

**Check:** `pytest --version`

### 4. Code editor

Any editor is fine (VS Code, Cursor, Neovim, etc.). Install a Python extension if you use VS Code/Cursor.

### 5. PDF reader for quizzes

Use a reader that can fill AcroForm PDFs (many browsers work; Preview / Adobe Reader / Okular also fine). Save finished PDFs under `my-work/quizzes/`.

---

## Install when you reach that module

### Node.js (Modules 08, 17)

- [Node.js LTS downloads](https://nodejs.org/)

**Check:** `node --version` · `npm --version`

### Go (Module 09)

- [Go install](https://go.dev/doc/install)

**Check:** `go version`

### Docker + Compose (Modules 13–14)

- [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/) (Windows/macOS) or [Docker Engine](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/) (Linux)

**Check:** `docker --version` · `docker compose version`

### Terraform (Module 13)

- [HashiCorp Terraform installs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install)

**Check:** `terraform version`

### kubectl + kind or minikube (Modules 14–16)

- [kubectl install](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/)
- [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/) or [minikube](https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/start/)

**Check:** `kubectl version --client` · `kind version` or `minikube version`

### GitHub + AWS (Modules 12+)

- [GitHub signup](https://github.com/signup)
- [AWS free tier](https://aws.amazon.com/free/) (or local stand-ins such as LocalStack/MinIO when a module allows)
- Optional: [AWS CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/getting-started-install.html) — `aws --version`

Never commit cloud secrets. Module READMEs describe least-privilege demos.

---

## OS tips

| OS | Notes |
|----|--------|
| **Windows** | Prefer PowerShell or Git Bash; WSL2 is excellent for Python/Docker/kind. |
| **macOS** | Homebrew simplifies Git, Python, Go, Terraform, kubectl. |
| **Linux** | Use your distro packages for Git/Python; follow upstream docs for Docker/Terraform/kind. |

---

## Final setup checklist

Confirm each item before marking Module 00 complete:

1. `git --version` works  
2. `python3 --version` (Windows: `py -3 --version`) shows 3.11+ (or current stable 3.x)  
3. `python3 -m venv` (Windows: `py -3 -m venv`) works; Challenge Gym venv installs `requirements.txt`  
4. `pytest --version` works inside that venv  
5. Editor + Git configured; you can commit  
6. Browser opens the course site  
7. You know *when* to add Node, Go, Docker, Terraform, kubectl/kind, GitHub, and AWS  

Then mark Module 00 complete in the site progress UI. Next are short **language/tool primers** (Bash, then Python) before Module 01 — read-only like this setup module. Later primers appear immediately before the first module that uses that tool (SQL, TypeScript/Vue, Go, Docker, GitHub Actions, Terraform, Kubernetes YAML, Svelte).

# Bash / shell primer

**Why this matters.** Almost every MailGuard lab starts in a terminal: create a venv, run `pytest`, call `go test`, or bring Compose up. Without shell fluency, the “how” of every later module stays blocked behind copy-paste. On the job, the same skill lets you reproduce CI failures, inspect logs, and keep secrets in the environment instead of committed files.

**How it works.**

1. You type a line; the shell expands variables and globs.
2. The shell runs the resulting program (or builtin).
3. Pipes (`|`) pass stdout of one command to stdin of the next; redirects send output to files.
4. Environment variables (`export VAR=…`) configure tools without hard-coding secrets into files you might commit.
5. Exit codes (`$?` / `$LASTEXITCODE`) tell scripts and CI whether the last command passed (0) or failed (non-zero).

### Worked example

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/mailguard-shell-demo && cd /tmp/mailguard-shell-demo
echo "hold" > decision.txt
grep -n hold decision.txt
echo "exit was $?"    # 0 if grep found a match
```

Same pattern CI uses: run a check, then branch on the exit code.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“The command printed nothing, so it failed.”** Many tools are quiet on success; check `$?` (or the pipeline status) instead of assuming silence means error.
- **“Putting the API token in the script is fine for a lab.”** Lab scripts get committed; use the environment so secrets stay out of git history.
- **“PowerShell and Bash are interchangeable copy-paste.”** Syntax for env vars, activation, and exit codes differs — follow the OS notes in Module 00 when a command fails oddly.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack — read, try the tiny example, mark complete, then continue.

---

## What Bash is

**Bash** (Bourne Again SHell) is a command language common on Linux/macOS. On Windows, **Git Bash**, **WSL**, or **PowerShell** cover the same lab ideas with slightly different syntax.

## Why industry uses it

Cloud and security work is automation-heavy: CI runners, remote bastions, and container entrypoints are shell-first. Guis help explore; shells make steps repeatable and reviewable in git.

## Key concepts for upcoming labs

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| `cd` / paths | Every module README assumes you are in the right folder |
| `export VAR=…` | Tokens and API URLs stay out of source when possible |
| pipes / redirects | Compose logs, `pytest -q`, filtering output |
| exit codes | Scripts and CI fail when a command returns non-zero |

## Install / open a shell

- **macOS / Linux:** Terminal.app, iTerm, or your desktop terminal — Bash or zsh both work for this course.
- **Windows:** [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) (Git Bash), [WSL2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install), or PowerShell (`py -3`, `python`, etc. as Module 00 notes).

**Check:** `echo $SHELL` (Git Bash/WSL/macOS/Linux) or `$PSVersionTable` in PowerShell.

## Tiny hands-on example

```bash
# Why: confirm the shell runs commands and prints exit status
mkdir -p /tmp/mailguard-shell-demo && cd /tmp/mailguard-shell-demo
echo "hold" > decision.txt
grep -n hold decision.txt && echo "exit was $?"
```

**How:** `mkdir` creates a sandbox, `echo` writes a file, `grep` searches it, `$?` shows the last exit code — the same pattern CI uses to fail a job.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Bash Scripting Full Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e7BufAVwDiM)**  
   Why it helps: shell literacy before Challenge Gym.

## Official docs

1. [GNU Bash manual](https://www.gnu.org/software/bash/manual/)
2. [Git for Windows](https://gitforwindows.org/)
3. [PowerShell docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`01-challenge-gym`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Python primer

**Why this matters.** MailGuard’s identity, email-auth, API, and capstone labs are Python-first. Without a working interpreter, venv, and pytest habit, Challenge Gym cannot prove the “how” behind TOTP, holds, and rules. On the job, the same loop — isolate deps, let tests define the contract — is how teams ship auth and email-security glue without “works on my machine.”

**How it works.**

1. Confirm a Python 3.11+ (or current stable 3.x) interpreter.
2. Create and activate a **virtual environment** so deps stay off the system Python.
3. Install from `requirements.txt` with `pip`.
4. Read the failing pytest for a kata stub under `katas/`.
5. Implement until the test passes; re-run often. That loop (read test → write code → re-run) is the course’s core practice: fail first, then make the stub match the spec.

### Worked example

```bash
python3 -m venv /tmp/mg-py-primer && source /tmp/mg-py-primer/bin/activate
python - <<'PY'
def hold_reason(score: int) -> str:
    return "hold" if score >= 80 else "allow"
print(hold_reason(90))  # → hold
PY
```

A pure function returning a decision string is the same shape as later hold-rule katas, without frameworks yet.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“I’ll install packages globally to save time.”** Global site-packages drift from CI and classmates; always use a venv for course work.
- **“Green means I understand the crypto/auth.”** Tests are the contract for the stub — still read the Why/How in each module so you can explain the mechanism in an interview.
- **“Type hints are optional fluff.”** Light hints in kata stubs document the expected shapes; ignoring them often causes the first confusing pytest failures.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Python is

**Python** is a high-level language widely used for APIs, automation, and security tooling. This course targets **Python 3.11+** (or current stable 3.x).

## Why industry uses it

Teams choose Python for fast iteration on auth, data, and glue code: readable modules, rich libraries (`cryptography`, web frameworks), and excellent test ergonomics. Cloud-security prototypes often start here before hardening.

## Key concepts for Module 01+

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| `venv` | Keeps course deps from fighting system Python |
| `pip install -r requirements.txt` | Reproducible lab installs |
| functions + type hints (light) | Clear kata stubs |
| `pytest` | Tests are the spec — fail first, then implement |

## Install and run

Follow Module 00 if needed, then:

```bash
# Why: confirm 3.x, then isolate this primer’s deps from system site-packages
python3 --version   # Windows: py -3 --version
python3 -m venv /tmp/mg-py-primer && source /tmp/mg-py-primer/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell: py -3 -m venv .venv ; .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
```

Official install: [python.org downloads](https://www.python.org/downloads/).

## Tiny hands-on example

```bash
cat > /tmp/mg_hello.py << 'EOF'
def hold_reason(score: int) -> str:
    # Why: small pure function — easy to unit test later
    return "hold" if score >= 80 else "allow"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(hold_reason(90))
EOF
python /tmp/mg_hello.py
```

**How:** A pure function returns a decision string — the same shape as later hold-rule katas, without frameworks yet.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Python for Beginners – Full Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eWRfhZAVOY8)**  
   Why it helps: venv/functions mindset before pytest katas.

## Official docs

1. [Python 3 tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/)
2. [venv docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html)
3. [pytest documentation](https://docs.pytest.org/)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`01-challenge-gym`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# HTTP primer

**Why this matters.** OIDC redirects, FastAPI routes, admin UIs, and health checks are all HTTP conversations. Without method/status/header literacy, every later “401 vs 403” or CORS failure becomes folklore. On the job, identity and email-security APIs are debugged first at the wire: request line, headers, status, then body.

**How it works.**

1. A client opens a **TLS** (or cleartext lab) connection to a host.
2. It sends a **request line** (method + path + HTTP version) plus **headers** and optional body.
3. The server responds with a **status code**, response headers, and optional body.
4. **Cookies** may store session state the browser sends back on later requests (scope/path/Secure/HttpOnly matter).
5. **CORS** is a browser rule set: servers advertise which origins may read responses from script; curl ignores CORS.
6. APIs document this surface (OpenAPI); browsers and SPAs must still respect same-origin / CORS.

```text
Client --TLS--> Server
  REQUEST: METHOD /path HTTP/1.1 + headers + body?
  RESPONSE: status + headers + body?
```

### Worked example

```bash
# Why: see method + status without a framework
curl -sI https://example.com | head -n 5
# Look for HTTP/2 200 (or 301) and security headers (e.g. Strict-Transport-Security)
```

Idempotent sketch: repeating `GET /healthz` should not change server state; repeating `POST /rules` usually creates another rule unless the API defines idempotency keys.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“401 and 403 are the same.”** 401 = not authenticated (or bad credentials); 403 = authenticated but not allowed — different fixes.
- **“CORS protects the server.”** CORS constrains *browsers*; non-browser clients can still call the API — authz still required.
- **“Cookies are fine without Secure/HttpOnly.”** Lab shortcuts leak sessions on HTTP or to JavaScript XSS.
- **“TLS is optional once we have OAuth.”** Tokens on cleartext HTTP are still stealable in transit.

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## Methods and status codes

| Method | Typical use | Safe? | Idempotent? |
|--------|-------------|-------|-------------|
| GET | Read | Yes | Yes |
| HEAD | Headers only | Yes | Yes |
| POST | Create / RPC-style | No | Usually no |
| PUT | Replace | No | Yes |
| PATCH | Partial update | No | Usually no |
| DELETE | Remove | No | Yes |

| Status | Meaning (literacy) |
|--------|--------------------|
| 2xx | Success (`200` OK, `201` Created, `204` No Content) |
| 3xx | Redirect (`301`/`302`/`307`/`308`) |
| 4xx | Client error (`400` bad request, `401` authn, `403` authz, `404` missing, `409` conflict) |
| 5xx | Server error |

## Headers, cookies, CORS, TLS

- **Headers** carry metadata (`Authorization`, `Content-Type`, `Cache-Control`).
- **Cookies** are `Set-Cookie` / `Cookie` pairs; prefer `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, and tight `SameSite` for sessions.
- **CORS** uses `Origin` + `Access-Control-Allow-*` for browser cross-origin reads.
- **TLS** authenticates the server (and optionally the client in mTLS) and encrypts the bytes.

## Tiny hands-on example

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://example.com
# → 200 (or a redirect code if the client does not follow)
```

## Official docs

1. [MDN — HTTP overview](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Overview)
2. [MDN — HTTP response status codes](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status)
3. [MDN — CORS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS)
4. [RFC 9110 — HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

## Videos (verified)

1. **[HTTP Crash Course & Exploration](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iYM2zFP3Zn0)** — Traversy Media  
   Why it helps: methods, status codes, and headers in one pass before OIDC/API labs.

## Done when

You can explain **why** HTTP shows up before OIDC and the MailGuard API and **how** to read a status line. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue.

# Reading — Basic auth JSON client

## Learning objectives

1. Build an HTTP Basic `Authorization` header (RFC 7617).
2. Parse a minimal JSON token response safely.
3. Reason about clock skew when pairing auth with TOTP.

**Why this matters.** Many lab and legacy APIs still gate calls with HTTP Basic. Without understanding how the header is built — and why cleartext HTTP fails — you either leak credentials or silently accept broken token JSON. On the job, pairing Basic (or any password-bearing header) with TOTP and clock-skew checks is a common “authenticated client + MFA” interview and integration pattern.

**How it works.**

1. Form the credential string as `username:password` (one string, colon separator).
2. Base64-encode that **single** string (encoding, not encryption).
3. Send `Authorization: Basic <encoded>` over **TLS only** (RFC 7617).
4. Parse the JSON body as an object and require an explicit `token` field — fail closed if missing or the body is not an object.
5. When the same client also verifies TOTP, compare client/server Unix time against a `max_skew` budget so modest clock drift does not look like an attack.

### Worked example

```text
username:password  →  Base64  →  dXNlcm5hbWU6cGFzc3dvcmQ=

GET /token HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Basic dXNlcm5hbWU6cGFzc3dvcmQ=

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"token":"lab-session-token-example","expires_in":3600}
```

If the body were `{"access":"..."}` without `token`, a fail-closed parser rejects it instead of treating a missing key as success.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Base64 hides the password.”** Anyone who sees the header can decode it; without TLS the credential is plaintext on the wire.
- **“Any JSON with a string field is a token.”** Accepting the wrong key or a bare string lets broken servers pass; require an object with an explicit `token`.
- **“Client and server clocks must match exactly for TOTP.”** A small `max_skew` budget covers ordinary drift; treating any skew as attack (or ignoring skew entirely) breaks real users or accepts stale codes.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 7617](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617)
2. [MDN — Authorization](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Authorization)
3. [httpx Auth](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/authentication/) or [requests Auth](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/authentication/)

## Next step

Assignment → `katas/basic_auth_client.py` → quiz.

# Reading — Crypto hygiene

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Explain why a bare hash is the wrong tool for message **integrity** when an attacker can modify bytes — and why Hash-based Message Authentication Code (**HMAC**) binds a secret key to the hash.
2. Describe Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (**AEAD**) as “encrypt + authenticate in one construction,” and name Transport Layer Security (**TLS**) as the everyday place AEAD (and certificates) show up.
3. State a short **key lifecycle** checklist (generate, store, rotate, revoke) and refuse to invent ciphers — use reviewed libraries instead.

**Why this matters.** A bare hash looks like “integrity” until an attacker rewrites both the bytes and the digest. Without keyed integrity (HMAC) or authenticated encryption (AEAD), webhooks, audit blobs, and secrets-at-rest can be forged or silently altered. On the job, TLS already uses AEAD for every hop you trust — the same misuse rules (nonce reuse, inventing ciphers, skipping auth) show up in application crypto for email and identity services.

Time-based One-Time Password (**TOTP**) already taught “don’t hand-roll HMAC.” This kata widens the lens: integrity tags for audit-style blobs, and AEAD for secrets at rest and for app-level envelopes. You will call Python’s `hmac` module and the `cryptography` library’s AES-GCM — not design modes yourself.

**How it works.**

1. **Bare hash (wrong for authenticity).** `H(message)` can be recomputed by anyone who can change the message — so it does not prove a trusted party produced the bytes.
2. **HMAC.** Bind a secret key to a hash (`HMAC(K, message)`). Only key holders produce a valid tag; verify with a constant-time compare (`hmac.compare_digest`).
3. **AEAD (e.g. AES-GCM).** Encrypt and authenticate in one construction. Associated data is authenticated but not encrypted. Seal with a fresh nonce; open fails closed if the ciphertext or AAD was tampered.
4. **Libraries.** Prefer reviewed APIs (`hmac`, `cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM`) — do not invent modes or “raw AES-ECB then ship.”
5. **Key lifecycle.** Generate with a CSPRNG → store outside git → rotate on schedule or after suspicion → revoke compromised keys. Never reuse a nonce with the same key.

![Comparison of bare hash, HMAC, and AEAD plus a generate-store-rotate-revoke key lifecycle](images/crypto-hygiene.svg)

*Figure. A bare hash is not authenticity when an attacker can change bytes; **HMAC** binds a secret key; **AEAD** encrypts and authenticates together (TLS is the everyday place this shows up). Notice the key lifecycle strip — generate, store, rotate, revoke — and the rule to use reviewed libraries. Original course diagram (CC0).*

**TLS** (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol that protects HTTP and SMTP connections: the server presents an X.509 **certificate** (a signed binding of public key ↔ name), the client verifies the chain to a trusted root, then the peers agree on a cipher suite. TLS 1.3 uses only AEAD suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305); TLS 1.2 also allowed non-AEAD CBC suites. You will not implement TLS here; you *will* practice the same misuse rules TLS libraries already enforce — never reuse a nonce with the same key, never skip authentication, never treat “encrypt with raw AES-ECB” as done.

### Worked example

Webhook integrity tag (illustrative):

```python
import hmac, hashlib

secret = b"whsec_lab_only"
body = b'{"event":"hold.created","id":"h_42"}'
tag = hmac.new(secret, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
# Authorization-style header a receiver might check:
# X-Signature: sha256=<tag>
assert hmac.compare_digest(tag, hmac.new(secret, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest())
```

If an attacker changes `"h_42"` to `"h_99"` without the secret, the tag will not match. A bare `sha256(body)` published beside the body would match the attacker’s rewritten digest too — that is why the key matters.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Hashing the file proves nobody changed it.”** Without a key (or signature), the attacker updates both content and digest.
- **“Encrypt-then-ship without a MAC is fine.”** Unauthenticated ciphertext can be bit-flipped; AEAD (or encrypt-then-MAC done correctly) is the fix TLS already standardized on.
- **“Nonce reuse is rare so we can hard-code IV=0.”** AES-GCM with a repeated nonce under one key catastrophically fails confidentiality and authenticity — libraries expect a unique nonce per seal.
- **“I’ll roll my own AES mode for learning.”** Learning belongs in crypto courses; product paths consume reviewed libraries so misuse stays visible in code review.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[Public Key Cryptography - Computerphile](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSIDS_lvRv4)** — Computerphile (feat. Dr Mike Pound)  
   Why it helps: mental model for public/private keys before certificates feel magical.

2. **[TLS Handshake Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=86cQJ0MMses)** — Computerphile (feat. Dr Mike Pound)  
   Why it helps: certificate check → key agreement → encrypted application data, without drowning in RFCs. Written companion: [Cloudflare Learning — What happens in a TLS handshake?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/ssl/what-happens-in-a-tls-handshake/).

3. **[AES Explained (Advanced Encryption Standard)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O4xNJsjtN6E)** — Computerphile (feat. Dr Mike Pound)  
   Why it helps: intuition for the block cipher under AES-GCM — then remember this kata uses **AEAD** (GCM), not raw ECB.

## Read these (verified)

### Specs & libraries

1. [RFC 2104 — HMAC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2104) — keyed hashing for integrity/authenticity.
2. [Python `hmac` — cryptographic message authentication](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hmac.html) — `hmac.new`, `compare_digest`.
3. [PyCA cryptography — AESGCM](https://cryptography.io/en/latest/hazmat/primitives/aead/#cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead.AESGCM) — AEAD seal/open API you will call.

### Concepts & security literacy

4. [OWASP Cryptographic Storage Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cryptographic_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html) — algorithms, key management, common failures.
5. [MDN — Transport Layer Security (TLS)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Transport_Layer_Security) — what browsers verify and why mixed content breaks the model.
6. [Latacora — Cryptographic Right Answers](https://www.latacora.com/blog/2018/04/03/cryptographic-right-answers/) — opinionated “what to use” list (pair with current library docs).

### Why this kata exists (career prep)

7. Cloud security SaaS work expects engineers to *consume* crypto correctly (TLS termination, secret storage, HMAC webhooks) — not invent primitives.
8. MailGuard’s audit and secure-transfer paths need integrity and confidentiality literacy even when the product story is DLP, not a crypto product.

## Optional deepeners

- [NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 — Recommendation for Key Management](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/57/pt1/r5/final) — lifecycle vocabulary (generate, distribute, store, rotate, destroy).

# Reading — Hold rules

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Describe email Data Loss Prevention (DLP) as ordered policy: match conditions → action (allow / hold-suspend / reject-discard).
2. Implement **first-match-wins** evaluation over a small rule list without inventing a Domain-Specific Language (DSL).
3. Connect the toy engine to real product language (Microsoft Purview / Google Workspace DLP and similar SaaS email guards) so you can explain trade-offs in an interview.

**Why this matters.** Without outbound policy, sensitive mail leaves the org the moment someone hits Send — autocomplete mistakes and rushed CCs are expensive. Email Data Loss Prevention (DLP) exists so messages are inspected and acted on *before* delivery. On the job, SaaS email guards and security gateways all share the same inspect → match → act shape; this kata trains that vocabulary without a product lock-in.

Email DLP products sit between sender and recipient and apply **policy**: allow, temporarily hold (suspend), or reject/discard. Admins express rules; engines evaluate messages in a defined order. This kata is a **tiny** version of that idea — domain and substring predicates, **first match wins**, no DSL. The point is clear specs and concise Python, not a production rule language.

**How it works.**

1. Inspect the outbound message (recipients, subject, body — whatever predicates the engine supports).
2. Walk an **ordered** rule list from top to bottom.
3. For each rule, evaluate its predicates (e.g. recipient domain, substring in subject/body).
4. On the **first** matching rule, apply its action: **allow**, **hold/suspend**, or **reject/discard** — then stop.
5. If nothing matches, apply the engine’s default (documented in the kata/tests). Order *is* policy: swapping two rules can change outcomes for the same mail.

![Ordered hold rules evaluating a message with first-match-wins allow, hold, or reject outcomes](images/hold-rules-flow.svg)

*Figure. Inspect the message, walk the ordered rule list, and stop at the **first match**. Notice the three actions — allow, hold/suspend, reject/discard — and that evaluation order is part of the policy, not an afterthought. Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Worked example

```text
Rules (top → bottom):
  1. if subject contains "payroll"     → hold
  2. if any recipient domain != org.com → reject
  3. else                              → allow   (or default)

Message: To: alice@org.com, Subject: "Q4 payroll draft"
Evaluation: rule 1 matches → hold (rule 2 never runs)
```

If rule 2 were listed first, an internal payroll draft to `alice@org.com` would **allow** (no external domain) and never reach the payroll hold — same predicates, different order, different outcome.

Real email DLP products share this shape: rules that allow, suspend, or discard to prevent costly mis-sends of sensitive information. MailGuard later folders reuse the same allow / hold / reject vocabulary.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“All matching rules fire.”** First-match-wins means later rules are invisible once one matches — that is why order is part of the policy, not cosmetic.
- **“A hold engine replaces SPF/DKIM/DMARC.”** Holds catch *outbound* mistakes; domain authentication stops *inbound* spoof. Different problems.
- **“More predicates always mean better security.”** An unreadable DSL you cannot explain in an interview (or debug at 2 a.m.) fails operationally; start with clear order and tiny predicates.
- **“Default allow with no final rule is fine.”** Undocumented defaults surprise operators; tests should pin what happens when nothing matches.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[What is Data Loss Prevention (DLP)?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=meWpZCmV0dg)** — Google Workspace  
   Why it helps: short official intro to DLP as **rules** that scan content and enforce an action when a rule matches.

2. **[Data Loss Prevention across endpoints, apps, & services | Microsoft Purview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hvqq8L_0kgI)** — Microsoft Mechanics  
   Why it helps: shows how one DLP policy idea spans email and other channels — same “inspect → match → act” loop as this kata, at product scale.

3. **[Plan and design Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Policies | SC-401 | Episode 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Agp8I97XHlk)** — Microsoft Learn  
   Why it helps: policy design (what to monitor, where, conditions, actions) maps cleanly onto ordered hold/allow/reject rules.

## Read these (verified)

### Product / domain context

1. [What is Data Loss Prevention (DLP)? — Google Workspace](https://support.google.com/a/answer/9646351) — rules that scan content and enforce actions.
2. [Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/dlp-learn-about-dlp) — protection, detection, and response framing for email and sharing.
3. Challenge bar for this kata: short, elegant solutions — keep the engine interview-explainable.

### Engineering craft for this kata

4. [Python `dataclasses`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/dataclasses.html) — frozen message/rule records as used in the stub.
5. [pytest — Get Started](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/getting-started.html) — tests are the contract; run them often.

### Missend / privacy literacy (why “hold” exists)

6. [NZ Privacy Commissioner — prevent privacy breaches through email](https://www.privacy.org.nz/resources-and-learning/knowledge-base/view/516/) — wrong recipient is a top reported breach; check recipients; delays/reminders help.
7. [OVIC — tips to reduce data breaches when sending emails](https://ovic.vic.gov.au/privacy/resources-for-organisations/tips-to-reduce-data-breaches-when-sending-emails/) — human error, verify full addresses, delay-send patterns.

## Keep in mind

Production DLP adds attachment inspection, admin UX, queues, and richer matching. Your kata stays dumb on purpose — interview-explainable order and predicates first. Later MailGuard folders (API, Go workers, Vue admin, AWS) extend this toy engine toward a fuller SaaS shape.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

# Reading — Recipient risk

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Classify recipients as internal / external / invalid against an org domain after simple normalization.
2. Explain why **mixed** or **invalid** recipient sets are a missend / data-loss signal that can feed a hold rule.
3. Distinguish accidental missends from **Business Email Compromise (BEC)** / phishing — same “verify the recipient” habit, different attacker model.

**Why this matters.** Accidental missends (internal + external in one To/Cc) and invalid addresses leak data or bounce into the wrong inbox. Without a recipient-risk signal, hold rules have nothing principled to trigger on. On the job, the same “verify the recipient” habit shows up in DLP products and in Business Email Compromise (BEC) playbooks — different attacker models, same classification step.

A common missend pattern: a message meant for **internal** colleagues also includes an **external** address (or a typo’d / invalid address). Classifying recipients against an org domain and flagging **mixed** or **invalid** sets is the seed of a hold decision. This kata uses a **simple** `local@domain` normalizer — enough to practice specs and string discipline, not full RFC 5322 parsing.

**How it works.**

1. Take each recipient address from To/Cc (and Bcc if in scope).
2. **Normalize**: strip surrounding whitespace; lowercase the domain part.
3. Classify against the org domain: **internal** (exact org domain), **external** (other valid `local@domain`), or **invalid** (missing `@`, empty local, etc. — per kata tests).
4. Aggregate the set: all-internal → lower risk; **mixed** (internal + external) or any **invalid** → missend / data-loss signal.
5. Feed that signal into a hold-rule engine (pair with the hold-rules kata) so policy can hold or reject before send.

![Recipient classification into internal, external, or invalid, then a set outcome that can feed hold rules](images/recipient-risk.svg)

*Figure. Normalize first, then classify each address against the org domain. Notice that **mixed** or **invalid** set outcomes are the missend signal — the same “verify the recipient” habit applies to accidents and to BEC pressure, with different attacker models. Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Worked example

Org domain: `org.com`

```text
To: Alice <alice@org.com>, Bob <bob@partner.io>
Normalized domains: org.com, partner.io
Classes: internal, external
Set outcome: mixed  →  candidate for hold
```

```text
To: alice@org.com, not-an-email
Classes: internal, invalid
Set outcome: invalid present  →  candidate for hold/reject
```

Accidental missend: user meant only `alice@org.com` but autocomplete added `bob@partner.io`. BEC: attacker pressure uses lookalike external addresses — still “verify the recipient,” different attacker model.

Pair this with the hold-rules kata: risk signals often feed “should we hold?” policies in email Data Loss Prevention (DLP) products.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Case in the domain doesn’t matter so skip normalization.”** Without lowercasing domains, `Alice@Org.COM` and `alice@org.com` disagree and classification flakes.
- **“Mixed recipients are always malicious.”** Mixed is a *signal* (often autocomplete), not a verdict — policy may hold for review rather than hard-reject.
- **“This kata’s regex is production-ready.”** Real mail needs proper parsers, display names, and IDN (see OWASP); documenting the gap is part of the literacy.
- **“BEC and missend need different classifiers.”** Both start from “who are the recipients?” — attacker model differs after classification.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[FBI Warns of Business Email Compromise Scams](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cBcjTJmxgh4)** — FBI – Federal Bureau of Investigation  
   Why it helps: official framing of BEC — lookalike addresses and payment requests; reinforces **verify the recipient** before trusting mail.

2. **[PSA: Business E-Mail Compromise Scams](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u3nAeVNSV24)** — FBI – Federal Bureau of Investigation  
   Why it helps: short dramatization of a rushed wire on a suspicious “boss” email — same urgency/missend pressure DLP holds interrupt.

3. **[Recognize and Report Phishing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9pTW-F6V2N0)** — CISA  
   Why it helps: quick checklist for sender/address mismatch and odd urgency — literacy that pairs with programmatic recipient classification.

## Read these (verified)

### Email address handling

1. [Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Email Validation and Verification Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Email_Validation_and_Verification_Cheat_Sheet.html) — normalize before compare; don’t invent brittle regex empires; domain lowercasing.
2. [RFC 5321 — SMTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321) — skim address / mailbox concepts (optional depth after the kata is green).
3. [RFC 5322 — Internet Message Format](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5322) — full address syntax is richer than this kata; know the gap.

### Missend / DLP motivation

4. [NZ Privacy Commissioner — prevent privacy breaches through email](https://www.privacy.org.nz/resources-and-learning/knowledge-base/view/516/) — wrong recipient as a leading breach type.
5. [OVIC — tips to reduce data breaches when sending emails](https://ovic.vic.gov.au/privacy/resources-for-organisations/tips-to-reduce-data-breaches-when-sending-emails/) — verify full addresses; delay-send as a practical control.
6. [Microsoft Purview Data Loss Prevention](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/purview/dlp-learn-about-dlp) — product framing for protection / detection / response on email and sharing.

### Career prep (honest)

7. DLP / secure-transfer engineering roles care about missend prevention and policy engines — portfolio work shows fluency; calendar years are separate.
8. Challenge quality and stack familiarity matter in screening for cloud security SaaS roles.

## Keep in mind

Real mail needs proper parsers, display-name handling, and Unicode/IDN awareness (see OWASP). Document that production gap in your trade-offs; don’t pretend the kata is RFC-complete.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

# Reading — Parametrized TOTP (RFC 6238)

## Learning objectives

1. Implement HOTP dynamic truncation (RFC 4226 §5.3) yourself.
2. Parametrize TOTP by digest (SHA-1/256/512), digits (6–10), step, and T0.
3. Validate against RFC 6238 Appendix B vectors and the errata on seed lengths.
4. Optionally port the same logic to Go (`crypto/hmac`, `encoding/binary`).

**Why this matters.** Library wrappers are fine for product MFA — but screening-style tasks (and debugging interop) often require you to **derive the counter, HMAC, and truncate** correctly. Without the RFC 6238 errata on seed lengths, SHA-256/512 vectors fail mysteriously even when truncation looks right. On the job, knowing *how* TOTP is built helps you validate vendor libraries and clock-skew edge cases instead of treating OTP as a black box.

Appendix B publishes known answers; the errata clarifies that the shared secret length matches the hash (20 / 32 / 64 bytes), not a single 20-byte seed for every digest.

**How it works.**

1. Choose parameters: digest (SHA-1 / SHA-256 / SHA-512), `digits` (6–10), time step `X` (usually 30s), and epoch offset `T0` (usually 0).
2. Derive counter `T = floor((t − T0) / X)` from Unix time `t`.
3. Encode `T` as an 8-byte **big-endian** integer; compute `HMAC(K, counter_bytes)` with the shared secret `K`.
4. **Dynamic truncation** (RFC 4226 §5.3): take the low nibble of the **last** HMAC byte as offset; read four bytes from that offset; clear the high bit (`& 0x7FFFFFFF`); reduce mod `10^digits`.
5. Compare to Appendix B vectors — and use the errata seed lengths (20 / 32 / 64 bytes) so SHA-256/512 cases match.

```text
t, T0, X  →  T = floor((t-T0)/X)
K, T      →  HMAC → truncate → N-digit code
```

### Worked example

RFC 6238 Appendix B style (SHA-1, 8 digits, step 30, T0=0) — shape of the evaluation:

```text
t = 59
T = floor((59 - 0) / 30) = 1
counter (8-byte BE) = 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01
HMAC-SHA1(K, counter) → 20-byte digest
offset = digest[-1] & 0x0f
code = (packed_4_bytes & 0x7fffffff) % 10**8
```

Use the Appendix B published codes as the oracle. If SHA-256 vectors disagree, check seed length first (errata: 32-byte seed for SHA-256, not the 20-byte SHA-1 seed).

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“One 20-byte seed works for every digest in Appendix B.”** The errata requires seed length to match the hash; wrong length makes SHA-256/512 vectors fail even with correct truncation.
- **“Truncate from the first HMAC byte.”** Dynamic truncation uses the **last** byte’s low nibble as the offset — using the wrong end silently mismatches every vector.
- **“Little-endian counter is fine on x86.”** The RFC counter is big-endian; native endianness bugs pass local toys and fail Appendix B.
- **“Digits and step are always 6 and 30.”** Parametrized TOTP must honor the configured digits/step/T0 or interop with authenticators breaks.

## Short note

Pair this with the Basic-auth JSON client kata when you need an authenticated call that also tolerates small clock skew.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 4226 — HOTP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4226) — §5.3 truncation.
2. [RFC 6238 — TOTP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238) — §4 + Appendix B.
3. [RFC 6238 errata](https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=6238) — seed length per hash.
4. [RFC 7617 — HTTP Basic](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7617) — Authorization header.

## Keep in mind

Never paste employer challenge text into public repos. Publish only your own generic implementation and keep secrets out of gists.

## Next step

Assignment → implement `katas/totp_rfc6238.py` → optional `go-totp/` → quiz.

# Reading — TOTP verify

## Learning objectives

By the end of this kata’s reading + assignment + implementation, you should be able to:

1. Explain Time-based One-Time Password (TOTP) as HMAC-based One-Time Password (HOTP) with a time-derived counter (shared secret + time step → short code).
2. State why a small verification **window** exists (clock skew) and what it does *not* replace (rate limits, replay controls).
3. Verify codes with `pyotp` instead of hand-rolling Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) — and point to RFC 6238 / Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) literacy in an interview.

**Why this matters.** Passwords alone fail when credentials leak or phishing succeeds. TOTP adds a second factor so a stolen password is not enough — but without understanding clock skew, replay, and why you should not hand-roll HMAC, MFA implementations break users or invent bugs. On the job, identity and email-security products expect this literacy when you wire MFA into admin consoles and APIs.

TOTP lets a server and an authenticator app compute the same short code from a **shared secret** and the **current time** (usually a 30-second step). You do **not** need to reimplement HMAC-SHA1 for a short challenge — understand the model, then use a well-regarded library (`pyotp`) to verify codes, including a small **window** for clock skew. Production MFA still needs replay protection, rate limits, and secret storage discipline; those belong later (`02-mailguard-mfa/`).

**How it works.**

1. Server and authenticator share a secret **K** (provisioned once, often via `otpauth://` URI / QR).
2. Both derive counter **T** from Unix time ÷ step (usually 30s): `T = floor(unix_time / step)`.
3. Both run HMAC over the counter, truncate to a short decimal code (RFC 6238 / HOTP truncation).
4. Server compares the presented code to the expected code, optionally accepting ±N neighboring steps (**window**) for clock skew only.
5. Prefer `pyotp.TOTP.verify(..., valid_window=...)` over reinventing crypto; add rate limits and replay tracking in later modules.

![TOTP flow from shared secret and time counter through HMAC to a short code, with a server verification window](images/totp-flow.svg)

*Figure. Shared secret **K** and time counter **T** feed HMAC; truncation yields the short code both the app and server compute. The verify **window** only covers clock skew — notice it does not replace rate limits or replay controls. Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Worked example

```python
import pyotp

totp = pyotp.TOTP("JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP")  # lab Base32 secret only
code = totp.now()                       # e.g. "123456" for current step
assert totp.verify(code, valid_window=1)  # accepts previous/current/next step
```

If the phone clock is ~20s behind the server, `valid_window=1` (one 30s step) often still accepts; `valid_window=0` rejects. The window does **not** stop an attacker from replaying a just-phished code — that needs a replay store and rate limits.

Challenge-style hiring tasks often pair a short coding exercise with **MFA/One-Time Password (OTP) research**, and prefer elegant solutions over over-engineering. That is the bar this kata trains.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“A bigger window is more user-friendly, so set it huge.”** Large windows widen the replay/guess surface; keep skew tolerance small and add rate limits.
- **“verify() already stops replay.”** Accepting the same code twice in one window is still possible without a used-code store.
- **“I should hand-roll HMAC to ‘really understand’ it for product MFA.”** Product paths use reviewed libraries; deep truncation work belongs in the parametrized TOTP kata, not in every verify call site.
- **“TOTP replaces passwords.”** It is a second factor — phishing can still harvest a live code (see passkeys reading for phishing-resistant authenticators).

## Videos (verified)

1. **[2FA: Two Factor Authentication](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZXFYT-BG2So)** — Computerphile (feat. Dr Mike Pound)  
   Why it helps: crisp mental model of MFA factors (know / have / are) before you touch libraries.

2. **[How HOTP and TOTP work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=46AKWNOJ3-Y)** — loops  
   Why it helps: walks HMAC → truncation → counter vs Unix-time step, plus the validation **window** you’ll use in `verify`.

3. **[A Tale of Two Factors: A Deep Dive into Two Factor Authentication](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4wZ9jM4coV4)** — Kelley Robinson @ PyGotham 2019  
   Why it helps: compares SMS vs TOTP soft tokens and includes Python-oriented TOTP implementation notes aligned with this kata.

## Read these (verified)

### Specs & library

1. [RFC 6238 — TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6238) — the standard behind authenticator apps (period, digits, time counter).
2. [RFC 4226 — HOTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4226) — TOTP builds on HOTP; skim security requirements / throttling ideas.
3. [PyOTP documentation](https://pyauth.github.io/pyotp/) — `TOTP.verify(..., valid_window=...)`, provisioning URIs; prefer this over reinventing crypto.

### Concepts & security literacy

4. [MDN — One-time passwords (OTP)](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Authentication/OTP) — email/SMS/TOTP comparison; why TOTP is preferred among OTP channels.

# Reading — TOTP enroll and recovery codes

## Learning objectives

1. Enroll a TOTP secret and verify codes with a small clock window.
2. Issue **one-time recovery codes** and consume them safely.
3. Keep secrets out of git; document what production still needs (rate limits, attestation).

**Why this matters.** MFA enrollment is where secrets are born. A leaked base32 secret or reusable recovery code is as bad as no MFA. Without a clear enroll → verify → recover story, helpdesk resets become account-takeover paths. On the job, identity and email-admin portals implement the same lifecycle before they federate to passkeys.

**How it works.**

1. Generate a high-entropy **shared secret** (base32 for authenticator apps).
2. Show the student a provisioning URI / QR (lab) so the app can compute TOTP.
3. **Verify** a current code before marking enrollment complete (proves the secret was stored).
4. Issue **recovery codes** (random, single-use); store only hashes in production.
5. On lost device: consume one recovery code, then force re-enrollment — never email a new TOTP secret in the clear.

```text
enroll(secret + recovery codes) → verify TOTP → store hashed recovery
lost phone → consume_recovery once → re-enroll
```

### Worked example

Contract shape (see `katas/mfa_enroll.py`):

```python
enrollment = enroll(recovery_count=5)   # secret + 5 codes
assert verify_totp(enrollment, code_from_app)
assert consume_recovery(enrollment, enrollment.recovery_codes[0]) is True
assert consume_recovery(enrollment, enrollment.recovery_codes[0]) is False  # one-time
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Commit a demo secret for classmates.”** Even “test” secrets in git get copy-pasted into real apps — use local-only fixtures and `.env`.
- **“Recovery codes can be reused until we rotate.”** Reuse enables silent takeover after phishing one code.
- **“Verify is optional if the QR scanned.”** Without a challenge code, you may have stored a secret the user never controlled.
- **“TOTP enroll finishes MFA.”** Passkeys/WebAuthn resist phishing better — see the passkeys reading.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[Make Your Accounts Safer with Multifactor Authentication (MFA)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XIlF2qkav5c)** — CISA  
   Why it helps: places MFA factors in plain language before you implement enroll.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 6238 — TOTP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238)
2. [OWASP — MFA](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html)
3. Module 01 `totp_verify` reading (shared secret + window)

# Reading — Passkeys / WebAuthn (beside TOTP MFA)

## Learning objectives

1. Explain **Web Authentication (WebAuthn)** as a browser API for public-key credentials scoped to a relying-party **RP ID** (a registrable domain suffix), not exactly the full origin string alone.
2. Contrast phishing risk of **TOTP** (user can type a code into a fake site) vs **passkeys** (origin-bound assertion).
3. Place passkeys next to MailGuard’s TOTP path as a *next* factor — not a rewrite of Challenge Gym.

**Why this matters.** TOTP proves “something you have,” but a convincing phishing page can still harvest the live code and replay it. Without phishing-resistant authenticators, identity and cloud admin portals stay one lookalike domain away from account takeover. On the job, passkeys / WebAuthn are how teams raise assurance beside (or instead of) OTP — without claiming TOTP literacy alone is enough.

TOTP proves “something you have” via a shared secret — but a convincing phishing page can still harvest the live code. Passkeys use WebAuthn: the browser/OS authenticator signs a challenge for *this* origin, so a lookalike domain should not get a usable assertion.

**How it works.**

1. **Registration.** The relying party (RP) sends a challenge; the authenticator creates a public-key credential bound to the **RP ID** (a registrable domain suffix, not merely “whatever string the page typed”).
2. **Storage.** The RP stores the credential id + public key (and related metadata); the private key stays in the authenticator / platform.
3. **Assertion.** At login, the RP sends a new challenge; the browser/OS asks the authenticator to sign only if the request matches that RP ID / origin.
4. **Verify.** The RP verifies the signature with the stored public key and checks challenge, origin/RP ID, and flags per WebAuthn.
5. **Recovery.** Lost device, backup passkey, and IT-assisted reset are operational design problems — plan them before turning off TOTP/recovery codes.

![TOTP code typed into a fake site versus a WebAuthn passkey bound to the relying-party origin](images/passkeys-vs-totp.svg)

*Figure. On the left, a typed TOTP code can be harvested and replayed. On the right, the authenticator signs only for the real relying-party origin — notice a lookalike domain does not get a usable assertion. Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Worked example

```text
RP ID:  example.com
Origin: https://login.example.com

Registration ceremony (shape):
  navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey: {
    rp: { id: "example.com", name: "Example" },
    user: { id: ..., name: "alex@example.com", displayName: "Alex" },
    challenge: <serverBytes>,
    pubKeyCredParams: [{ alg: -7, type: "public-key" }, ...]
  }})

Assertion on https://evil-example.com:
  authenticator should refuse — RP ID / origin binding does not match.
```

A phished TOTP code typed into `evil-example.com` still works at the real site until it expires; a passkey assertion for the wrong RP does not.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Passkeys are just better passwords in the cloud.”** The private key never goes to the RP; the phishing resistance comes from origin/RP-bound signatures, not from longer secrets.
- **“RP ID equals the full origin including scheme and path.”** Credentials are scoped to a registrable domain suffix (RP ID); misunderstanding that breaks registration or weakens the threat model — see W3C WebAuthn.
- **“Turn off TOTP the day passkeys ship.”** Without recovery (second device, backup passkey, IT reset), lockouts become outages.
- **“This replaces Challenge Gym TOTP work.”** Passkeys sit *beside* TOTP literacy; the course still needs OTP for labs and for estates that have not moved yet.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[Understand passkeys in 4 minutes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2xdV-xut7EQ)** — Google / passkeys overview  
   Why it helps: phishing-resistant passkeys mental model in under five minutes.

2. **[Passkeys: A simpler and more secure way to log in](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3BmYR--3z8M)** — Google  
   Why it helps: how passkeys relate to platform authenticators without building an IdP.

Prefer MDN + W3C links below if a video moves.

## Read these (verified)

1. [MDN — Web Authentication API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Authentication_API) — ceremonies and browser support.
2. [W3C WebAuthn Level 3](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/) — Candidate Recommendation track; Level 2 is the current W3C Recommendation. Credentials are scoped to the **RP ID** (a registrable domain).
3. [passkeys.dev](https://passkeys.dev/) — practitioner-oriented passkey guidance.
4. [OWASP MFA Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html) — factors and phishing-resistant authenticators.
5. [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/63/b/4/final) (final, 31 Jul 2025; incorporates syncable authenticators / passkeys) — authenticator assurance high-level.

# Reading — Identity depth (SAML, device certs, password managers)

## Learning objectives

1. Compare **SAML** and **OIDC** for enterprise single sign-on (**SSO**) at a high level.
2. Explain device certificates / posture as *additional signals*, not magic.
3. Threat-model an enterprise password manager for apps that still use passwords (non-SSO).

**Why this matters.** Enterprises rarely run “OIDC only.” Without SAML literacy, device-posture signals, and a threat model for password managers on non-SSO apps, identity work stops at the happy path and fails in real estates of legacy apps. On the job, cloud and email-security admins still federate with both SAML and OIDC, and still protect vaults where SSO never arrived.

This module’s coding path is OIDC-shaped. Enterprises still run Security Assertion Markup Language (**SAML**) for many apps, issue device certificates for posture, and deploy password managers where SSO never arrived. This reading builds interview literacy without claiming you built a full Identity Provider (**IdP**).

**How it works.**

1. User authenticates at an **IdP** (password + MFA, passkey, etc.).
2. For **OIDC** apps: IdP runs an OAuth 2.0-based flow and issues identity tokens (typically JWT-shaped) the app validates (issuer, audience, signature, expiry).
3. For **SAML** apps: IdP issues a signed XML **assertion**; the service provider checks signature, audience, recipient/ACS, and time conditions, then creates a session.
4. **Device certificates / posture** add admission *signals* (managed device, healthy agent) — they do not replace user authentication.
5. Where SSO is missing, a **password manager** reduces reuse; you still model vault compromise, phishing-unlock, and shared-folder risks.

![Identity provider federating SSO to applications via OIDC JSON tokens or SAML XML assertions](images/oidc-vs-saml.svg)

*Figure. One IdP, two common SSO wires: **OIDC** (identity layer on OAuth 2.0, JWT-shaped tokens) vs **SAML** (XML assertions). Notice the coding path here is OIDC-shaped, while enterprises still run both. Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Worked example

```text
OIDC id_token claims (shape):
  iss: https://idp.example.com/
  aud: mailguard-admin
  sub: user-42
  exp: 1730003600
  email: alex@example.com

SAML assertion checks (shape):
  Signature present + trusted cert
  Audience == SP entity ID
  Recipient/ACS == registered ACS URL
  NotOnOrAfter within skew budget
```

Same user, two wires: JSON token validation vs XML assertion conditions. Device posture might additionally require a client cert before the app accepts either.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“OIDC replaced SAML everywhere.”** Many enterprise apps still speak SAML; literacy for both is table stakes.
- **“A device certificate means the user is authenticated.”** Device proof is a signal; without user auth (or with a stolen unlocked device) it is not enough.
- **“Password managers eliminate phishing.”** They reduce reuse and typing into random forms, but unlock phishing, malware, and shared-vault mistakes remain — model them (OWASP secrets / MFA sheets).
- **“If SSO works in demo, federation is done.”** Audience/ACS mismatches and cert rollover are how production SSO breaks after the happy path.

## Logout and revocation (OIDC)

Login without logout design leaves sessions and refresh tokens alive after the user thinks they are done. Treat sign-out as an identity-control problem, not only a UI button.

**Why this matters.** Clearing a local cookie does not end the IdP SSO session, and an unrevoked **refresh token** can mint new access tokens. On the job, admin portals and DLP consoles need honest logout notes: RP-initiated logout, token revocation, and what you still cannot kill (already-issued access tokens until they expire).

**How logout / revocation works.**

1. **App session end.** The relying party deletes its own session cookie / server session.
2. **RP-initiated logout.** Redirect the browser to the IdP `end_session_endpoint` with `id_token_hint` and a registered `post_logout_redirect_uri` so the IdP session ends too ([OIDC RP-Initiated Logout](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-rpinitiated-1_0.html)).
3. **Refresh-token revoke.** Call the IdP `revocation_endpoint` with the refresh token ([RFC 7009](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009)) so silent renew fails after logout.
4. **Access-token lifetime.** Short-lived access tokens still work until `exp` unless you add introspection or a denylist — document that gap honestly.
5. **Lab practice.** Use the local Keycloak lab ([`keycloak_lab.md`](./keycloak_lab.md)) to click through end-session and revocation against discovery document URLs.

### Worked example (logout shape)

```text
1. User clicks Sign out in MailGuard admin
2. App deletes local session
3. Browser → GET {end_session_endpoint}
     ?id_token_hint=<current id_token>
     &post_logout_redirect_uri=http://127.0.0.1:3000/
4. App → POST {revocation_endpoint}
     token=<refresh_token>&token_type_hint=refresh_token
5. Result: IdP SSO cookie cleared; refresh renew fails; access token dies at exp
```

### Misconceptions (logout)

- **“Logout is only a front-end route change.”** Without IdP logout + refresh revoke, SSO bounce-back and renew keep the user in.
- **“Revoking the refresh token kills the current access token instantly.”** Access tokens are usually bearer until expiry unless you add extra controls.
- **“Back-channel logout is required for every lab.”** Useful in multi-tab estates; start with RP-initiated logout + revoke, then read Keycloak/OIDC back-channel docs as a deepen.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (in plain English)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=996OiexHze0)** — OktaDev  
   Why it helps: OIDC as identity layer on OAuth — revisit before SAML compare.

2. Prefer the OWASP SAML + OAuth cheat sheets below for the SAML vs OIDC compare (video IDs bitrot). Optional: search “SAML vs OIDC” from IdP vendor developer channels and cross-check against OWASP.

Prefer written RFCs/docs below if videos move.

## Read these (verified)

1. [OWASP — SAML Security Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SAML_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html)
2. [OWASP — OAuth 2.0 / OIDC related cheat sheets](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/OAuth2_Cheat_Sheet.html)
3. [OASIS — SAML 2.0 Technical Overview](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/Post2.0/sstc-saml-tech-overview-2.0.html) — assertions, bindings, and SSO flows.
4. [MDN — Authentication overview](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Authentication) — browser auth landscape; for mTLS see [Cloudflare Learning — What is mutual TLS?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/access-management/what-is-mutual-tls/).
5. [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/63/b/4/final) (final, 31 Jul 2025; incorporates syncable authenticators / passkeys) — authenticators & federation high-level. Companion HTML: [pages.nist.gov/800-63-4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html).
6. [OWASP — Secrets Management Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html) — why vaults beat spreadsheets (for apps still on passwords). For server-side password hashing see [Password Storage Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html).

## Quiz (required)
[`../quizzes/identity_depth.md`](../quizzes/identity_depth.md)

# Reading — Local Keycloak lab (OIDC + logout / revocation)

## Learning objectives

1. Run **Keycloak** locally with Docker as a lab Identity Provider (**IdP**).
2. Create a realm and a public OpenID Connect (**OIDC**) client with **Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)**, exact redirect URIs, and a logout redirect.
3. Practice **RP-initiated logout** and **refresh-token revocation** so “logout” is more than clearing a cookie.
4. Connect the lab to `jwt_checks` (id_token claims) and the PKCE / redirect katas.

**Why this matters.** SSO demos that only show “login works” hide the hard parts: redirect URI mismatches, missing PKCE, and sessions that survive after the user thinks they logged out. Without a local IdP you cannot safely break and fix those controls. On the job, cloud and email-admin portals federate to real IdPs — Keycloak in Docker is a vendor-neutral way to rehearse realm/client config, logout, and token revocation before you touch production tenants.

**How it works.**

1. Start Keycloak in Docker (dev mode is fine for a laptop lab; never expose it to the internet).
2. Create a **realm** (isolated tenant of users, clients, and keys) separate from the built-in `master` realm.
3. Register a **client** for MailGuard admin (or a local callback app): public client, standard flow + PKCE (S256), exact **Valid redirect URIs**, and a **Valid post logout redirect URI**.
4. Run an authorization-code + PKCE login; redeem the code; validate the **id_token** (`iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `nonce`, `alg`) — see the `jwt_checks` kata.
5. **Log out / revoke:** call RP-initiated logout so the IdP session ends, and revoke refresh tokens so silent renew cannot mint new access tokens after logout.

```text
Browser → Keycloak authorize (PKCE) → redirect_uri?code=…
App → token endpoint (code + code_verifier) → id_token + refresh_token
App validates id_token claims (+ JWKS signature in production)
Later: RP-initiated logout and/or refresh_token revoke
```

### Worked example

**1. Start Keycloak (Docker).** Use a lab-only admin password from your environment — do not commit real credentials.

```bash
# Lab only — bind to localhost. Set KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD in your shell
# to a local throwaway value (never a production secret).
docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  -e KEYCLOAK_ADMIN=admin \
  -e KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD \
  quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.0 start-dev
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8080` → Administration Console → sign in with the lab admin you set.

**2. Realm + client (OIDC, PKCE).**

| Setting | Lab value (example) |
|---------|---------------------|
| Realm | `mailguard-lab` |
| Client ID | `mailguard-admin` |
| Client authentication | Off (public client) |
| Standard flow | On |
| Direct access grants | Off (avoid password grant in the lab) |
| PKCE method | S256 |
| Valid redirect URIs | `http://127.0.0.1:3000/callback` (exact) |
| Valid post logout redirect URIs | `http://127.0.0.1:3000/` |
| Web origins | `http://127.0.0.1:3000` |

**3. Discovery document (shape).** After the realm exists:

```text
http://127.0.0.1:8080/realms/mailguard-lab/.well-known/openid-configuration
```

Note `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `end_session_endpoint`, `revocation_endpoint`, and `jwks_uri`.

**4. RP-initiated logout (shape).** Relying Party (**RP**) redirects the browser to the IdP end-session endpoint with `id_token_hint` and `post_logout_redirect_uri` that matches registration. Why: clearing the app cookie alone leaves the IdP SSO session alive — the next visit may silently sign the user back in.

**5. Refresh-token revocation (shape).** `POST` to the revocation endpoint with `token=<refresh_token>&token_type_hint=refresh_token` (and client auth if the client is confidential). Why: stolen refresh tokens otherwise keep minting access tokens after “logout.”

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Wildcard redirect URIs are fine for labs, so they are fine in prod.”** Open redirects and token theft follow loose matching — register exact URIs (RFC 9700).
- **“Logout = delete the session cookie.”** Without IdP logout and/or refresh-token revoke, SSO and refresh keep the user effectively signed in.
- **“PKCE is optional for a public SPA.”** Stolen authorization codes are usable without the verifier; turn on S256 for public clients (RFC 7636).
- **“id_token signature is enough; skip iss/aud/nonce.”** Mix-up and replay succeed when claims are not checked — pair JWKS verify with claim checks (`jwt_checks`).

## Videos (verified)

1. **[OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (in plain English)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=996OiexHze0)** — OktaDev  
   Why it helps: mental model for authorize → code → tokens before you click through Keycloak screens.

2. **[Keycloak + Docker Compose: Setup & Authentication Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WGcgiegv0W0)**  
   Why it helps: realm and client UI orientation; cross-check every click against current Keycloak docs (UI moves between versions).

Prefer the Keycloak guides below if a video moves.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Keycloak — Getting started](https://www.keycloak.org/guides#getting-started)
2. [OpenID Connect Core 1.0 — ID Token](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html#IDToken)
3. [OpenID Connect RP-Initiated Logout 1.0](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-rpinitiated-1_0.html)
4. [RFC 7009 — OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7009)
5. [RFC 7636 — PKCE](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7636)
6. [RFC 9700 — OAuth 2.0 Security BCP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700)

## Next step

Implement [`../katas/jwt_checks.py`](../katas/jwt_checks.py) until `pytest -q` is green, then revisit logout/revocation notes in [`identity_depth.md`](./identity_depth.md). Pair with [`saml_oidc_lab.md`](./saml_oidc_lab.md) for SAML vs OIDC.

# Reading — SAML 2.0 + OIDC lab deepen

## Learning objectives

1. Run **Keycloak** locally as an IdP (lab only).
2. Contrast auth-code + **PKCE** (OIDC) with SAML SP/IdP-initiated flows.
3. Check assertion conditions: audience, recipient/ACS, time window, InResponseTo, signature present.
4. Know headline attacks: XML Signature Wrapping, unsigned assertions, open redirects; OAuth mix-up / redirect URI mismatch.

**Why this matters.** Federation bugs are not theoretical: unsigned assertions, loose ACS/redirect matching, and missing PKCE turn “we have SSO” into account takeover. Without checking audience, time windows, and InResponseTo, replay and mix-up attacks succeed. On the job, identity engineers validate these conditions every time a new app joins the IdP.

**How it works.**

**SAML (SP-initiated shape):**

1. User hits the SP; SP redirects to the IdP (often with `RelayState`).
2. IdP authenticates the user and returns a signed XML assertion (POST or redirect binding) to the Assertion Consumer Service (**ACS**).
3. SP verifies: signature present and trusted, **audience**, **recipient/ACS**, time window (`NotOnOrAfter` + skew), and **InResponseTo** (binds to the authn request).
4. On success, SP creates an application session.

**OIDC auth-code + PKCE (RFC 7636):**

1. Client creates `code_verifier` / `code_challenge` and redirects to the IdP authorize endpoint with an exact **redirect_uri**.
2. User authenticates; IdP returns an authorization `code` to that redirect URI.
3. Client redeems the code at the token endpoint, proving possession of `code_verifier`.
4. Client validates tokens (issuer, audience, signature, nonce where used). Exact redirect matching and issuer checks blunt mix-up (RFC 9700).

Lab IdPs like Keycloak let you break and fix these checks safely.

### Worked example

```text
SAML condition checklist (fixture-style):
  ✔ Signature: RSA-SHA256 over Assertion, cert matches IdP metadata
  ✔ Audience:  https://sp.example.com/metadata
  ✔ Recipient: https://sp.example.com/acs
  ✔ Time:      NotOnOrAfter = now+5m, skew allowance ±2m
  ✔ InResponseTo: matches AuthnRequest ID _abc123

OIDC token request (shape):
  POST /token
  grant_type=authorization_code
  code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA
  redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback   # must match authorize request exactly
  code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
```

If `redirect_uri` differs by a trailing slash, honest clients fail closed — and open redirect / mix-up bugs get blocked when registration enforces exact match.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Signature on the Response is enough; skip Assertion checks.”** XML Signature Wrapping and unsigned assertions exploit incomplete verification — check the assertion the SP will trust (OWASP SAML cheat sheet).
- **“PKCE is only for mobile.”** Public and many confidential clients use PKCE so a stolen code alone is useless (RFC 7636 / RFC 9700).
- **“Clock skew of a few minutes can be ignored.”** Too-tight windows lock out users; too-loose windows widen replay — document skew like cert rollover.
- **“IdP-initiated SAML is always safer.”** Without careful RelayState/ACS handling it enables open redirects; treat it as an operational choice with controls, not a free upgrade.


## Videos (verified)
