# Reading — mTLS, device certs, ZTNA

## Learning objectives

1. Issue a lab client certificate from a private CA (`openssl` or `step-ca`).
2. Enforce mTLS in front of the admin (nginx/Caddy) and discuss CRL/OCSP pain.
3. Tie identity-bound access to ZTNA ideas; read **NIST SP 1800-35**.

**Why this matters.** Server TLS alone proves the *server* to the client. Without mutual TLS (mTLS) or another device signal, any client that reaches the port can speak — stolen cookies or a leaked URL may be enough. On the job, admin consoles and ZTNA-style admission often require a client certificate so only enrolled devices complete the handshake; revocation (CRL/OCSP) is the hard operational part.

**How it works.**

1. Stand up a **private CA** (lab: `openssl` or `step-ca`) and define who may receive client certificates.
2. Issue a **client certificate** (and private key) to an enrolled device or user.
3. Configure the reverse proxy (nginx/Caddy) to **require and verify** the client cert during the TLS handshake for the admin vhost.
4. On successful verify, optionally forward identity headers to the app; reject the handshake otherwise.
5. Operate **revocation** (CRL and/or OCSP): document lag — a stolen cert stays trusted until revocation data is published and fetched. Map the admission signal to ZTNA: identity + device proof → per-app access ([NIST SP 1800-35](https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/projects/implementing-zero-trust-architecture) for patterns, not a commercial mesh mandate).

```text
Client --TLS+client cert--> Proxy (verify vs private CA) --headers?--> Admin app
                \-- fail handshake if cert missing/untrusted/revoked
```

### Worked example

```text
# Conceptual checks a proxy performs (lab):
TLS ClientHello + Certificate message presents CN=device-42, issuer=Lab Client CA
Proxy: chain to Lab Client CA? ✔
       notAfter still valid?   ✔
       CRL/OCSP status?        good (or "unknown" — decide fail-open vs fail-closed)
Result: handshake completes; X-Client-DN: CN=device-42 forwarded
```

Why CA → issue → require that order: without a CA and issued cert first, “require client cert” only produces handshake failures you cannot debug.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Server HTTPS already proves the client.”** Server TLS authenticates the server; without mTLS (or another client proof) any TCP client can still connect.
- **“Revocation is automatic once we issue certs.”** CRL/OCSP lag and fail-open defaults leave stolen certs trusted — document the workflow.
- **“mTLS replaces SSO/MFA.”** It is a strong *device* signal; user identity still comes from the IdP for ZTNA-style admission.
- **“Any client cert in the trust store is fine forever.”** Missing rotation/revocation turns a lost laptop into a permanent admin key.

## Read these (verified)

1. [NIST SP 1800-35 — Implementing a ZTA](https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/projects/implementing-zero-trust-architecture)
2. [step-ca](https://smallstep.com/docs/step-ca/)
3. [Mozilla — TLS client auth overview](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Transport_Layer_Security)

## Lab idea — openssl (or step-ca) + nginx/Caddy

Private CA → client cert → require certificate on the admin vhost; document revocation workflow.

Why that order: without a CA and issued cert first, “require client cert” only produces handshake failures you cannot debug.

### Option A — openssl lab CA + client cert

```bash
# Lab-only keys — never reuse outside your laptop; do not commit private keys
mkdir -p /tmp/mtls-lab && cd /tmp/mtls-lab
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout lab-ca.key -out lab-ca.crt \
  -days 365 -subj "/CN=MailGuard Lab Client CA"
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout client.key -out client.csr \
  -subj "/CN=device-42"
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA lab-ca.crt -CAkey lab-ca.key -CAcreateserial \
  -out client.crt -days 90
```

### Option B — step-ca (sketch)

```bash
# After step-ca is initialized in your lab (see smallstep docs):
step ca certificate device-42 client.crt client.key
step certificate inspect client.crt
```

### nginx — require client cert on admin vhost

```nginx
server {
  listen 443 ssl;
  server_name admin.mail.example;
  ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/server.crt;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/server.key;
  ssl_client_certificate /etc/nginx/tls/lab-ca.crt;
  ssl_verify_client on;
  location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
    proxy_set_header X-Client-DN $ssl_client_s_dn;
  }
}
```

### Caddy — client auth snippet

```caddy
admin.mail.example {
  tls {
    client_auth {
      mode require
      trust_pool file /etc/caddy/lab-ca.crt
    }
  }
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080
}
```

Document CRL/OCSP: how you revoke `device-42` and how long clients keep a stolen cert trusted.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[Transport Layer Security (TLS) — Computerphile](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0TLDTodL7Lc)** — literacy backdrop for client vs server certs  
   Why it helps: clarifies what mTLS adds after ordinary HTTPS.

## Next step

[`../assignments/mtls_ztna.md`](../assignments/mtls_ztna.md) → `mtls_checks` kata → quiz.

# Reading — ZTNA lite

## Learning objectives

1. Define **Zero Trust** as “never trust, always verify” with continuous evaluation — not a single product SKU.
2. Contrast network-level **VPN** admission with application-level **ZTNA**.
3. Name Policy Engine / Policy Enforcement Point ideas from National Institute of Standards and Technology (**NIST**) SP 800-207 at a high level.

**Why this matters.** Classical VPN admission parks a client on a flat corporate LAN. After credential theft or malware, **lateral movement** reaches many internal services. Without per-app verification, “we have SSO” still leaves a wide network path open. On the job, cloud and identity teams pair IdPs with Zero Trust Network Access (**ZTNA**) so contractors and admins reach *one* app, not the whole estate.

Classical remote access: join a VPN, then reach wide internal ranges. If malware or a stolen laptop lands on that network, **lateral movement** is easier. ZTNA aims to grant access to *specific applications* after verifying user identity, often device posture, and context — ideally without parking the client on a flat corporate LAN.

**How it works.**

1. User requests an application (not “the corporate network”).
2. Identity is verified (often MFA / OIDC via an IdP); device posture and context may be collected.
3. A **policy engine** (NIST SP 800-207 vocabulary) evaluates allow/deny for *that* app and session.
4. A **policy enforcement point** grants a narrow path to the application — ideally without broad LAN admission.
5. Evaluation continues (session risk, posture change); access is not a one-time VPN ticket for the whole estate.

```text
VPN:   Client → VPN concentrator → flat LAN → many services
ZTNA:  Client → identity/posture → Policy Engine → PEP → one app
```

MailGuard modules already practice app identity (TOTP, OIDC). ZTNA is the *network/access path* story that enterprises pair with identity providers.

![Side-by-side contrast of VPN network admission versus ZTNA application-level access with policy engine](images/ztna-vs-vpn.svg)

*Figure. VPN admits the client onto a broad LAN (lateral movement risk). ZTNA checks identity/posture/context, then a Policy Engine / Enforcement Point grants **per-app** access — notice “never trust, always verify,” not a single product SKU. Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Worked example

```text
Request: contractor needs https://admin.mail.example (only)
Signals: OIDC login + MFA OK; device posture = managed; location = expected country
Policy:  allow app=admin.mail.example; deny lateral routes to hr-db.internal
PEP:     issues app-scoped access; no RFC1918 “full tunnel” to 10.0.0.0/8
```

Same user on a classical VPN might route to `hr-db.internal` after a phish; ZTNA never admitted that path.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Zero Trust is a product SKU we can buy once.”** It is an architecture of continuous verification (NIST SP 800-207); products implement pieces.
- **“SSO means we already have Zero Trust.”** SSO authenticates the user to an app; without per-app enforcement you may still have VPN-style lateral paths.
- **“ZTNA replaces MFA.”** ZTNA consumes identity/MFA (and often posture); it does not make weak auth strong.
- **“After first admit, trust the session forever.”** Continuous evaluation is the point — posture loss or risk change should revoke or step-up.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[What Is Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)? NIST 800-207 Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5Kq64vOgE10)**  
   Why it helps: policy engine vs enforcement point vocabulary.

2. **[Zero Trust, Before The Cloud (Bsides-style talk)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M0Pb8GNxWl8)** — Ben Lintern  
   Why it helps: identity-aware networking vs “VPN then flat access,” with practical skepticism.

## Read these (verified)

1. [NIST SP 800-207 — Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final) — abstract + section on ZTA components.
2. [NIST Zero Trust Architecture portal](https://www.nist.gov/publications/zero-trust-architecture) — publication landing.
3. [NCSC (UK) — Zero trust architecture design principles](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/zero-trust-architecture) — pragmatic principles.
4. [Cloudflare Learning — What is ZTNA?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/access-management/what-is-ztna/) — plain-language ZTNA vs VPN (vendor learning site; read for concepts).

## Quiz (required)
[`../quizzes/ztna_lite.md`](../quizzes/ztna_lite.md)

# Reading — Email authentication & SMTP/TLS literacy

## Learning objectives

1. Explain Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (**SMTP**) as the store-and-forward *sending* protocol, and why Transport Layer Security (**TLS**) on SMTP encrypts a hop but does **not** by itself prove the `From:` domain is legitimate. Server-to-server STARTTLS is **opportunistic**: an active attacker can strip it, and certificates are often not validated. **MTA-STS** (RFC 8461) or **DANE** (RFC 7672) make TLS required and authenticated for a receiving domain, and **TLS-RPT** (RFC 8460) reports failures. Implicit TLS (port 465) applies to client submission (RFC 8314), not MX-to-MX.
2. Distinguish Sender Policy Framework (**SPF**), DomainKeys Identified Mail (**DKIM**), and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance (**DMARC**) — what each checks and how they combine. DMARC passes if **at least one** of SPF or DKIM passes **and** aligns with the visible `From:`.
3. Read a DMARC DNS policy (`p=`, `rua=`, and RFC 9989 tags such as `t=` / `np=` / `psd=`) and say what hold/DLP rules **cannot** fix alone when attackers spoof lookalike mail.

**Why this matters.** Hold/DLP rules catch *outbound* mistakes (missend, policy); they do not stop attackers who **spoof** your (or a partner’s) domain into someone else’s inbox. Without SPF/DKIM/DMARC, receivers cannot tell authorized mail from lookalike fraud. On the job, email and cloud-security teams publish DNS auth, read aggregate reports, and step `p=` carefully — TLS on SMTP encrypts a hop but does not prove `From:`.

Attackers also **spoof inbound or lookalike domains**. SPF publishes which hosts may send for the **envelope sender (MAIL FROM / Return-Path) or HELO domain** — it does **not** check the header `From:`. DKIM adds a cryptographic signature over selected headers/body with a public key in DNS. DMARC adds the **alignment** check that ties SPF or DKIM to the visible `From:` domain, tells receivers what to do on failure (`p=`), and where to send aggregate reports (`rua`).

**How it works.**

1. **SMTP hop.** The sending MTA transfers the message to the next hop (often the receiving MX). Optional TLS on that connection encrypts the pipe for *that* hop only.
2. **SPF check.** The receiver looks up the SPF TXT for the envelope sender domain (MAIL FROM / Return-Path) or HELO identity and asks: is this connecting IP authorized? SPF does **not** inspect the header `From:`.
3. **DKIM verify.** The receiver finds a `DKIM-Signature` header, fetches the public key from DNS (`selector._domainkey.domain`), and verifies the signature over the signed headers and body.
4. **DMARC alignment.** The receiver takes the visible `From:` domain and asks whether SPF and/or DKIM **passed and aligned** with that domain (organizational or strict, per policy). At least one aligned pass is enough for DMARC pass.
5. **Policy + reports.** On failure, the published `p=` (`none` / `quarantine` / `reject`) guides disposition; `rua=` collects aggregate reports so operators can fix legitimate senders before tightening.

```text
Sender MTA --SMTP(+TLS?)--> Receiver MTA
                              |-- SPF: envelope/HELO vs IP (DNS TXT)
                              |-- DKIM: signature vs DNS pubkey
                              `-- DMARC: align SPF|DKIM with From: → p=/rua
```

**SMTP + TLS** literacy: encrypting the pipe (TLS) stops casual eavesdropping on that hop; it does not replace SPF/DKIM/DMARC. Between MTAs, STARTTLS is opportunistic unless MTA-STS or DANE enforces authenticated TLS. Domain authentication is how receivers decide “did this domain authorize this message?”

### Worked example

DNS (illustrative):

```text
example.com.            TXT  "v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.10 -all"
selector._domainkey.example.com.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIj..."
_dmarc.example.com.     TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"
```

Message shape the receiver sees:

```text
Return-Path: <bounce@example.com>
From: Billing <billing@example.com>
DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=example.com; s=selector;
    h=from:to:subject:date; bh=...; b=...
```

If the connecting IP is `203.0.113.10`, SPF can pass for `example.com`. If the DKIM signature verifies with `d=example.com`, DKIM passes. DMARC then checks alignment of those results with header `From:` (`example.com`). A spoofed `From: billing@example.com` sent from an unauthorized IP *without* a valid aligned DKIM signature fails DMARC even if the hop used TLS.

![SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks from sending MTA through receiving MTA with DNS-published controls](images/spf-dkim-dmarc.svg)

*Figure. SMTP+TLS protects the hop; **SPF** authorizes envelope hosts, **DKIM** signs content, **DMARC** aligns results with the visible `From:` and sets `p=` policy. Notice hold/DLP and domain auth solve different problems (outbound mistakes vs inbound spoof). Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“TLS on SMTP means the From: is trusted.”** TLS encrypts (and maybe authenticates) the *transport hop*; it says nothing about who is allowed to use the domain in `From:`. That is SPF/DKIM/DMARC’s job.
- **“SPF checks the From: header.”** SPF evaluates the envelope sender / HELO against the connecting IP. Attackers can put any address in `From:` while using a different MAIL FROM — without DMARC alignment, SPF alone does not stop that.
- **“STARTTLS between MTAs is always enforced.”** Server-to-server STARTTLS is opportunistic unless MTA-STS or DANE require authenticated TLS; an active attacker can strip it, and many hops never validate certificates.
- **“Flip to p=reject on day one.”** Aggregate reports (`rua=`) exist so you find legitimate relays missing SPF/DKIM/alignment before reject breaks payroll or marketing.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[SPF, DKIM and DMARC Protocols Explained](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2eR6996cQvY)** — PowerDMARC  
   Why it helps: end-to-end picture of the three DNS-published controls receivers combine.

2. **[Email Trust and Antispoofing: DKIM, SPF, and DMARC](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZFg691hXDzk)** — Salesforce Support  
   Why it helps: operator-oriented setup narrative (`p=none` → stricter policies) without requiring their product.

3. **[Set up email authentication](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YdWgHAcD91E)** — Google Workspace  
   Why it helps: SPF/DKIM publish steps and where DMARC fits for modern receivers.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 7208 — SPF](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208) — skim abstract + mechanism overview (MAIL FROM / HELO identity).
2. [RFC 6376 — DKIM](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6376) — signature + public key in DNS.
3. [RFC 9989 — DMARC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9989) — current protocol (Standards Track; obsoletes RFC 7489 and RFC 9091). Companion: [RFC 9990](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9990) (aggregate reports), [RFC 9991](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9991) (failure reports). RFC 9989 removes `pct`/`rf`/`ri` and adds `t` (test mode), `np`, and `psd`; the Public Suffix List is replaced by a DNS tree walk.
4. [DMARC.org overview](https://dmarc.org/overview/) — plain-language diagram.
5. [Cloudflare Learning — What are DMARC, DKIM, and SPF?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/email-security/dmarc-dkim-spf/) — concise comparison.
6. [Google — Email sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126) — modern receiver expectations (SPF/DKIM/DMARC).
7. [Cloudflare Learning — What is SMTP?](https://www.cloudflare.com/learning/email-security/what-is-smtp/) — SMTP + why encryption ≠ authentication.
8. [RFC 8461 — MTA-STS](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8461) · [RFC 8460 — TLS-RPT](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8460) · [RFC 7672 — DANE for SMTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7672) — authenticated/required SMTP TLS and failure reporting.

### Aggregate reports (DMARC report literacy)

Receivers email XML **aggregate reports** to `rua=` addresses summarizing pass/fail by source IP. Operators use them to find legitimate senders missing SPF/DKIM (or alignment) before flipping `p=reject`. This course does not require a live domain — parse policies in the kata and describe what a report would tell you on the assignment.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

# Reading — Mail flow + DMARC aggregate analytics

## Learning objectives

1. Place a cloud **email security gateway** relative to Microsoft 365 / Google Workspace (MX vs outbound smart-host).
2. Explain connectors/transport rules, journaling/archive, ARC (RFC 8617), and why SPF often fails after relay while DMARC may still pass via DKIM.
3. Parse DMARC aggregate reports (RFC 9990-shaped) and recommend the next `p=` step.
4. Know bulk-sender receiver mandates (Google/Yahoo 2024; Outlook.com high-volume expectations).

**Why this matters.** Real mail rarely goes “MUA → final MX” in one hop. Gateways, relays, and journaling rewrite paths so SPF breaks even for legitimate senders — and without aggregate analytics you either stay on `p=none` forever or flip to `p=reject` and break payroll/marketing. On the job, email-security engineers read RFC 9990-shaped reports, preserve DKIM (or ARC), and place MX vs outbound smart-hosts deliberately.

**How it works.**

1. **Inbound placement.** MX for the domain points at the security gateway (or directly at the workspace). Mail is inspected (spam, malware, policy), then delivered into the mailbox store.
2. **Outbound placement.** The workspace sends via a smart-host / gateway connector. Envelope data or the connecting IP may change after relay — SPF for the original MAIL FROM often fails at the final receiver.
3. **Authentication across intermediaries.** Aligned **DKIM** (signature survives if headers/body are preserved) can still make **DMARC** pass when SPF fails. **ARC** (RFC 8617) seals prior authentication results so downstream receivers can trust them across hops.
4. **Aggregate feedback.** Receivers send XML aggregate reports (RFC 9990-shaped) to `rua=` summarizing pass/fail by source IP. Operators climb `none → quarantine → reject` only when reports show legitimate senders are covered.
5. **Bulk-sender mandates.** High-volume senders are expected to publish SPF/DKIM/DMARC at minimum (see Google/Yahoo 2024 guidance and Outlook.com postmaster expectations).

```text
Inbound:  Internet → [gateway MX] → workspace
Outbound: workspace → smart-host/gateway → Internet MX
Auth:     SPF often fails after relay; aligned DKIM (± ARC) can still pass DMARC
```

### Worked example

A marketing ESP sends as `news@example.com` from `198.51.100.50`. Aggregate report row (shape simplified):

```text
<source_ip>198.51.100.50</source_ip>
<count>1200</count>
<policy_evaluated>
  <disposition>none</disposition>
  <dkim>pass</dkim>
  <spf>fail</spf>
</policy_evaluated>
<header_from>example.com</header_from>
```

SPF fails because the ESP IP is not in `example.com`’s SPF (or the envelope domain differs). DKIM `d=example.com` aligns with `From:`, so DMARC can still pass. Next `p=` step: keep `p=none` until every high-volume source shows aligned pass; then move to `quarantine`, then `reject`.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“SPF failed, so the mail is forged.”** After a legitimate relay, SPF often fails while aligned DKIM still authorizes the message for DMARC.
- **“Gateway in the path always breaks DMARC.”** Gateways break SPF when they change the connecting IP/envelope; they break DMARC only if they also invalidate or strip aligned DKIM (or you lack ARC where needed).
- **“Aggregate reports are optional fluff.”** Without them you guess which IPs are yours; flipping `p=reject` blind breaks real senders.
- **“ARC replaces SPF/DKIM.”** ARC conveys prior results across intermediaries; receivers still need a trustworthy ARC chain and underlying authentication story.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 8617 — ARC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8617)
2. [RFC 9990 — DMARC aggregate](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9990) (and related DMARC reporting RFCs)
3. [Google bulk sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126)
4. [Outlook.com postmaster](https://postmaster.outlook.com/)
5. [Exchange Online mail flow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/exchange/mail-flow-best-practices/mail-flow-best-practices)
6. [aiosmtpd](https://aiosmtpd.readthedocs.io/)

## Lab idea

Python **aiosmtpd** relay applying hold rules, then reinjecting allowed mail to MailHog/Mailpit.

Why local-only: an open relay on the public internet becomes abuse infrastructure; the lab proves flow mechanics without sending real mail.

## Next step

`mail_flow` + `dmarc_aggregate` katas → quiz.

# Reading — Email threats beyond SPF/DKIM/DMARC

## Learning objectives

1. Place **BIMI**, **MTA-STS**, **TLS-RPT**, and **DANE** next to SPF/DKIM/DMARC without confusing logos for authentication.
2. Analyze phishing **headers** and attachment risk at a literacy level (sandboxing concepts).
3. Contrast **S/MIME / PGP** end-to-end crypto with **time-of-click** URL rewriting.

**Why this matters.** DMARC can pass and the message can still be hostile: malicious attachments, credential links, or downgraded SMTP TLS. Without transport policy (MTA-STS/DANE), reporting (TLS-RPT), and human-layer controls, “we have DMARC” becomes a false sense of safety. On the job, email-security reviews ask what you do *after* authentication succeeds.

**How it works.**

1. **SPF/DKIM/DMARC** answer “is this domain authorized for this message path?”
2. **BIMI** can show a logo when DMARC is enforced — brand indicator, not a crypto proof by itself.
3. **MTA-STS** publishes a policy so sending MTAs prefer STS-validated TLS to your MX; **TLS-RPT** receives failure reports.
4. **DANE** (DNSSEC + TLSA) binds MX certs in DNS — powerful where DNSSEC is real; operationally heavier.
5. **Header analysis** (Received, Authentication-Results, URL paths) supports phishing triage without attacking third parties.
6. **Attachment sandboxing** detonates or statically inspects files off the user desktop.
7. **S/MIME/PGP** encrypt/sign content end-to-end; **time-of-click** rewriting proxies links at click time (privacy/availability trade-offs).

```text
Auth (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) → transport policy (MTA-STS/DANE) → content controls
                      → human triage (headers) → sandbox / rewrite / E2E crypto
```

### Worked example

MTA-STS policy host sketch (conceptual):

```text
# DNS: _mta-sts.example.com TXT "v=STSv1; id=20261114"
# HTTPS: https://mta-sts.example.com/.well-known/mta-sts.txt
version: STSv1
mode: enforce
mx: mail.example.com
max_age: 86400
```

Why reports (`rua` for DMARC, TLS-RPT for STS) before `enforce`: you learn which senders break before you drop them.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“BIMI proves the message is safe.”** BIMI is a brand indicator tied to DMARC enforcement — not malware scanning.
- **“TLS on port 25 is enough.”** Opportunistic TLS can be stripped; MTA-STS/DANE raise the bar for SMTP hop security.
- **“Sandboxing means zero risk.”** Evasion and time bombs exist; combine with type blocks and user reporting.
- **“URL rewriting is free.”** It breaks some links, centralizes click metadata, and must not become a phishing page itself.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[Email Authentication Explained (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SN5-DnOH8RQ)** — practical backdrop before BIMI/STS  
   Why it helps: refreshes Module 05 so the “beyond auth” controls have a base.

## Read these (verified)

1. [MTA-STS (RFC 8461)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8461)
2. [TLS-RPT (RFC 8460)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8460)
3. [BIMI Group — overview](https://bimigroup.org/)
4. [DANE (RFC 6698)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6698)
5. [S/MIME (RFC 8551)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8551)

## Lab idea — MTA-STS / TLS-RPT

1. Publish a **testing** STS policy (`mode: testing`) for a lab domain you control.
2. Configure TLS-RPT so failure reports have somewhere to go.
3. Move to `enforce` only after reports look clean.
4. Document who owns DNS + HTTPS for `mta-sts.` — split ownership is a common outage.

## Next step

Assignment + required quiz. Stay vendor-neutral: mechanisms over product names.

# Reading — Threat modeling & lightweight secure SDLC

## Learning objectives

1. Apply a **STRIDE**-lite pass to MailGuard’s hold/release path (who can spoof an operator? tamper with rules? deny the queue?).
2. Relate findings to mitigations you already ship (MFA, audit logs, first-match rules, CI) and gaps you document honestly.
3. Skim **OWASP SAMM** as a maturity *map*, not a certificate — pick one practice to improve next.

**Why this matters.** Shipping hold/release without naming abuse stories leaves gaps that MFA, audits, and CI cannot invent for you. Teams that skip threat modeling discover spoofed operators, silent rule tampering, and held-body disclosure in production — after users are affected. A lightweight pass costs a page of Markdown; a missed elevation path costs incident response.

**How it works.**

1. **What are we working on?** Sketch the hold/release path and trust boundaries (browser → admin/API → rule store → queue → next hop).
2. **What can go wrong?** Walk **STRIDE** against each element: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege (Microsoft-origin checklist — see [STRIDE reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/develop/threat-modeling-tool-threats)).
3. **What are we doing about it?** Map each abuse story to a mitigation you ship (MFA, audit logs, first-match tests, least privilege) or mark an honest gap.
4. **Did we do a good job?** Revisit when the design changes; Secure Software Development Life Cycle (**SDLC**) means these questions recur in requirements, design, implementation, test, and operate — not only in a final pen-test fantasy.
5. **Privacy sibling:** **LINDDUN** is privacy-oriented; for MailGuard, focus on disclosure of held message bodies and audit access ([LINDDUN](https://www.linddun.org/)).
6. **Maturity map:** **OWASP SAMM** maps five business functions (Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations) so you pick *one* practice to improve — not claim enterprise maturity ([OWASP SAMM](https://owasp.org/www-project-samm/)).

```
Shostack four questions
  → STRIDE (or LINDDUN-lite) rows on the diagram
  → mitigations / gaps
  → SAMM: one practice to raise next
```

### Worked example

One STRIDE-lite row for MailGuard’s hold path:

| Element | STRIDE | Abuse story | Mitigation or gap |
|---------|--------|-------------|-------------------|
| Operator session | Spoofing | Attacker uses a stolen session to approve holds | MFA + short-lived session; gap if admin has no step-up on release |
| Rule store | Tampering | Quiet edit flips first-match order to silent allow | Audit log on rule write + CI tests for evaluate order |
| Held body | Information disclosure | Support role reads full message body | Least privilege / redacted preview; document if full body is required |
| Release API | Elevation of privilege | Low-privilege user calls `POST /holds/{id}/release` | Authz check on hold id (tenant + role); 403 on miss |

**On the job.** Email and identity gateways always have privileged operator actions (release, rule edit). Interviewers and security reviews expect you to walk a trust-boundary diagram and name STRIDE rows with mitigations or honest gaps — vendor-neutral vocabulary that transfers across cloud mail and SaaS admin consoles.

## Short intro

Threat modeling asks “what can go wrong?” before or while you build. Secure Software Development Life Cycle (**SDLC**) means security activities show up in requirements, design, implementation, test, and operate — not only in a final pen-test fantasy.

**STRIDE** (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) is a Microsoft-origin checklist still useful as interview vocabulary. **LINDDUN** is a privacy-oriented sibling; for MailGuard, focus on disclosure of held message bodies and audit access. Prefer a short table over an unused enterprise tool: six abuse stories tied to MailGuard’s hold path beat a blank “we follow best practices.”

![STRIDE-lite checklist with example questions for a hold and release path](images/stride-lite.svg)

*Figure. Six STRIDE categories as a lightweight checklist on the hold/release path. Notice each tile pairs a threat question with a mitigation you may already ship (MFA, audit logs, least privilege) — document gaps honestly. Original course diagram (CC0).*

### Trade-offs

| Approach | When it helps | Cost / limit |
|----------|---------------|--------------|
| STRIDE-lite table | Fast feature reviews | Misses privacy-specific linking threats (use LINDDUN-lite) |
| Full threat-modeling tools | Regulated programs | Overhead for a student kata |
| Pen-test only at the end | Finds some bugs | Too late for design-level trust boundaries |

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“We have MFA and audit logs, so we already threat-modeled.”** Controls without named abuse stories leave blind spots (e.g. rule-order tampering) that MFA never covers.
- **“STRIDE is obsolete / only for Microsoft stacks.”** It is a vocabulary checklist; the point is coverage of spoof/tamper/disclose/elevate on *your* diagram, not a product allegiance.
- **“SAMM means we are mature.”** SAMM is a map of practices. Inflating scores without evidence fails reviews; pick one practice and show a concrete next step.
- **“Privacy is separate from security threat modeling.”** Held bodies and audit access are disclosure risks — LINDDUN-lite belongs on the same page as STRIDE for a gateway.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[Threatmodcon keynote (segment)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4ngYKVAs22c)** — Adam Shostack  
   Why it helps: threat modeling as a practice; pairs with the four-question frame in writing.

2. **[Keynote: Stop Trying to "Manage Risk"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=THSfJIlPGPk)** — Adam Shostack  
   Why it helps: connects threat modeling judgment to delivery — not spreadsheet theater.

Also skim: [Shostack + Associates — threat modeling beginner guide](https://adam.shostack.org/resources/threat-modeling) (four questions).

## Read these (verified)

1. [OWASP Threat Modeling](https://owasp.org/www-community/Threat_Modeling) — community overview.
2. [OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Threat_Modeling_Cheat_Sheet.html) — practical steps.
3. [Microsoft — STRIDE](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/develop/threat-modeling-tool-threats) — threat categories reference.
4. [OWASP SAMM](https://owasp.org/www-project-samm/) — five business functions: **Governance**, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations (15 practices).
5. [LINDDUN](https://www.linddun.org/) — privacy threat categories (skim).
6. [Shostack four-question frame (GitHub)](https://github.com/adamshostack/4QuestionFrame) — one-pager.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment.

entries.body:
# SQL primer

**Why this matters.** Hold/release queues need **durable** state: who held a message, when, and whether it was released. In-memory demos lose that story on restart; without a queryable store you cannot prove “who released this hold?” after an incident. Document stores or logs alone rarely give the same transactional constraints for account/rule/audit rows — SQL remains the default for that shape of SaaS data.

**How it works.**

1. Model entities as **tables** (rows + columns) with constraints (`NOT NULL`, keys).
2. Identify rows with **primary keys** so holds/rules stay addressable across restarts.
3. Change data with declarative statements (`SELECT` / `INSERT` / `UPDATE`) — the engine plans how, you declare what.
4. Evolve schema with **migrations** (Alembic later) so deploys do not hand-edit production tables.
5. The MailGuard API module starts in-memory, then asks you to *sketch* a Postgres-shaped design — this primer is that vocabulary. On the job, the same pattern backs email-security and identity APIs: durable holds, rules, and audit trails operators can query.

### Worked example

Sketch that answers “what is held?” without an app server:

```sql
-- Why: one table can answer "what is held?" without an app server
CREATE TABLE holds (
  id          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  state       TEXT NOT NULL,  -- held | released | rejected
  created_at  TEXT NOT NULL,
  actor       TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO holds (id, state, created_at, actor)
VALUES ('msg-1', 'held', '2026-11-13T12:00:00Z', 'api');

SELECT id, state FROM holds WHERE state = 'held';
-- → msg-1 | held
```

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What SQL is

**SQL** (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and cloud variants).

## Why industry uses it

Relational stores give strong consistency for account, rule, and audit data. Security products lean on queryable audit trails — “who released this hold?” — which tables express well.

## Key concepts for Module 07

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| Primary key | Stable id for a held message |
| Foreign keys | Rules/holds point at real accounts — orphan rows break audits |
| `CHECK` constraints | Reject impossible `state` values early |
| Indexes | Fast lookup by state / created_at for operator queues |
| Transactions | Approve+audit insert commits together or not at all |
| Parameterized queries | Stop SQL injection from operator/search input |
| Migrations (awareness) | Schema changes ship with app versions (Alembic later) |

## Parameterized queries (SQL injection)

**Why:** String-concatenating user input into SQL lets an attacker change the query (classic injection). **How:** pass values as bound parameters:

```sql
-- Bad (never): "SELECT * FROM holds WHERE id = '" + user_id + "'"
-- Good (shape):
SELECT id, state FROM holds WHERE id = ?;   -- SQLite-style placeholder
-- or $1 / %(id)s depending on the driver
```

## Transactions

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE holds SET state = 'released' WHERE id = ? AND state = 'approved';
INSERT INTO audit(hold_id, actor, action) VALUES (?, ?, 'release');
COMMIT;
-- On error: ROLLBACK so you never release without an audit row (or the reverse)
```

## CHECK, foreign keys, indexes

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE holds (
  id          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id  TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  state       TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (state IN ('held', 'approved', 'released', 'rejected')),
  created_at  TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX holds_state_idx ON holds (state);
```

Why FKs: deleting an account should not leave holds that point nowhere (or should cascade deliberately). Why CHECK: typos like `relased` fail closed. Why index: operator UIs filter `WHERE state = 'held'` constantly.

## Install and run

You do **not** need a live database for this primer — the vocabulary above is enough to start Module 07. Optional (why: muscle memory for `psql` / SQLite before the stretch persistence lab): install [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/download/) or use SQLite for experiments. Module 07 keeps the kata in-memory; persistence is a stretch with SQLAlchemy/Alembic links in readings.

## Tiny hands-on example

Use the SQL sketch in **Worked example** above (`CREATE` → `INSERT` → `SELECT`). **How:** `CREATE TABLE` defines the shape; `INSERT` records a hold; `SELECT` filters — the same questions operators ask in an admin UI.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Logs are enough for audit.”** Append-only logs help forensics, but hold/release needs queryable current state with constraints — tables answer “is this still held?” in one row.
- **“In-memory is fine until launch.”** Restarts wipe holds; multi-instance APIs disagree on state. Sketch SQL early even if the kata stays in-memory.
- **“Any string in `state` is fine.”** Without CHECK constraints, typos (`relased`) become silent bugs; treat legal states as part of the schema design.
- **“Escaping by hand is as good as parameters.”** Drivers’ bound parameters are the reliable fix; hand escaping misses encodings.
- **“Indexes are free.”** They speed reads and slow writes — index the filter columns operators actually use.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[SQL Tutorial - Full Database Course for Beginners](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HXV3zeQKqGY)**  
   Why it helps: tables/constraints before MailGuard persistence sketches.

## Official docs

1. [PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/)
2. [SQLAlchemy ORM quick start](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/quickstart.html) (stretch after Module 07)
3. [Alembic tutorial](https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/tutorial.html)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`07-mailguard-api`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Reading — Hold / approve / release

## Learning objectives

1. Model a first-class hold queue with explicit state transitions.
2. Separate **approve** (human decision) from **release** (send onward).
3. Reject illegal transitions instead of silently no-oping.

**Why this matters.** Collapsing “approve” and “release” into one click is how held mail leaves without a recorded human decision — or how a bug silently no-ops and operators think work finished. Illegal transitions that return 200 hide missends. Explicit states (`held` → `approved` → `released`, or `rejected`) exist so audits answer “who decided?” separately from “did it leave?”

**How it works.**

1. A hold starts in state **held** (message parked for review).
2. An operator **approves** (policy OK) or **rejects** (do not send).
3. Only **approved** items may **release** to the next hop (MTA / downstream).
4. The API rejects illegal jumps (e.g. held → released) with a client error (often **409 Conflict**), not a silent 200.
5. Stretch: persist rows in Postgres via SQLAlchemy; **Alembic** migrations version the schema so deploys do not hand-edit production tables ([Alembic tutorial](https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/tutorial.html)).
6. Auto-bcc / delete-on-condition are explicit **action kinds**, not silent side effects of allow — so least privilege and audit stay possible.

```
held --approve--> approved --release--> released
  \--reject--> rejected
```

### Worked example

State transition table (illegal cells must error):

| From \ Action | approve | reject | release |
|---------------|---------|--------|---------|
| held | → approved | → rejected | **409** (must approve first) |
| approved | **409** | → rejected (policy: may still reject before release) | → released |
| rejected | **409** | **409** | **409** |
| released | **409** | **409** | **409** |

This course’s `hold_state` kata treats **approved → reject** as legal so operators can stop a previously approved item before release. Document any stricter policy in your own lab notes.

```http
POST /holds/msg-1/release
→ 409 {"detail": "hold msg-1 is held; approve before release"}
```

**On the job.** Every email-security and DLP review queue uses a similar state machine. Cloud identity/admin tools likewise separate “decision recorded” from “side effect executed.” Being able to draw the diagram and defend illegal-transition errors is day-one literacy for gateway work.

## Short intro

An email-security gateway often **holds** outbound mail for review. Operators approve or reject; only approved items are released to the next hop. Keep vocabulary vendor-neutral: hold, approve, release, reject.

Persistence (Postgres + SQLAlchemy/Alembic) belongs in your stretch lab — the kata stays a pure state machine you can unit-test.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Approve and release are the same button.”** Then audits cannot separate human judgment from send — and a UI bug can release without a decision record.
- **“Illegal transitions can no-op with 200.”** Operators and monitors treat 200 as success; use 4xx so clients retry or surface the error.
- **“We’ll add states later; strings are fine.”** Unchecked free-text states drift (`aproved`); model an enum/FSM early and test every edge.
- **“Alembic is optional busywork.”** Hand-edited production schemas diverge across environments; migrations are how schema changes travel with the app.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[FastAPI Tutorial for Beginners – Full Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VirndPTeRaw)**  
   Why it helps: HTTP handlers around the hold state machine.

2. [SQLAlchemy 2.0 — ORM quick start](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/quickstart.html)
3. [Alembic tutorial](https://alembic.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/tutorial.html)

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page (`hold_state` + `rule_actions` katas). The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

# Reading — MailGuard API

## Learning objectives

1. Sketch a small HTTP API that stores ordered hold/allow/reject rules.
2. Evaluate a message against those rules with **first-match-wins** semantics.
3. Cover happy path and edge cases with automated tests.

**Why this matters.** Without a rules API, operators cannot encode “hold external domains” or “reject secret substrings” as durable policy — every decision becomes a one-off script. First-match-wins without tests drifts into silent allow; an in-memory-only store vanishes on restart and cannot support multi-instance or audit. History of mail gateways is full of policy engines that grew from ad-hoc filters; a thin, tested evaluate function is the trade-off that keeps the kata honest before Postgres and authn.

**How it works.**

1. Operators **create** ordered rules (predicates + decision: `hold` / `allow` / `reject`).
2. On evaluate, the service walks the list **top-down**.
3. Stop at the **first** match; return that decision (or a documented default if none match).
4. Keep evaluation as a **pure function** separate from FastAPI handlers so pytest covers edge cases without HTTP.
5. Pydantic models shape requests; OpenAPI documents the surface ([FastAPI first steps](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/first-steps/)).
6. Persistence, authn/z, and pagination stay out of the kata on purpose — stretch labs add Postgres later.

```
Client → POST /rules  → store (ordered list)
Client → POST /evaluate(message) → walk rules → first match → decision
```

### Worked example

Rules and one evaluate call (conceptual JSON):

```json
[
  {"id": "r1", "recipient_domain": "external.example", "decision": "hold"},
  {"id": "r2", "contains": "SECRET", "decision": "reject"}
]
```

A rule with **no predicates** (neither `recipient_domain` nor `contains`) **never matches**. Use the evaluate call’s documented **default** (usually `allow`) when nothing matches — do not invent a catch-all empty `match: {}` rule.

```http
POST /evaluate
{"to": "user@external.example", "subject": "Q3", "body": "hi"}

→ 200 {"decision": "hold", "matched_rule": "r1"}
```

If a broad allow rule were listed *before* the domain hold, the same message would silently allow — **order is policy**.

**On the job.** Email DLP and identity-adjacent gateways expose the same pattern: policy CRUD + evaluate on the message path. Interviewers care that you can explain first-match vs scoring, why pure evaluation is testable, and what an in-memory store cannot prove in production — vendor-neutral skills for any cloud mail or SaaS security API.

## Short intro

MailGuard’s product thread needs a **rules API**: operators create rules; the service decides whether an outbound message is allowed, held for review, or rejected. This module is a thin FastAPI-shaped service with an in-memory store and a pure evaluation function you can unit-test without standing up a database.

Keep the public vocabulary vendor-neutral: rules, holds, allow, reject — not a commercial product clone.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Last-match or score-sum is the same as first-match.”** Different semantics produce different outcomes for the same rule list; document and test the one you chose.
- **“Evaluation inside the route handler is fine.”** Mixing HTTP and policy makes edge-case tests slow and fragile; pure `evaluate(rules, message)` is the contract.
- **“In-memory means production-ready.”** Restarts wipe rules; two API instances disagree. Production needs authn/z, persistence, pagination, and audit logs — the kata stays small **why:** prove the decision engine before infrastructure hides policy bugs.
- **“No match → hold for safety.”** Maybe — but only if documented. Silent defaults are how missends (or false blocks) ship.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[FastAPI Tutorial for Beginners – Full Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VirndPTeRaw)** — Tech With Tim (2025)  
   Why it helps: routes, models, docs UI, and a runnable API shape that matches this module’s starter.


## Read these (verified)

1. [FastAPI — First steps](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/first-steps/) — routing and OpenAPI.
2. [Pydantic — Models](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/models/) — request/response shapes.
3. [pytest — Get Started](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/getting-started.html) — tests as contract.
4. Challenge Gym [`hold_rules`](../../01-challenge-gym/readings/hold_rules.md) — same decision vocabulary.

## Keep in mind

Production APIs add authn/z, persistence, pagination, and audit logs. Your kata stays small on purpose — **why:** prove the decision engine before wiring infrastructure that hides policy bugs.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

## Phase 3 deepen

Add Postgres persistence in your lab environment, plus the `hold_state` and `rule_actions` katas for approve/release and auto-bcc/delete actions.

Untyped form state is where “allow” vs “hold” bugs hide; **TypeScript** makes illegal states harder to represent, and **Vue 3** is how Module 08 structures that admin SPA. Plain JavaScript + ad-hoc DOM updates can work for demos — until a typo ships the wrong decision label into production. **How it works.** 1. **Node.js** runs the toolchain (`npm` installs packages and scripts). 2. **TypeScript** compiles typed `.ts` to JavaScript the browser (or Node) runs. 3. **Vue 3** binds reactive state to templates so a hold-queue table updates when the API returns new rows. 4. Forms and row models use interfaces/unions so `"hold" | "allow" | "reject"` stays consistent with the API. 5. On the job, the same stack backs many SaaS security admin consoles: typed forms, clear dangerous actions, no cloud secrets in the browser bundle. ### Worked example A decision union that rejects typos at compile time: ```ts export type Decision = "hold" | "allow" | "reject"; export function labelFor(d: Decision): string { // Why: exhaustive-ish union — typos become compile errors return d.toUpperCase(); } console.log(labelFor("hold")); // → HOLD // labelFor("hodl") → TypeScript error before a reviewer sees it ``` This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack. --- ## What these tools are - **Node.js** — JavaScript runtime + npm for frontend tooling - **TypeScript** — JavaScript with types - **Vue 3** — progressive UI framework (Composition API in modern apps) ## Why industry uses them Admin consoles for security products need accessible forms, clear dangerous actions (release), and fewer runtime surprises. # Go primer

**Why this matters.** Module 09’s worker consumes queue messages and applies hold/allow/reject. **Go** fits small, explicit network services: fast compile, static binaries, and straightforward concurrency — useful when a Python API owns HTTP and a worker owns async decisions. You *could* keep everything in one Python process; splitting a worker is how teams isolate retries, DLQs, and deploy cadence without blocking the API.

**How it works.**

1. Install the Go toolchain and confirm with `go version`.
2. Create a module (`go mod init`) so imports and tests resolve.
3. Write packages with exported (`TitleCase`) names for the worker’s public surface.
4. Describe ports with **interfaces** (e.g. a queue) so the kata stays in-memory before cloud SQS.
5. Verify with `go test ./...` — table-driven tests lock decisions the same way pytest does for the API.
6. On the job, the same pattern shows up in email and identity pipelines: thin consumers, table-driven tests, swap local fakes for cloud queues later.

### Worked example

Tiny decision function + test (same shape Module 09 uses):

```go
package primer

func Decision(score int) string {
        // Why: tiny pure function — easy to unit test in Module 09
        if score >= 80 {
                return "hold"
        }
        return "allow"
}
```

```go
func TestDecision(t *testing.T) {
        if Decision(90) != "hold" {
                t.Fatalf("expected hold")
        }
}
```

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Go is

**Go** is an open-source language from Google, common for CLIs, proxies, and cloud workers.

## Why industry uses it

Ops-friendly deploy (single binary), good standard library for HTTP/JSON, and predictable performance for queue consumers. Many security and platform teams keep Go beside Python services.

## Key concepts for Module 09

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| `go.mod` / packages | Reproducible module layout |
| exported names (`TitleCase`) | Public API of your worker package |
| interfaces | Swap in-memory queue for SQS later |
| `go test ./...` | Same red/green loop as pytest |

## Install and run

1. [Go install docs](https://go.dev/doc/install)
2. Check: `go version`

```bash
# Why: scratch module outside the course repo
mkdir -p /tmp/mg-go-primer && cd /tmp/mg-go-primer
# Why: go.mod pins the module path so imports and `go test` resolve
go mod init example.com/mgprimer
```

## Tiny hands-on example

```bash
cat > /tmp/mg-go-primer/decision.go << 'EOF'
package primer

// Decision is a MailGuard-style outcome.
func Decision(score int) string {
        // Why: tiny pure function — easy to unit test in Module 09
        if score >= 80 {
                return "hold"
        }
        return "allow"
}
EOF
cat > /tmp/mg-go-primer/decision_test.go << 'EOF'
package primer

import "testing"

func TestDecision(t *testing.T) {
        if Decision(90) != "hold" {
                t.Fatalf("expected hold")
        }
}
EOF
cd /tmp/mg-go-primer && go test ./...
```

**How:** Production code + `_test.go` live side by side; `go test` compiles and runs them — Module 09 uses the same pattern.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Go replaces the Python API.”** The split is intentional: HTTP/policy in one process, async side effects in another — shared JSON vocabulary, not a rewrite.
- **“Call the cloud SDK from every package.”** Interfaces keep LocalStack/in-memory fakes testable; sprinkle SDK calls and unit tests need the network.
- **“Tests are optional until SQS.”** Table-driven `go test` locks the decision contract before any broker exists.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Learn Go Programming - Golang Tutorial for Beginners](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YS4e4q9oBaU)**  
   Why it helps: Go toolchain before the worker module.

## Official docs

1. [Go install](https://go.dev/doc/install)
2. [A Tour of Go](https://go.dev/tour/)
3. [go test docs](https://pkg.go.dev/testing)

---

# Reading — MailGuard Worker

## Learning objectives

1. Consume queued messages and apply rule decisions.
2. Keep a queue interface so local demos and cloud queues share code.
3. Document the contract with the Python API.

**Why this matters.** Synchronous HTTP-only gateways choke under burst mail and couple every retry to a client timeout. Without a worker, hold persistence, notifications, and release-to-MTA pile into the API process — and a crash mid-send has no clear redelivery story. History of mail pipelines favors async consumers with shared decision vocabulary (`hold` / `allow` / `reject`) so Python and Go do not drift.

**How it works.**

1. The API (or an ingest path) **enqueues** work as a JSON message.
2. A Go **worker** pulls messages behind a **queue interface** (in-memory / LocalStack now; cloud SQS later — [SQS overview](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html)).
3. The worker applies the same decision vocabulary as Module 07 (`hold` / `allow` / `reject`).
4. It performs side effects (persist hold, notify, release toward an MTA).
5. On success it **acks/deletes** the message; on crash, at-least-once delivery redelivers — so handlers must be **idempotent**.
6. Table-driven `go test` locks the JSON contract with the Python API.

```
Producer / API → Queue → Go worker → apply decision → side effects → ack
                              ↑ interface: in-memory now, SQS later
```

### Worked example

Shared queue message JSON (API producer ↔ Go `QueueMessage` in `worker/sqs_contract.go`):

```json
{
  "id": "msg-42",
  "subject": "Q3 forecast",
  "body": "Confidential numbers…",
  "attempt": 1
}
```

The worker applies hold/allow/reject using the **same decision vocabulary** as Module 07 (rules evaluate / hold state). Do not invent parallel field names like `message_id` / `to` in the queue envelope — keep the Go struct and the producer JSON identical.

```
Receive → ParseQueueMessage → evaluate / apply decision
  hold   → persist hold row (idempotent on id)
  allow  → forward / no-op if already forwarded
  reject → record rejection
→ DeleteMessage / ack (attempt increments on failure; see DLQ reading)
```

**On the job.** Cloud email security, identity provisioning, and DLP all use workers + queues. Interviewers ask about idempotency, shared JSON contracts, and why you do not sprinkle cloud SDK calls through every package — vendor-neutral platform skills.

## Short intro

API services accept operator input; **workers** apply decisions asynchronously — hold persistence, notifications, or release to an MTA. This module is a Go worker with an in-memory queue interface and table-driven tests.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Ack before side effects finish.”** A crash after ack loses the work; ack after success (and design for duplicate delivery).
- **“Exactly-once is guaranteed.”** Most queues are at-least-once; idempotency keys (`id` / hold id) are mandatory.
- **“Python and Go can invent their own field names.”** Field drift causes silent parse failures; document and test one JSON contract.
- **“The worker can call evaluate with different rules.”** Divergent policy engines are how allow/hold disagree across services — share vocabulary and fixtures.


## Videos (verified)

   Why it helps: Go concurrency/packages backdrop for the worker.

# Reading — Queue consumer + DLQ

## Learning objectives

1. Consume work from a queue behind an interface (LocalStack SQS in lab).
2. Make processing idempotent; route poison messages to a **dead-letter queue**.
3. Share a JSON contract with the API module.

**Why this matters.** Poison messages that never succeed will retry forever without a **dead-letter queue (DLQ)** — burning compute and blocking the main queue’s visibility window. Handlers that are not idempotent double-send mail on redelivery after a crash. Field drift between API JSON and Go structs causes silent parse failures in production. DLQs exist so humans can inspect failures without losing the original payload.

**How it works.**

1. A consumer **receives** a message (visibility timeout hides it from other workers).
2. It **processes** the payload (parse JSON, apply decision, side effects).
3. On success it **deletes** the message.
4. On failure the message becomes visible again (**at-least-once** redelivery; attempt count increments).
5. After `maxReceiveCount` / max attempts, the broker moves it to a **DLQ** ([SQS dead-letter queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html)).
6. Your kata’s `ShouldDLQ(attempt, maxAttempts)` encodes that threshold (typically `attempt >= maxAttempts`). Idempotency keys (message id / hold id) prevent double side effects. Parse shared JSON carefully — same fields as Module 07.

```
Main queue → worker
   │ fail / redeliver (attempt++)
   └─ attempt >= max → DLQ (inspect, fix, replay)
```

### Worked example

Threshold helper + a poison payload:

```go
// ShouldDLQ: move to DLQ when attempt reaches max (inclusive)
func ShouldDLQ(attempt, maxAttempts int) bool {
    return attempt >= maxAttempts // why: attempt==max means last try failed
}
```

| attempt | maxAttempts | ShouldDLQ? |
|---------|-------------|------------|
| 1 | 3 | false (retry) |
| 2 | 3 | false (retry) |
| 3 | 3 | **true** → DLQ |

```json
{
  "id": "",
  "subject": "poison",
  "body": "bad",
  "attempt": 5
}
```

If `id` is empty, `ParseQueueMessage` must error — that poison payload retries until DLQ rather than blocking the main queue forever. Fix the producer; do not silently invent an id.

**On the job.** SQS-style DLQs are standard in cloud mail and identity pipelines. Knowing when to DLQ vs retry — and how LocalStack demos the same shape — is day-to-day platform security engineering, not a single-vendor trick.

## Short intro

Queue consumers must survive crashes and bad payloads. Idempotency plus a DLQ turns “retry forever” into “park and investigate.”

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Use `attempt > maxAttempts`.”** Off-by-one leaves one extra burn on the main queue (or never DLQs); the kata expects `>=` — test both edges.
- **“DLQ means delete the problem.”** DLQ parks the payload for humans; without inspection/replay you just move the outage.
- **“Redelivery is rare.”** Crashes and timeouts are normal; non-idempotent handlers double-send.
- **“LocalStack is optional busywork.”** Proving the interface locally catches contract bugs before cloud credentials and cost enter the story.

## Local queue compose

Bring up an SQS-compatible broker on your laptop (ElasticMQ):

```bash
cd 09-mailguard-worker/starter
docker compose -f docker-compose.queue.yml up
```

- Compose file: [`../starter/docker-compose.queue.yml`](../starter/docker-compose.queue.yml)
- Config (main + DLQ): [`../starter/elasticmq.conf`](../starter/elasticmq.conf)
- API endpoint: `http://127.0.0.1:9324`
- Queues: `mailguard-hold` → DLQ `mailguard-hold-dlq` after `maxReceiveCount = 3`

Module 07 can enqueue the shared JSON contract via
[`../../07-mailguard-api/starter/app/queue_producer.py`](../../07-mailguard-api/starter/app/queue_producer.py)
(in-memory by default; comments show the ElasticMQ/LocalStack boto3 shape).


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Amazon SQS DLQ Setup Guide](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p4t0-_POkrI)**  
   Why it helps: redrive / DLQ mental model (pair with local ElasticMQ).

## Read these (verified)

1. [AWS SQS dead-letter queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html)
2. [LocalStack SQS](https://docs.localstack.cloud/user-guide/aws/sqs/)
3. [ElasticMQ](https://github.com/softwaremill/elasticmq) — SQS-compatible local broker used by the compose file above
4. [encoding/json](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json)

## Next step

Continue with the assignment, then implement `ShouldDLQ` / `ParseQueueMessage` and run `go test ./...` (**why:** red/green on the threshold and contract before wiring real SQS).

# Reading — File / cloud-share DLP

## Learning objectives

1. Explain why **email hold** alone does not cover files shared via cloud links.
2. List controls: link visibility (org / specific users / public), expiry, app-level revoke, download audit. Note: a raw S3 **presigned URL** cannot be revoked individually — it stays valid until expiry (or until signing credentials / object policy are revoked). Real share-DLP revoke needs app-level indirection.
3. Relate Secure Drop’s expiring link to a minimal share-DLP story.

**Why this matters.** Outbound email hold catches messages on the mail path; it does nothing when someone pastes an “anyone with the link” URL into chat. Without visibility limits, expiry, revoke, and download audit, missent shares stay reachable until someone notices. Presigned URLs feel like revoke-able magic — until you learn a raw S3 presign is a **bearer** link that cannot be killed one-by-one. That trade-off is why production share-DLP puts an app check in front of short-lived presigns.

**How it works.**

1. Upload creates a **share object**: owner, visibility (org / specific users / public), `expires_at`, optional `revoked_at`, and audit hooks.
2. Recipient requests download through **your app** (not a naked long-lived storage URL).
3. App checks: not expired, not revoked, caller authorized for that visibility.
4. Only then issue a **short-lived** storage fetch (presign or stream) and log who/when/object id — **not** file bytes ([presigned URL docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html)).
5. On missend, set `revoked_at` (or equivalent) so further app checks fail even if someone copied an old link.
6. Email hold and share-DLP are complementary: hold is about SMTP content; share-DLP is about object links after the fact.

```
Upload → ShareLink (visibility, expiry, revoked_at)
Download → app authz check → short-lived fetch → audit metadata
Missend → set revoked_at → further downloads fail
```

### Worked example

Minimal share record + revoke effect:

```json
{
  "share_id": "sh_9f3a",
  "object_key": "drops/q3-forecast.pdf",
  "visibility": "specific_users",
  "allowed": ["alex@example.com"],
  "expires_at": "2026-11-20T00:00:00Z",
  "revoked_at": null
}
```

| Event | App check | Result |
|-------|-----------|--------|
| Alex downloads before expiry | ok | short-lived URL + audit row |
| Public guess of URL | visibility fail | 403 |
| After operator sets `revoked_at` | revoked | 403 even with copied link |
| Raw S3 presign issued for 7 days, no app front | n/a | **cannot** revoke that URL alone until it expires |

**On the job.** Cloud Drive/SharePoint/S3-backed secure transfer shows up in every email and collaboration security review. Explaining why email DLP ≠ link DLP — and why revoke needs indirection — is vendor-neutral literacy for SaaS and cloud security roles.

## Short intro

Outbound email DLP catches messages and attachments on the mail path. People also paste cloud-share URLs into chat or leave “anyone with the link” open. File / cloud-share DLP is about **governing those shares**: who can open them, for how long, and what the audit log shows when someone downloads. Note again: a raw object-storage **presigned URL** is a bearer token until expiry (or until signing credentials / object policy change) — real revoke needs an app-level check in front of short-lived fetches.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Email hold covers Drive links.”** Hold never sees a URL pasted in chat; share visibility/expiry/revoke are a different control plane.
- **“Presigned URL = revocable share.”** Individual S3-style presigns cannot be killed one-by-one; use app indirection + short TTL.
- **“Audit should store the file bytes.”** Log metadata (who/when/object id); storing content duplicates sensitive data and expands breach scope.
- **“Public link with a long random path is secret enough.”** Guessing is hard; forwarding is easy — treat “anyone with the link” as public.

## Videos (verified)

Credited DLP overview talks rotate often — prefer the written links below. Optional: search YouTube for “Data Loss Prevention explained” from IBM Technology / NIST-oriented channels and confirm the title matches before watching.

Prefer written vendor-neutral docs below if a video ID drifts.

1. [OWASP — File Upload Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html) — upload risks adjacent to secure drop.
2. [NIST SP 800-171 / access control concepts](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/171/r3/final) — skim access-control family vocabulary (optional depth).
3. [Google Workspace — Manage external sharing for your organization](https://support.google.com/a/answer/60781) — org-level Drive/Docs link sharing controls (generic literacy).
4. [Microsoft Learn — SharePoint / OneDrive sharing overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sharepoint/external-sharing-overview) — external sharing concepts (read for patterns, not product lock-in).
5. [AWS — Presigned URLs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html) — mechanism behind many expiring links (bearer URLs; max lifetime and revoke limits).

## Next step

# Reading — Insecure password-ZIP transfer → Secure Drop

## Learning objectives

1. Explain the **global** insecure pattern: password-protected archive in one message, password in another on the **same channel**.
2. Why it fails: same-channel secrecy, blocks malware scanning, abused by malware loaders historically.
3. Prefer portal-style secure transfer: link + **recipient OTP**, expiry, and **revoke-after-missend**.

**Why this matters.** Sending a passworded ZIP and the password on the **same email channel** looks like encryption theater: anyone who compromised the mailbox gets both. Gateways cannot malware-scan encrypted archives, which is why loaders historically abused the pattern. Some regions nicknamed it “PPAP”; treat it as a **worldwide** anti-pattern, not a culture lesson. Secure Drop-style delivery exists because expiry, recipient proof, and **revoke-after-missend** beat hoping the wrong recipient deletes a ZIP.

**How it works.**

1. Sender **uploads** the file to object storage (not as a passworded ZIP in mail).
2. Service creates a share with **expiry** and a **hashed** recipient OTP (never store the OTP in plaintext).
3. Recipient opens the link and proves possession of the OTP; compare with a constant-time helper such as `hmac.compare_digest`.
4. On success, issue a **short-lived** download (see [presigned URL limits](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html)) and write an audit event.
5. On missend, operator **revokes** immediately so further downloads fail even if the URL was copied.
6. Prefer this over same-channel ZIP+password; S/MIME or portal encryption may fit when you need end-to-end crypto with different threat models. Upload risks still apply — skim [OWASP File Upload](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html).

```
Sender uploads → Secure Drop link + OTP challenge
Recipient OTP OK → download → audit
Missend → revoke → further downloads fail
```

### Worked example

Share + OTP verify (conceptual):

```json
{
  "share_id": "sd_77",
  "object_key": "secure/contract.pdf",
  "expires_at": "2026-11-14T18:00:00Z",
  "otp_hash": "sha256$…",
  "revoked_at": null
}
```

| Step | What happens |
|------|----------------|
| Email A | “Your file is ready: https://drop.example/sd_77” (no password in this channel ideal; OTP out-of-band or separate channel) |
| Recipient posts OTP | `compare_digest(hash(input), otp_hash)` → true |
| Download | short-lived URL; audit `{share_id, actor, at}` |
| Missend | `revoked_at = now` → next OTP/download → 403 |

Same-channel ZIP+password failure mode: mailbox compromise yields **both** ciphertext and key; scanners see opaque blobs.

**On the job.** Secure file transfer and email DLP reviews always ask: can you revoke after missend, and can scanners see content? Answering with portal+OTP+revoke (and knowing ZIP+password fails) is core email/cloud security literacy.

## Short intro

Some regions nicknamed this pattern “PPAP”; treat it as a **worldwide** anti-pattern, not a culture lesson. The insecure pattern is a password-protected archive in one message and the password in another on the **same channel** — same-channel secrecy, blocked malware scanning, and historical abuse by malware loaders. Secure Drop-style delivery converts attachments to expiring download URLs with recipient verification and revocation.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Passworded ZIP is encrypted email.”** Same-channel password delivery collapses the secrecy; it also blinds malware scanners.
- **“Store the OTP in the database in plaintext for support.”** Support can reset; a breach then reprints every code — hash and compare constant-time.
- **“Revoke is optional if expiry is short.”** Missend to the wrong person needs immediate kill; waiting for TTL is still a window of exposure.
- **“Long-lived presign to the object is fine after OTP.”** OTP then a week-long bearer URL undoes the control; keep post-auth fetches short-lived.

## Read these (verified)

1. [IIJ — PPAP report (English)](https://www.iij.ad.jp/en/dev/iir/pdf/iir_vol51_report_EN.pdf) — historical context
2. Module Secure Drop reading + object-storage [presigned URL docs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html) for mechanism limits
3. [OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html)

## Next step

Continue with the assignment (extend Secure Drop with recipient OTP + revoke). The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment.

# Reading — OWASP Top 10 / API Top 10 lab

## Learning objectives

1. Map findings from a **local-only** lab (OWASP Juice Shop or crAPI) to Top 10 / API Top 10.
2. Tie each finding to a MailGuard mitigation.
3. Add supply-chain CI hints: pip-audit, govulncheck, Dependabot, Syft SBOM.

**Why this matters.** Broken access control on hold release (IDOR / BOLA) ships silent cross-tenant leaks; injection and misconfiguration turn a rules API into an incident. Supply-chain CVEs in Python/Go deps ship unnoticed if CI never runs `pip-audit` / `govulncheck` or produces an **SBOM** (Software Bill of Materials). Labs without mitigations teach tourism; mapping to MailGuard teaches transfer. Corporate shared clusters are out of scope — unauthorized testing is not a learning feature.

**How it works.**

1. Reproduce a finding in a **local** Juice Shop / crAPI container only.
2. Label with Top 10 / API Top 10 (e.g. A01:2021 Broken Access Control; API1:2023 BOLA) — [OWASP Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/), [API Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/API-Security/).
3. Write the MailGuard fix (authz on hold id, input validation, least privilege) you can point to in-repo or in a test.
4. For supply chain: CI runs dependency audits ([pip-audit](https://pypi.org/project/pip-audit/), [govulncheck](https://go.dev/security/vuln/), Dependabot).
5. **Syft** (or similar) emits an **SBOM** so when a CVE drops you can answer “are we affected?” quickly ([Syft](https://github.com/anchore/syft)).

```
Local Juice Shop / crAPI → categorize → MailGuard mitigation
CI: pip-audit / govulncheck / Dependabot + Syft SBOM
```

### Worked example

Mapping + CI sketch:

| Lab finding | Category | MailGuard mitigation |
|-------------|----------|----------------------|
| Change `orderId` in URL, see another user’s order | API1:2023 BOLA | `assert hold.tenant_id == caller.tenant_id` before release; pytest for cross-tenant 403 |
| SQLi in search | A03:2021 Injection | Parameterized queries / ORM binds; never string-format SQL |
| Outdated `requests` with known CVE | Supply chain | `pip-audit` on PR + Syft SBOM artifact |

```yaml
# Conceptual CI fragment — why: fail the PR before a known-bad dep merges
- name: pip-audit
  run: pip-audit -r requirements.txt
- name: sbom
  run: syft dir:. -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
```

**On the job.** AppSec reviews of email/identity APIs start with access control and injection; platform teams expect SBOM + audit in CI. This module is that workflow in miniature — vendor-neutral.

## Short intro

Map local lab findings to named categories and ship mitigations you can show. Never attack systems you do not own. Local containers only.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“IDOR is only a web app bug.”** Hold release by id without tenant checks is the same BOLA class on an API.
- **“SBOM is paperwork.”** Without an inventory you cannot answer CVE blast-radius quickly; Syft (or similar) makes that queryable.
- **“Auditing deps once at kickoff is enough.”** New CVEs land weekly; run audits on every PR.
- **“The lab is the deliverable.”** Tourism without a MailGuard mitigation row fails the learning goal.

## Read these (verified)

1. [OWASP Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/)
2. [OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023)](https://owasp.org/API-Security/)
3. [pip-audit](https://pypi.org/project/pip-audit/) · [govulncheck](https://go.dev/security/vuln/) · [Syft](https://github.com/anchore/syft)

## Keep in mind

Never attack systems you do not own. Local containers only.

Continue with the assignment (`owasp_map` kata). The quiz is required after you attempt the assignment and tests.

# Reading — Security notes

## Learning objectives

1. Map findings to OWASP Top 10 / API Top 10 categories.
2. Tie each finding to a MailGuard mitigation you can show in-repo.
3. Stay ethical: local labs only; no attacks on systems you do not own.

**Why this matters.** Vague “we should be careful” does not survive a security review or an interview. Unmapped screenshots of a vulnerable lab do not prove you can fix a rules API. Without ethics boundaries, “practice” becomes unauthorized access. Security notes exist so each risk has a **name**, a **category**, and a **mitigation you can show** — the same discipline used in email, identity, and cloud SaaS engineering.

**How it works.**

1. Run an intentionally vulnerable app (e.g. OWASP Juice Shop) **only on localhost** ([Juice Shop getting started](https://pwning.owasp-juice.shop/companion-guide/latest/part1/running.html)).
2. Capture a finding with a short title and evidence (screenshot path / request id in your notes).
3. Label it with [OWASP Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/) or [API Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/API-Security/).
4. Map to a MailGuard mitigation you can show (authn, hold rules, least privilege, input validation).
5. Prefer five solid mapped notes over a laundry list of unrelated CVEs. Use [CWE Top 25](https://cwe.mitre.org/top25/) when you need finer defect vocabulary.

**OWASP Top 10 edition note.** Many labs and older notes still cite **2021** labels (e.g. A01 Broken Access Control, A03 Injection). The [OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/) list reorders and renames some categories — notably elevating **security misconfiguration**, introducing **software supply chain failures**, and **mishandling of exceptional conditions**. When you write notes, prefer **2025** category names when they fit; if you reuse a 2021 label from a lab guide, add a one-line mapping to 2025 so reviewers know you are current.

| 2021 (common in labs) | 2025 (prefer in new notes) |
|-----------------------|----------------------------|
| A01 Broken Access Control | A01 Broken Access Control |
| A05 Security Misconfiguration | A02 Security Misconfiguration |
| (supply chain often under A08/A06) | A03 Software Supply Chain Failures |
| A02 Cryptographic Failures | A04 Cryptographic Failures |
| A03 Injection | A05 Injection |
| A04 Insecure Design | A06 Insecure Design |
| A07 Identification and Authentication Failures | A07 Authentication Failures |
| A08 Software and Data Integrity Failures | A08 Software or Data Integrity Failures |
| A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures | A09 Security Logging and Alerting Failures |
| A10 SSRF (2021) | A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (2025; SSRF still matters — map via CWE when needed) |

```
Local lab finding → OWASP/API category → MailGuard mitigation → evidence
         ↑ never point tools at systems you do not own
```

One security-note row:

| Field | Example |
|-------|---------|
| Title | IDOR on order endpoint returns another user’s data |
| Category | API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) |
| MailGuard mitigation | Authz check: caller may only release/approve holds in their tenant; tests for cross-id 403 |
| Evidence | `notes/juice-idor.png` + request showing `/api/Orders/7` with victim id |
| Ethics | Local Docker only; no corporate/shared targets |

**On the job.** Writing actionable findings tied to product mitigations is how AppSec and product security communicate. Vendor-neutral OWASP/API Top 10 literacy transfers across gateways, admin APIs, and cloud identity surfaces.

## Short intro

Security notes turn vague “we should be careful” into **named risks + concrete fixes**. Use a local intentionally vulnerable app (e.g. OWASP Juice Shop) *only on localhost*, capture findings, and map them to MailGuard controls (authn, hold rules, least privilege, input validation).

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“A CVE list counts as notes.”** Without category + product mitigation, reviewers cannot act; map to MailGuard controls you can show.
- **“Screenshots alone prove understanding.”** Notes need the OWASP/API label and the fix path — tourism vs transfer.
- **“Shared staging is fine for practice.”** Unauthorized testing is out of scope; local containers only.
- **“Everything is A01.”** Mis-labeling hides the real fix (e.g. injection vs access control); use the right Top 10 / API row.
