# Docker primer

**Why this matters.** “Works on my machine” fails CI and demos. **Containers** package an app with its runtime so Module 12 image builds and Module 13 Compose demos look the same on every laptop. VMs can isolate too, but images are the usual unit security teams scan and CI rebuilds — baking secrets into layers is the anti-pattern to avoid.

**How it works.**

1. Write a **Dockerfile**: base image → install deps → copy app → set start command (each instruction is a **layer**).
2. `docker build` produces an **image** (layered filesystem + metadata).
3. `docker run` starts a **container** (running instance of that image).
4. **Compose** declares multi-service stacks (API + DB + mail dependencies) in YAML so `docker compose up` tells a story, not twelve manual steps.
5. Pass secrets at **runtime** (env / secret mounts) — never `ENV AWS_SECRET=…` in a layer. On the job, email/identity services ship as images from laptop → CI → cloud with the same artifact.

### Worked example

Layer idea for a tiny API image (conceptual):

```dockerfile
# Why: slim base keeps scan surface smaller
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
# Why: copy requirements first so dependency layer caches when only app code changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY app/ ./app/
# Why: secrets stay out of the image — inject at run time
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
```

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Docker is

**Docker** is a popular container toolchain (Engine/Desktop + CLI). **Docker Compose** orchestrates multiple containers locally.

## Why industry uses it

Identical artifacts from laptop → CI → cloud; fewer “missing library” incidents; security reviews can scan images. Local stacks approximate cloud topology without full accounts.

## Key concepts for Modules 12–13

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| Image vs container | Build once, run many |
| Dockerfile (awareness) | CI may build an image for a service you own |
| Compose services | MailGuard demo wiring |
| No secrets in images | Pass env at runtime; never bake cloud keys into layers |

## Install and run

- macOS / Windows: [Docker Desktop](https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/)
- Linux: [Docker Engine install](https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/)

**Check:** `docker --version` · `docker compose version` — **why:** confirm Engine + Compose plugins before Module 12/13, so “command not found” is not your first CI failure.

## Tiny hands-on example

```bash
# Why: prove the daemon runs without pulling a whole MailGuard stack yet
docker run --rm hello-world
```

**How:** The CLI pulls (if needed) a tiny image, starts a container, prints a confirmation message, and removes it (`--rm`) — the same pull/run lifecycle CI uses.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Containers are VMs.”** They share the host kernel; isolation model and patching story differ — still scan images.
- **“Bake credentials into the image for easier demos.”** Layers are extractable; use runtime env/secrets.
- **“Compose is only for production orchestration.”** Local Compose approximates topology; production may use other schedulers later (Module 13+).


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Docker Tutorial for Beginners](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fqMOX6JJhGo)**  
   Why it helps: images/containers before Compose demos.

## Official docs

1. [Docker overview](https://docs.docker.com/get-started/overview/)
2. [Docker Compose overview](https://docs.docker.com/compose/)
3. [Dockerfile reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`12-ci-aws`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# GitHub Actions primer

**Why this matters.** Reviews catch some bugs; **CI** catches the rest on every push. Module 12 expects a workflow that runs tests (and optionally builds an image) **without** committing cloud secrets. Long-lived cloud keys in git are a classic incident; **OIDC to cloud roles** is the usual modern alternative when you deploy.

**How it works.**

1. Add a YAML file under `.github/workflows/`.
2. Declare **when** to run (`on: pull_request`, `push`, etc.).
3. Define **jobs** on runners (`runs-on: ubuntu-latest`).
4. List **steps**: checkout → setup language → test (and later build/push image).
5. Keep secrets in the host’s secret store; prefer **OIDC to cloud roles** over long-lived keys when you deploy. On the job, email/identity/cloud security pipelines use the same pattern: PR checks, pinned actions, least-privileged tokens.

### Worked example

Minimal PR workflow (Module 12 expands this):

```yaml
# Conceptual minimal workflow — Module 12 expands this for real tests
name: primer-ci
on:
  pull_request:
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Why: prove the runner clone worked before real tests"
      # Later: pytest / go test / npm test — never commit cloud keys here
```

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What GitHub Actions is

**GitHub Actions** is GitHub’s integrated CI/CD: workflows as code beside your repository.

## Why industry uses it

Same git history as the product; PR checks block merges; matrix tests across languages. Security teams care that workflows are pinned, least-privileged, and secret-clean.

## Key concepts for Module 12

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| `on: pull_request` | Test before merge |
| jobs / steps | Clear failure logs |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` / secrets | Credentials never in YAML git history |
| Pinning actions (awareness) | Prefer immutable versions/SHAs in real pipelines |

## Install and run

1. A [GitHub](https://github.com/signup) account and a repo you control
2. No local daemon required — workflows run on GitHub-hosted runners (or self-hosted later)

Skim: [GitHub Actions documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/actions).

## Tiny hands-on example

Use the YAML in **Worked example** above. **How:** A PR event starts a VM, checks out your commit, then runs steps — replace the `echo` with `pytest` / `go test` / `npm test` in Module 12.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Put cloud access keys in the workflow YAML.”** Git history leaks them; use secrets + OIDC roles ([security hardening](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions)).
- **“`actions/checkout@main` is fine forever.”** Unpinned tags move; prefer version tags or SHAs in real pipelines.
- **“CI only needs to run on main.”** PR checks catch breakage before merge — Module 12 expects that habit.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[GitHub Actions Certification – Full Course to PASS the Exam](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tz7FsunBbfQ)** — freeCodeCamp / Andrew Brown  
   Why it helps: workflow YAML, jobs/steps, and secrets hygiene before Module 12.

## Official docs

1. [GitHub Actions docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions)
2. [Workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions)
3. [Security hardening for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/security-guides/security-hardening-for-github-actions)

---

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`12-ci-aws`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Reading — CI + cloud deploy

## Learning objectives

1. Run tests (and optionally build an image) on every PR/push.
2. Prefer federated OIDC roles over long-lived cloud keys in git.
3. Document a deploy path a stranger can follow.

**Why this matters.** Without Continuous Integration (**CI**), broken hold/allow rules and dependency regressions land on `main` and only surface in a demo or production. Long-lived cloud access keys in git (or even in Actions secrets) are a classic incident source: history, forks, and logs leak them, and rotation is slow. On the job, email and identity SaaS teams treat PR CI plus short-lived deploy credentials as table stakes — not optional polish.

**How it works.**

1. A workflow YAML under `.github/workflows/` declares **when** to run (`on: push` / `pull_request`) and which paths matter.
2. A runner checks out the PR tree, sets up the language toolchain, installs locked deps, and runs tests/lint — the contract must fail on stubs or broken rules.
3. Optionally a later job builds a container image from the same commit.
4. Deploy (if any) should exchange an OpenID Connect (**OIDC**) token for a cloud role instead of storing `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / secret keys.
5. The kata checks workflow hygiene: forbidden secret-like patterns and a required test job name.

```text
PR/push → runner checkout → install deps → pytest/lint
                ↓ (optional)
         OIDC assume-role → push image / update service
```

### Worked example

Copy ideas from [`../starter/ci-sample.yml`](../starter/ci-sample.yml) into a workflow you own — never commit live secrets.

```yaml
# Why path filters: skip unrelated modules so CI stays fast and cheap
name: sample-mailguard-ci
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["07-mailguard-api/**"]
jobs:
  unit-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4   # Why: runner starts empty; need the PR tree
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"    # Why: match the course Python pin
      - run: pip install -r 07-mailguard-api/requirements.txt  # Why: reproducible deps
      - run: pytest -q              # Why: contract must fail on stubs / broken rules
        working-directory: 07-mailguard-api
```

Prefer pinning third-party Actions by commit SHA in production (supply-chain hardening) — see [OWASP CI/CD Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/).

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Green CI means the deploy is safe.”** A unit-test job can pass while a later job still embeds static cloud keys or an over-broad deploy role — hygiene and OIDC are separate checks.
- **“Secrets in Actions are as good as OIDC.”** Repository secrets still leak via mis-logged env dumps, forks with write permissions, and compromised maintainers; rotation is slow compared to short-lived STS credentials.
- **“One workflow for the whole monorepo is fine.”** Without path filters, unrelated module noise burns minutes and hides real failures in the module you care about.
- **“`:latest` Action tags are fine.”** Mutable tags can change under you; pin by commit SHA so supply-chain reviews have a fixed digest.

## Short intro

Continuous Integration catches broken rules engines before merge. Cloud deploy should use short-lived credentials — GitHub Actions OIDC to a cloud role is the modern default. This module’s kata validates workflow hygiene helpers (detect forbidden secret patterns; require a test job name).


## Videos (verified)

1. **[GitHub Actions Certification – Full Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tz7FsunBbfQ)**  
   Why it helps: CI before OIDC-to-AWS deploys.

## Read these (verified)

1. [GitHub Actions — Workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions)
2. [GitHub Actions — OIDC with cloud providers](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/about-security-hardening-with-openid-connect)
3. [AWS — IAM best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)
4. [OWASP — CI/CD Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/)

## On the job

Identity and mail-security products ship often. Reviewers ask: “Did CI run the real tests?” and “Can this deploy role only touch the intended account/service?” Document the deploy path so on-call can replay it without tribal knowledge.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page.

# Reading — OIDC to AWS + ECS

## Learning objectives

1. Prefer **GitHub Actions OIDC** over long-lived `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` secrets.
2. Constrain role trust by `sub` (repo + ref).
3. Sketch an ECS Fargate deploy from CI.

**Why this matters.** Static AWS keys in repository secrets still leak via mis-logged env dumps, overly broad `permissions:`, and compromised maintainers. Federation with OpenID Connect (**OIDC**) issues **short-lived** credentials only when a trusted workflow runs. Without a tight trust policy (`sub` = this repo + `main`), any branch or fork workflow that can request the token becomes a cloud admin path. On the job, cloud-security reviews almost always ask how CI authenticates to the account that runs gateways, queues, and mail workers.

**How it works.**

1. Register GitHub’s OIDC issuer (`token.actions.githubusercontent.com`) as an Identity and Access Management (**IAM**) OIDC provider in AWS.
2. Create an IAM role whose trust policy allows `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` only when JWT claims match (commonly `sub` like `repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main`).
3. In Actions, set workflow `permissions:` so the job can mint an OIDC token — at minimum `id-token: write` (and usually `contents: read`). Without `id-token: write`, `configure-aws-credentials` cannot request the JWT.
4. Request an ID token, call AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (often via `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`), then push an image and update **Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS)** on **Fargate** (serverless tasks — no EC2 capacity management for the task itself).
5. Task definition pins image digest/tag, CPU/memory, and task role (least privilege to queues/buckets — not `AdministratorAccess`).

```text
GitHub job → OIDC JWT → AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
       → short-lived keys → ECR push / ECS service update
```

Trade-off vs long-lived keys: slightly more IAM/OIDC setup up front; far less key-rotation and leak blast radius. Trade-off vs “deploy from a laptop”: CI is auditable and repeatable; laptop tokens are not.

### Worked example

Trust fragment (conceptual — align with [`../starter/oidc-aws-ecs.tf.example`](../starter/oidc-aws-ecs.tf.example); do not apply blindly):

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
    "Condition": {
      "StringEquals": {
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com"
      },
      "StringLike": {
        "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main"
      }
    }
  }]
}
```

Example `sub` shapes (pin the tightest that fits the job):

| Intent | Example `sub` |
|--------|----------------|
| Production deploys from `main` only | `repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main` |
| A protected GitHub Environment | `repo:ORG/REPO:environment:production` |
| A single workflow file (when using `job_workflow_ref`) | `repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main` plus workflow filters in the job |

Minimal Actions permissions for the deploy job:

```yaml
permissions:
  id-token: write   # required to mint the OIDC JWT
  contents: read
```

Why constrain `sub` to `main`: a feature-branch or fork job must not assume the production deploy role. Why Terraform for the trust: the condition is a reviewable diff — console clicks drift.
### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“OIDC alone is least privilege.”** Federation only answers *who can assume*; the role’s **permission** policy still decides blast radius (queues, buckets, ECS update). An open trust + admin role is worse than static keys you knew to rotate.
- **“Any `repo:ORG/REPO:*` subject is fine.”** Wildcard refs let a PR from a compromised branch request the token; pin `ref:refs/heads/main` (or an environment-gated subject) for production deploys.
- **“Forks inherit the same deploy path.”** Pull requests from forks may still request OIDC depending on permissions — treat `pull_request_target` and write tokens as high risk; see GitHub’s OIDC hardening docs.
- **“Task role = deploy role.”** The CI deploy role updates the service; the **task** role is what the running mail worker uses — keep them separate so a compromised container cannot redeploy itself as admin.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[GitHub Actions Certification – Full Course](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tz7FsunBbfQ)**  
   Why it helps: OIDC permissions context in Actions.

## Read these (verified)

1. [GitHub Actions — OIDC with AWS](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services)
2. [AWS ECS on Fargate](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/AWS_Fargate.html)
3. [Terraform AWS provider — IAM OIDC](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/resources/iam_openid_connect_provider)

## Starter sketch (do not apply blindly)

See [`../starter/oidc-aws-ecs.tf.example`](../starter/oidc-aws-ecs.tf.example). Why Terraform here: the trust condition and role are reviewable diffs — console clicks drift. Why constrain `sub`: so a feature-branch job cannot assume the production deploy role.

## On the job

Mail/identity services often land on ECS/Kubernetes behind CI. Interview and incident questions converge on the same mechanism: **who can assume the deploy role, from which repo/ref, and what can that role do afterward?**

## Next step

`oidc_aws` kata + starter Terraform sketch → quiz.

# Reading — Practical secrets management

## Learning objectives

1. Prefer cloud **Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store** (or equivalent) over plaintext env in git.
2. Use **SOPS** (or similar) for encrypted-at-rest secrets in git when needed.
3. Plan **rotation** and least-privilege access to secret material.

**Why this matters.** Long-lived keys in repositories and chat logs are a top incident class for CI and cloud mail/identity workloads. Without a secrets store and rotation story, every laptop and Actions runner becomes a potential leak. On the job, reviewers ask where the secret lives, who can read it, and how often it rotates.

**How it works.**

1. Classify secrets (DB passwords, API tokens, webhook HMAC keys) — never commit real values.
2. Store production secrets in a managed store (**AWS Secrets Manager** or **SSM SecureString**).
3. Grant IAM roles (OIDC deploy role / task role) `GetSecretValue` / `ssm:GetParameter` on *named* resources only.
4. For git-held config, encrypt with **SOPS** + KMS/age so the ciphertext can live in-repo while keys stay in KMS.
5. Rotate on a schedule and on suspicion; update consumers via redeploy, not by editing old commits.

```text
Developer → (no plaintext in git)
CI OIDC role → Secrets Manager / SSM → runtime env / file mount
Optional: SOPS ciphertext in git → decrypt with KMS in CI
```

### Worked example

IAM fragment (conceptual — tighten ARNs to your account):

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["secretsmanager:GetSecretValue"],
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:secretsmanager:REGION:ACCOUNT:secret:mailguard/prod/*"]
}
```

SOPS sketch (do not commit real keys):

```bash
# Encrypt a values file for git (age or KMS backend in real labs)
sops --encrypt --age "$AGE_PUBLIC_KEY" secrets.enc.yaml > secrets.enc.yaml
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“`.env` in the repo is fine if gitignored on my machine.”** Teammates and CI will copy it; use examples with placeholders only.
- **“Base64 is encryption.”** Encoding is not confidentiality.
- **“Rotation means wait for expiry.”** Also rotate after personnel changes and suspected leaks.
- **“The deploy role can read all secrets.”** Scope to named prefixes; separate task role from deploy role.

## Read these (verified)

1. [AWS Secrets Manager](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/)
2. [AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)
3. [SOPS](https://github.com/getsops/sops)

## Next step

Document where *your* lab secrets live (local `.env` vs cloud store) in the Module 12/13 assignments — never paste real values into the course repo.

# Terraform / HCL primer

**Why this matters.** Clicking a cloud console does not review well and drifts silently. **Terraform** expresses buckets, IAM, and queues as code so Module 13 can `plan` changes before they hit a real account. On the job, reviewers read the plan — not a console screenshot — when mail/identity infra changes.

**How it works.**

1. Write **HCL** (HashiCorp Configuration Language) describing desired resources (providers + `resource` blocks).
2. Run `terraform init` to download providers declared in the config.
3. Run `terraform plan` to see the create/update/destroy diff **before** any mutation.
4. Run `terraform apply` only when the plan is intentional; **state** maps real IDs back to your config — and must not be committed when it contains secrets.

```text
HCL config → init (providers) → plan (diff) → apply (cloud APIs) → state
```

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Terraform is

**Terraform** is an infrastructure-as-code tool. Config files commonly use the `.tf` extension and HCL syntax.

## Why industry uses it

Reviewable infra diffs, repeatable environments, and clearer least-privilege IAM stories. Security reviews often start from the plan output, not from a console screenshot.

## Key concepts for Module 13

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| Providers | Talk to AWS (or others) via APIs |
| Resources | Bucket, queue, IAM policy blocks |
| `plan` vs `apply` | See blast radius before change |
| Remote state (awareness) | Team sharing without git-stored secrets |

## Install and run

1. [Terraform install](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install)
2. Check: `terraform version`

You do not need cloud credentials for this primer — Module 13 documents plan against *your* resources or local stand-ins.

## Tiny hands-on example

### Worked example

Local-only HCL (no cloud account) so `plan` still teaches blast-radius review:

```hcl
# Conceptual — do not apply without credentials and a backend you own
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
}

# Why: a local_file resource proves HCL parses without a cloud account
resource "local_file" "primer" {
  filename = "${path.module}/primer-note.txt"
  content  = "mailguard terraform primer\n"
}
```

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/mg-tf-primer && cd /tmp/mg-tf-primer
# Why /tmp: keep the primer throwaway; do not mix with real state
# paste the HCL into main.tf, then:
terraform init   # Why: download providers declared in the config
terraform plan   # Why: see the diff before any apply
```

**How:** `init` installs providers; `plan` shows it would create a local file — same discipline as planning IAM/bucket changes later.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“`plan` green means production is safe.”** Plan only shows *this* config’s diff; it does not prove least privilege, public-access blocks, or that remote state is locked down.
- **“Commit `terraform.tfstate` for the team.”** State often holds secrets and resource IDs — use a remote backend with access control, not git history.
- **“Skip plan and just `apply -auto-approve`.”** You lose the blast-radius review that makes Terraform worth using for mail/identity IAM.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Learn Terraform (and AWS) by Building a Dev Environment](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iRaai1IBlB0)** — freeCodeCamp  
   Why it helps: plan/apply mental model before Module 13.

## Official docs

1. [Terraform intro](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/intro)
2. [Terraform install](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install)
3. [HCL language resources](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language)

---

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`13-infra`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Reading — Cloud IAM & misconfiguration posture

## Learning objectives

1. Explain Identity and Access Management (**IAM**) as identities + permissions + resources.
2. Apply a least-privilege review to a MailGuard bucket/queue role.
3. Describe shared responsibility at a high level (provider secures cloud; you secure *in* cloud).

**Why this matters.** Broken cloud IAM — public storage, wildcard `*` actions, root-like keys in CI — causes real incidents more often than exotic crypto bugs. Hold queues, Secure Drop objects, and worker roles all inherit whatever permissions you grant. Without a posture checklist, Terraform/`apply` can look “green” while leaving world-readable buckets or admin-equivalent runtime roles. On the job, cloud-security and identity teams review IAM before they review application code.

**How it works.**

1. IAM binds **principals** (users, roles, services) to **actions** on **resources** via policies.
2. Least privilege means the MailGuard API/worker role can read/write only the buckets and queues it needs — not `s3:*` / `iam:*` on `*`.
3. Shared responsibility: the provider secures the platform (datacenters, hypervisor, managed control planes); you secure accounts, identities, network exposure, encryption choices, and data *in* the cloud.
4. Practice the review against Module 13 Terraform/Compose (and the Module 12 CI deploy identity) — National Institute of Standards and Technology (**NIST**) vocabulary welcome; no cert wall.

```text
Identity (role) → Policy (Allow/Deny actions) → Resource (bucket/queue)
                      ↑
              CI OIDC / app runtime assumes this role
```

Trade-offs: broad roles ship features faster and explode blast radius; narrow roles need more planning when new queues appear. Prefer plan-time checks over “we’ll tighten later.”

### Worked example

Runtime role for a hold-queue worker (conceptual — tighten ARNs to your account):

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "HoldQueueOnly",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": [
      "sqs:ReceiveMessage",
      "sqs:DeleteMessage",
      "sqs:GetQueueAttributes"
    ],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:REGION:ACCOUNT:mailguard-hold"
  }]
}
```

Why not `sqs:*` on `*`: a compromised worker should not purge unrelated queues or create new ones. Pair with bucket **Block Public Access** on and no `Principal: "*"` object policies.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Terraform applied cleanly, so IAM is fine.”** Apply success only means the API accepted the config — public buckets and `Action: "*"` still plan “green.”
- **“Shared responsibility means the cloud vendor owns my data exposure.”** The provider secures the *cloud*; you secure identities, policies, and data *in* the cloud.
- **“CI deploy role and app runtime role can be the same admin role.”** Separate them: deploy updates services; runtime talks to queues/buckets — compromise of the API process must not rewrite IAM.
- **“We’ll tighten wildcards after launch.”** Wildcard permissions rarely shrink later; posture checks belong in `plan`/CI, not a backlog ticket.

## Short intro

Broken cloud IAM (public storage, wildcard `*` actions, root-like keys in CI) causes real incidents more often than exotic crypto bugs. This reading prepares a checklist you will run against your Module 13 Terraform/Compose (and the Module 12 CI deploy identity) — National Institute of Standards and Technology (**NIST**) vocabulary welcome; no cert wall.

## Videos (verified)

1. Prefer [AWS IAM User Guide — Introduction](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction.html) first (authoritative). Optional video: search freeCodeCamp / AWS “IAM explained” and confirm the current title before watching.  
   Why it helps: users/roles/policies mental model.

2. Optional: search “cloud misconfiguration public S3” conference talks for incident stories — treat as case studies, not product ads.

Prefer official IAM docs below if videos move.

## Annotated posture moves

| Check | Why that way |
|-------|----------------|
| No long-lived keys in git | History/forks leak; prefer OIDC / short-lived creds |
| Bucket Block Public Access on | Default-deny stops accidental `Principal: "*"` exposure |
| Runtime role ≠ admin | Compromise of the API process should not rewrite IAM |
| Secrets in a store / env, not state jokes | Terraform state can contain sensitive values — lock down remote state |

Example mindset for a lab-only misconfig: turn Block Public Access off and add a public bucket policy — then detect with `terraform plan`, a policy scanner, or a Scout/Prowler-class tool, and remediate. Why intentionally break a *lab* bucket: muscle memory for detection before production.

## Read these (verified)

1. [AWS IAM — User guide (roles & policies)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/introduction.html) — core model.
2. [AWS — Security best practices in IAM](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html)
3. [CIS Amazon Web Services Foundations Benchmark](https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/amazon_web_services) — awareness of common hardened baselines (download may require form; skim public summaries OK).
4. [NIST CSF overview](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework) — identify/protect framing without exam prep.
5. [OWASP — Cloud Native Application Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/projects/cloud-native-application-security-top-10) — cloud-native risks adjacent to IAM/misconfig posture (also see [CI/CD Security Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-10-ci-cd-security-risks/)).

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page.

## Learning objectives

1. Build local Docker images for the API (`07`) and worker (`09`).
2. Wire those tags into Module 13’s Compose story (`mailguard-api:local`).
3. Keep secrets out of image layers.

**Why this matters.** Compose referencing `mailguard-api:local` fails until you build that tag. Without a Dockerfile, “compose up demos the MailGuard story” stays aspirational. On the job, the same habit — pin tags, pass secrets at runtime — is how email/identity services move from laptop demos to CI.

**How it works.**

1. Build the API image from Module 07’s Dockerfile.
2. Build the worker image from Module 09’s Dockerfile.
3. Point Compose `image:` fields at those local tags (or `build:` contexts).
4. Confirm `/healthz` on the API container.

```text
docker build (07) → mailguard-api:local
docker build (09) → mailguard-worker:local
compose up → api + db (+ optional queue) → curl /healthz
```

### Worked example

```bash
# From repo root

docker build -t mailguard-worker:local ./09-mailguard-worker
cd 13-infra/starter && docker compose up -d
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/healthz
# → {"status":"ok"}
```

# Reading — Terraform plan walkthrough

## Learning objectives

1. Explain **why** `terraform plan` exists before any cloud mutation.
2. Walk **how** init → validate → plan → (optional) apply works for MailGuard storage/queue/IAM.
3. Spot dangerous plan diffs (public bucket, wildcard IAM) before you type `yes`.

**Why this matters.** Clicking “create bucket” in a console does not produce a reviewable diff. Hold-queue workers and Secure Drop objects inherit whatever Identity and Access Management (**IAM**) you attach; a bad apply can leave a public bucket or an admin-equivalent role. `terraform plan` shows the intended create/update/destroy set so a reviewer can reject wildcards *before* the account changes. On the job, platform and security teams read the plan — not a console screenshot — when mail/identity infra changes.

**How it works.**

1. **Write** HCL for provider, (optional) remote backend, and resources (see [`../starter/main.tf.example`](../starter/main.tf.example)).
2. **`terraform init`** downloads providers and configures the backend (local by default; remote S3+lock when uncommented).
3. **`terraform validate`** checks syntax/types without talking to the cloud APIs for mutations.
4. **`terraform plan`** refreshes state, computes a diff, and prints `+` / `~` / `-` actions — still no apply.
5. Only if the plan is least-privilege and Block Public Access is on, run **`terraform apply`** (or apply a saved plan file).
6. Re-run plan after edits; treat unexpected destroys as stop-the-line.

```text
HCL → init (providers/backend) → validate → plan (diff) → apply (mutate)
                                      ↑
                         reject wildcards / public exposure here
```

Trade-off: local state is simplest for a solo lab and easy to lose or leak; remote state with locking is safer for teams but needs a bootstrapped bucket/table. Prefer plan-time review over “apply and fix later.”

### Worked example

Lab-safe walkthrough using the starter example (copy aside; do not commit secrets or real account IDs):

```bash
# Why a private copy: keep course git clean of terraform.tfstate and *.tfvars secrets
cp -r 13-infra/starter /tmp/mailguard-tf && cd /tmp/mailguard-tf
cp main.tf.example main.tf

# Why init first: providers are not vendored in the repo
terraform init

# Why validate before plan: catch typos without needing cloud credentials
terraform validate

# Why pass -var on the CLI for labs: avoids committing tfvars with account specifics
terraform plan \
  -var='bucket_name=mailguard-secure-drop-lab-UNIQUE' \
  -var='environment=dev'

# Read the plan:
#   + aws_s3_bucket.secure_drop
#   + aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.secure_drop   # must stay true/true/true/true
#   + aws_sqs_queue.hold
#   + aws_iam_role.mailguard_runtime
#   + aws_iam_role_policy.mailguard_runtime           # check Action lists — no "*"
```

Least-privilege IAM shape (also in [`../starter/iam_policy_mailguard.json`](../starter/iam_policy_mailguard.json)):

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": ["sqs:ReceiveMessage", "sqs:DeleteMessage", "sqs:GetQueueAttributes"],
  "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:REGION:ACCOUNT_ID:mailguard-hold-dev"
}
```

Why not `sqs:*` on `*`: a compromised worker should not purge unrelated queues. Pair with S3 Block Public Access on.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Plan is optional if I trust my HCL.”** Apply without plan skips the human diff review — wildcards and public policies still “succeed.”
- **“Terraform applied cleanly, so IAM is fine.”** Apply success only means the API accepted the config; posture is a separate checklist ([`cloud_iam_posture.md`](./cloud_iam_posture.md)).
- **“Commit terraform.tfstate for the team.”** State can hold sensitive attributes; use a remote backend with encryption + locking, never git.
- **“`Action: \"*\"` is fine for a weekend lab role.”** Lab habits leak into prod; start narrow and add statements when a new queue appears.
- **“Uncomment the S3 backend with placeholder names and apply.”** Backend config must point at buckets/tables *you* own — placeholders fail loudly; never paste real access keys into HCL.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Terraform — Command: plan](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan)
2. [Terraform — Backend: S3](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/backend/s3)
3. [AWS IAM — Policies and permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html)
4. [Amazon S3 — Blocking public access](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/access-control-block-public-access.html)

## Next step

Continue with the [cloud IAM posture assignment](../assignments/cloud_iam_posture.md) against *your* plan output.

# Kubernetes YAML primer

**Why this matters.** Compose is enough for a laptop story; **Kubernetes** is how many teams run the same containers with health probes, restarts, and resource requests. Module 14 puts MailGuard’s shape on kind/minikube before GitOps in Module 16. On the job, API/worker pods for mail and identity services live here — probes and requests are the difference between a quiet restart and a silent outage.

**How it works.**

1. Declare desired state in **YAML** (Deployment, Service, etc.).
2. Apply with **kubectl**; the control plane reconciles actual pods toward that state.
3. A **Deployment** keeps N replicas from a Pod template; a **Service** gives stable networking to matching pods.
4. **kind**/**minikube** give you a local cluster without a cloud bill — Module 14 adds probes and resource requests on this shape.

```text
YAML apply → API server → controllers → Pods running
                ↑ kubectl is the CLI to that API
```

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

---

## What Kubernetes YAML is

**Kubernetes** schedules containers across nodes. You rarely “SSH and start a process” — you apply manifests that describe replicas, probes, and networking.

## Why industry uses it

Self-healing workloads, consistent deploy APIs across clouds, and a clear path to policy/GitOps. Security teams care about resource limits, probes, and later NetworkPolicy/admission controls.

## Key concepts for Module 14

| Concept | Why you care |
|---------|----------------|
| Pod | Smallest runnable unit (usually one app container) |
| Deployment | Keeps N replicas; rolling updates |
| Service | Stable networking to pods |
| Probes / requests | Readiness and CPU/memory — Module 14 requires these |

## Install and run

1. [kubectl install](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/)
2. Cluster tools wait for Module 14: [kind](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/) or [minikube](https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/docs/start/)

**Check now:** `kubectl version --client`  
Why `--client` only: confirm the CLI is installed without needing a cluster API yet (Module 14 starts the cluster).

## Tiny hands-on example

### Worked example

Minimal Deployment shape (apply only inside Module 14’s cluster):

```yaml
# Conceptual snippet — apply only inside Module 14's cluster
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mailguard-api
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mailguard-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: mailguard-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: example/mailguard-api:primer
          # Why: probes come next in Module 14 — without them traffic may hit a dead process
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
```

**How:** The Deployment names a Pod template; Kubernetes creates pods matching the selector — Module 14 adds probes and resource requests on top of this shape.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“A Pod is the durable unit.”** Pods are ephemeral; Deployments (or similar controllers) recreate them — design for restarts.
- **“kubectl apply once and you’re done.”** Without probes/requests (Module 14) and later GitOps/policy (Module 16), laptop apply drifts from what production needs.
- **“Compose knowledge transfers 1:1.”** Labels/selectors and Service DNS are the Kubernetes networking contract — missing `matchLabels` means zero traffic.


## Videos (verified)

   Why it helps: Pod/Deployment/Service literacy.

## Official docs

2. [Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)

## Done when

You can explain **why** this tool shows up on the MailGuard path and **how** to install/run the tiny example. Mark this primer complete on the site, then continue to the next module (`14-k8s-local`).

This primer has **no** assignment, quiz, or download pack.

# Reading — kind + Helm/Kustomize deepen

## Learning objectives

1. Run the app on kind/minikube with probes and requests.
2. Prefer Helm or Kustomize overlays for env differences.
3. Name managed Kubernetes + GitOps as the production next step.

**Why this matters.** Copy-pasting raw YAML per environment (dev/stage/prod) drifts: one cluster gets probes, another does not. **Helm** charts and **Kustomize** overlays keep a shared base and patch only what must change (replicas, image tag, ingress host). Without that discipline, “works on kind” silently differs from “what we shipped.” On the job, platform teams expect env overlays — and then GitOps (Module 16) to sync them.

**How it works.**

1. Keep **base** manifests for Deployment/Service/probes shared across environments.
2. Express env diffs with **Helm** `values.yaml` (templates) or **Kustomize** overlays (patches).
3. **Render** first (`helm template` / `kustomize build`) so template errors fail before the cluster mutates.
4. Install into the local cluster and verify Ready pods.
5. Later: managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS-class) replaces the DIY control plane; a pull agent (Argo CD-class) replaces laptop `kubectl apply`.

```text
base YAML → Helm values / Kustomize overlay → rendered manifests → cluster
```

Trade-off: raw YAML is easiest to read for one file; overlays scale when env diffs grow. Prefer overlays over forked copies.

### Worked example

Dev vs prod image tag via Helm values (conceptual):

```yaml
# values-dev.yaml
image:
  repository: mailguard-api
  tag: "local"          # Why pin: reproducible restarts on kind
replicaCount: 1
```

```bash
# Why render before install: catch template errors without mutating the cluster
helm template myapp ./chart -f values-dev.yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# Kustomize (shipped under starter/ — preferred in this module):
kubectl kustomize starter/kustomize/overlays/dev   # Why: inspect rendered YAML first
kubectl apply -k starter/kustomize/overlays/dev    # Why -k: build overlay then apply

# kind load still required when the overlay pins mailguard-api:local
docker build -t mailguard-api:local ../07-mailguard-api
kind load docker-image mailguard-api:local
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Fork the whole YAML tree per env.”** Drift is inevitable — overlays/charts exist so probes and security fields stay in one base.
- **“Helm install without template is faster.”** Rendering first catches missing values and bad YAML before you break the cluster.
- **“Overlays replace GitOps.”** Env packaging is necessary but not sufficient; Module 16 adds sync + policy so prod is not another laptop apply.
- **“`:latest` in values is fine for prod.”** Mutable tags make rollbacks and incident timelines guesswork — pin digests or immutable tags.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Helm Package Manager for Kubernetes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fy8-G5H80uQ)**  
   Why it helps: charts vs overlays literacy.

## Read these (verified)

2. [Helm](https://helm.sh/docs/) / [Kustomize](https://kustomize.io/)

# Reading — K8s local

## Learning objectives

1. Run a Deployment + Service on kind or minikube.
2. Add liveness/readiness probes and CPU/memory requests.
3. Know what you have not automated yet (GitOps, policy).

**Why this matters.** A container that “runs on my laptop” is not enough for a mail/identity API: processes die, dependencies hang, and noisy neighbors steal memory. Without readiness probes, Services send traffic to pods that are not ready; without resource requests, the scheduler cannot place work fairly and a leak can OOM-kill neighbors. On the job, platform and security reviews ask for probes, requests/limits, and an honest gap list (no GitOps yet, no NetworkPolicy yet) before calling a chart “production-shaped.”

**How it works.**

1. Create a local cluster (**kind** or **minikube**).
2. Apply YAML for a **Deployment** (Pod template + replica controller) and a **Service** (stable virtual IP/DNS to matching pods).
3. The kubelet runs **probes**: readiness gates Service endpoints; liveness triggers restarts of stuck processes.
4. Set **requests** so the scheduler knows how much CPU/memory the pod needs.
5. Document gaps honestly — you are not yet doing pull-based GitOps or admission policy (Module 16).

```text
kubectl apply → API server → controllers create Pods
Pods pass readiness → Endpoints populate → Service routes traffic
liveness fail → kubelet restarts container
```

### Worked example

Probe + requests snippet aligned with [`../starter/deployment.yaml`](../starter/deployment.yaml):

```yaml
containers:
  - name: api
    image: mailguard-api:local   # Why pin a tag: :latest restarts are not reproducible
    ports:
      - containerPort: 8000
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8000 }
      initialDelaySeconds: 3
      periodSeconds: 5
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8000 }
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 10
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi }
```

```bash
# Why kind/minikube: practice the API without a cloud bill
kind create cluster   # or: minikube start

# --- kind load step (required for local tags) ---
# Why: kind nodes do not see images that only exist in your host Docker daemon.
# Build the Module 07 image, then import it into the kind cluster before apply.
docker build -t mailguard-api:local ../07-mailguard-api
kind load docker-image mailguard-api:local
# How it works: kind copies the image layers into each node’s container runtime
# so kubelet can start pods with image: mailguard-api:local (no registry pull).

kubectl apply -f starter/deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f starter/service.yaml
# Or Kustomize overlay (shared base + env patches):
# kubectl apply -k starter/kustomize/overlays/dev
kubectl get pods,svc   # Why: confirm Ready + ClusterIP before claiming the demo works
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Liveness and readiness are interchangeable.”** Readiness removes traffic until ready; liveness **restarts** a stuck process. Using liveness for slow startups can crash-loop a healthy app.
- **“No requests is fine on a laptop cluster.”** Without requests the scheduler cannot place fairly; a leak can OOM-kill neighbors — Module 14 checks expect requests.
- **“Pods Running means users are served.”** `Running` ≠ Ready; until readiness passes, the Service may have empty Endpoints.
- **“This is production GitOps.”** Laptop `kubectl apply` is practice — sync agents and policy come in Module 16; keep claims proportional.
- **“`docker build` is enough for kind.”** Without `kind load docker-image` (or a registry the nodes can pull), pods stay `ImagePullBackOff` for `:local` tags.

## Short intro

Containers need orchestration for restarts, probes, and resource requests. Start local (kind/minikube), keep manifests small, and document gaps honestly.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Kubernetes Course - Full Beginners Tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d6WC5n9G_sM)**  
   Why it helps: kind/minikube backdrop.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Kubernetes — Deployments](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/)
2. [Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/)
3. [kind — Quick Start](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/docs/user/quick-start/)
4. [Resource requests and limits](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/)

## On the job

Email gateways and identity sidecars often run as Deployments. Knowing **how** probes and requests behave under failure is more valuable than memorizing every kubectl flag.

## Starter layout

| Path | Role |
|------|------|
| [`../starter/deployment.yaml`](../starter/deployment.yaml) | Standalone Deployment (probes + requests) |
| [`../starter/service.yaml`](../starter/service.yaml) | ClusterIP Service for `mailguard-api` |
| [`../starter/kustomize/`](../starter/kustomize/) | Base + `overlays/dev` for env patches |

## Next step

Continue with the [assignment](../assignments/k8s_local.md). For overlays/Helm deepen, see [`k8s_helm_deepen.md`](./k8s_helm_deepen.md).

# Reading — Incident response & detection

## Learning objectives

1. Apply **NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3** as a **CSF 2.0** community profile — not the Rev. 2 four-phase checklist alone.
2. Triage identity alerts (e.g. impossible travel) at a conceptual level.
3. Write a **blameless English postmortem** (impact, timeline, actions) — no secondary-language summary line required.

**Why this matters.** Hold-queue privacy incidents, missend+revoke events, and admin “impossible travel” alerts do not wait for a perfect runbook. Without a shared vocabulary, teams skip preparation work under **Govern / Identify / Protect**, thrash during **Respond**, and write blame-heavy writeups that do not prevent recurrence. On the job, email and identity security teams are expected to triage signals quickly, contain access, and document impact in clear English for legal/privacy partners.

**How it works.** National Institute of Standards and Technology (**NIST**) [SP 800-61r3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final) (April 2025) is titled as a **Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 Community Profile**. It embeds incident response across CSF 2.0 functions rather than replacing them with a standalone four-box lifecycle.

**Historical note (Rev. 2):** SP 800-61 Rev. 2 taught a familiar four-phase story — *Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment, Eradication & Recovery → Post-Incident Activity*. That language still appears in many runbooks; treat it as history when reading older materials.

**CSF 2.0 functions (current r3 framing):**

| CSF 2.0 function | IR-oriented focus for MailGuard-shaped events |
|------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| **Govern** | Roles, policies, privacy duties for held content |
| **Identify** | Assets (hold queue, admin IdP, keys) and risk context |
| **Protect** | Hardening, least privilege, logging readiness before incidents |
| **Detect** | Alerts (impossible travel, anomalous hold access) |
| **Respond** | Contain sessions/keys, freeze risky releases, communicate |
| **Recover** | Restore service under least privilege; improve detections |

For MailGuard-shaped events:

1. **Govern / Identify / Protect** — logging, roles, contacts, SLIs that show hold/release health (the “preparation” work Rev. 2 named explicitly).
2. **Detect** — alert on anomalous admin sign-in (e.g. impossible travel) or sudden hold-queue access.
3. **Respond** — revoke sessions/keys, freeze risky releases, limit who can read held content; eradicate the cause (stolen token, misconfig).
4. **Recover** — restore service under least privilege; blameless postmortem with impact, timeline, root causes, and owners for actions.

```text
Signal → Detect/triage → Respond (contain + eradicate)
      → Recover service → postmortem + Govern/Protect improvements
```

Trade-off: aggressive auto-lockouts reduce attacker dwell time but can lock out legitimate travelers — document human review paths. Keep Endpoint Detection and Response (**EDR**) / Managed Detection and Response (**MDR**) discussion vendor-neutral.

### Worked example

Impossible-travel triage sketch (conceptual):

```text
Alert: admin Ada signed in from Region A at 10:00 UTC and Region B at 10:25 UTC
1. Detect — confirm IdP sign-in logs; check VPN/known travel; score severity
2. Respond — revoke active sessions / refresh tokens; temp step-up MFA; freeze hold-queue export
3. Notify — if held mail may contain personal data, loop privacy/security (why: transfer + access duties)
4. Recover / Govern — timeline, impact (accounts/queues touched), detection gap, owners + due dates
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“800-61r3 is still the Rev. 2 four phases.”** Rev. 3 is a CSF 2.0 profile — map Detect / Respond / Recover (with Govern / Identify / Protect for readiness), and cite Rev. 2 only as historical language.
- **“Jump straight to eradication.”** Without containment first, stolen sessions keep reading hold queues while you “investigate.”
- **“Auto-lockout every impossible-travel alert.”** Legitimate travel and VPN exit nodes create false positives — document human review so on-call does not disable detection.
- **“Postmortem = name who clicked.”** Blame-heavy writeups do not prevent recurrence; fix logging, access, and playbooks ([NIST SP 800-61r3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final)).
- **“EDR/MDR brand names are the course.”** Concepts matter; stay vendor-neutral and keep detection artifacts in English.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[NIST Cybersecurity Framework overview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S9KxqZ8q1kY)**  
   Why it helps: CSF backdrop for 800-61r3.

## Keep in mind

EDR/MDR are concepts here — stay vendor-neutral. Detection content is English-only for course artifacts.

## Read these (verified)

1. [NIST SP 800-61r3](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final) (CSF 2.0 Community Profile)
2. [NIST CSF 2.0](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework)
3. Existing module SRE / golden signals reading
4. Cloud identity sign-in log docs for the IdP you use in lab

## On the job

Interview and IR drills ask for **how** you decide severity and **why** you notify privacy/security stakeholders when held mail may contain personal data — not just which button you clicked in a vendor console.

## Next step

`ir_triage` kata → assignment → quiz.

# Reading — OpenTelemetry + Prometheus lab

## Learning objectives

1. Expose at least one **Prometheus** metric from a tiny MailGuard-shaped API.
2. Explain **how** scrape configs and `/metrics` cooperate (and where an OpenTelemetry collector fits).
3. Map golden signals (traffic, errors, latency, saturation) to hold-pipeline counters/histograms.

**Why this matters.** Logs alone do not tell you whether hold-enqueue latency is burning an error budget. Metrics give aggregatable SLI events; traces explain a single slow release. Without a local scrape path, “we will add observability later” stays aspirational. On the job, email/identity on-call expects named counters and latency histograms before paging on vibes.

**How it works.**

1. The app increments **counters** / observes **histograms** on the evaluate path.
2. It exposes Prometheus text format at **`GET /metrics`**.
3. **Prometheus** scrapes that path on an interval (see `starter/prometheus/prometheus.yml`).
4. Optionally, an **OpenTelemetry (OTel) collector** receives OTLP and re-exports metrics (compose service `otel-collector`) — useful when many languages speak OTLP but you still want Prometheus.
5. You query Prometheus (`rate()`, histograms) and feed SLI/SLO math from Module 15’s SRE reading.

```text
evaluate() → counters/histograms → /metrics
                                      ↑ scrape
                                 Prometheus ← (optional) OTel collector ← OTLP
```

Trade-off: app-exposed `/metrics` is the simplest lab; a collector adds a hop but standardizes export across services. Prefer working scrapes over a perfect topology diagram.

### Worked example

```bash
cd 15-observability/starter
docker compose -f otel-compose.yml up --build

# Why hit evaluate: create time series before opening the UI
curl -s -X POST localhost:8000/evaluate -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":"urgent wire transfer"}'
curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep mailguard_holds_total

# Prometheus UI: http://localhost:9090
# Example query: rate(mailguard_holds_total[1m])
```

Metric names in [`../starter/app/main.py`](../starter/app/main.py):

| Metric | Golden signal |
|--------|----------------|
| `mailguard_holds_total{decision=...}` | Traffic (hold/allow volume) |
| `mailguard_evaluate_errors_total` | Errors |
| `mailguard_evaluate_seconds` | Latency |

Saturation (queue depth) belongs on the worker/SQS side — document it even if this lab stub does not emit it yet.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Dashboards without scrape targets are observability.”** If Prometheus has no job for the API, charts are empty — verify `/metrics` and `up == 1` first.
- **“Traces replace metrics for SLOs.”** Traces explain individuals; SLOs need aggregatable good/bad events (usually metrics).
- **“Export every debug gauge.”** High-cardinality labels (`msg_id`, emails) explode series cost — label by decision/rule class, not message id.
- **“OTel collector alone scrapes the app.”** In this compose file the collector receives OTLP; Prometheus still scrapes `/metrics` (and optionally the collector’s exporter). Wire an OTLP SDK when you leave the lab stub.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Prometheus — Getting started](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/getting_started/)
2. [OpenTelemetry — Collector](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/collector/)
3. [Prometheus Python client](https://prometheus.github.io/client_python/)
4. [Google SRE — Golden signals](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/)

## Next step

Run the compose lab, then continue with the [SRE basics assignment](../assignments/sre_basics.md) using real series from `/metrics`.

# Reading — SRE basics (SLI / SLO / error budgets / postmortem)

## Learning objectives

1. Define **SLI**, **SLO**, and **error budget** and relate them to MailGuard’s hold pipeline.
2. Prefer user-visible indicators (e.g. successful release within N seconds) over vanity metrics.
3. Write a short **blameless postmortem** from telemetry.

**Why this matters.** Observability without objectives becomes dashboard tourism: lots of charts, no decision rule. When hold enqueue or release latency silently degrades, operators and users notice before vanity counters do. Site Reliability Engineering (**SRE**) popularized measuring reliability with Service Level Indicators (**SLI**s), targeting them with Service Level Objectives (**SLO**s), and spending **error budgets** when reality misses the target — then learning via postmortems. On the job, email/identity on-call uses those budgets to choose “ship features” vs “freeze and harden.”

**How it works.**

1. Pick user-visible **SLIs** (e.g. fraction of release API calls completing in < 30s; hold-enqueue success rate).
2. Set an **SLO** over a window (e.g. 99% over 28 days).
3. The **error budget** is the allowed failure fraction (here ~1%). Burn it → pause risky launches; recover budget → resume feature work.
4. Emit signals (metrics/traces/logs via OpenTelemetry-class tooling) so you can prove burn and write a **blameless** postmortem (systems/process fixes, not blame).

```text
User journey → SLI events (good/bad) → SLO compliance → error budget left?
                                                      ↓ burned
                                            reliability work / freeze
```

Trade-off: tight SLOs create more freezes; loose SLOs hide user pain. Prefer fewer meaningful SLIs over dozens of vanity gauges.

### Worked example

Error-budget burn for a release SLI (see [Google SRE Book — Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/)):

```text
SLO: 99% of releases complete in < 30s over 28 days
Error budget: 1% of events may be slow/fail

Suppose 10_000 release attempts in the window:
  Budget = 0.01 × 10_000 = 100 bad events
  Observed bad = 40
  Budget remaining = 60% → feature work OK
  If bad jumps to 120 → budget burned → freeze risky launches, fix reliability
```

```text
# Why count good/bad release events — not “CPU looks fine”:
release_success{le="30s"} / release_attempts
```

Alert on **burn rate over a window**, not every single failure — why: avoid pager fatigue that trains people to ignore real incidents.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“CPU/memory dashboards are SLIs.”** SLIs measure *user-visible* success; vanity gauges do not tell you whether to freeze a release.
- **“Alert on every failed release.”** Single-event pages burn attention; burn-rate alerts over a window distinguish noise from budget threat.
- **“Error budget is a stick for blameless people.”** Budgets are a *policy* for risk vs reliability; postmortems fix systems/process, not individuals ([Postmortem Culture](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/)).
- **“Tighter SLO is always better.”** Unrealistic targets force permanent freezes or silent SLO lies — pick targets you can measure and act on.

## Short intro

Observability without objectives becomes dashboard tourism. Site Reliability Engineering (**SRE**) popularized measuring reliability with Service Level Indicators (**SLI**s), targeting them with Service Level Objectives (**SLO**s), and spending **error budgets** when reality misses the target — then learning via postmortems. SRE vocabulary turns telemetry into release policy — not just pretty graphs.

## Videos (verified)

1. **[SLIs, SLOs, SLAs, oh my! (class SRE implements DevOps)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tEylFyxbDLE)** — Google Cloud Tech  
   Why it helps: canonical vocabulary with examples.

2. **[Risk and Error Budgets (class SRE implements DevOps)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y2ILKr8kCJU)** — Google Cloud Tech  
   Why it helps: how error budgets drive release vs reliability trade-offs; pair with written postmortem culture chapter.

Prefer the Google SRE book chapters below if a video moves.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Google SRE Book — Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) — SLI/SLO/error budgets.
2. [Google SRE Book — Postmortem Culture](https://sre.google/sre-book/postmortem-culture/) — blameless learning.
3. [OpenTelemetry docs — Concepts](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/) — signals you will emit in this module.
4. [Google — CRE life lessons / SLOs](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/sre-fundamentals-slis-slas-and-slos) — short companion.

## Next step

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page.

# Reading — Argo CD, policy-as-code, Crossplane intro

## Learning objectives

1. Explain **pull** GitOps (Argo CD app-of-apps) vs push pipelines.
2. Fail CI on bad manifests with Kyverno or Conftest.
3. Sketch a Crossplane claim for cloud resources (generic intro).

**Why this matters.** As services multiply (API, worker, admin UI), one flat folder of manifests becomes unreviewable. **App-of-apps** patterns let a root Application own child apps so each team’s repo/path stays clear. Without policy, privileged pods or missing probes still sync “successfully.” **Crossplane** (awareness-level here) brings cloud resources into the same Kubernetes control loop via claims — useful when identity/mail infra should be requested like any other API object. On the job, platform interviews often contrast pull vs push and ask how bad YAML is blocked.

**How it works.**

1. **Argo CD** (pull): controller compares live state to git; syncs when drifted.
2. **App-of-apps**: root Application manifests point at child Applications (API, worker, …).
3. **Policy-as-code**: Conftest/Kyverno reject privileged pods, `:latest`, missing probes in CI or admission.
4. **Crossplane claim**: a namespaced custom resource requests composed cloud infra (bucket/queue) without every app team learning raw cloud consoles — Terraform remains valid; Crossplane is another composition style.
5. Recover from a bad sync by reverting the git commit (desired state) and letting the agent reconcile — why git-first: the fix is reviewable and replayable, not a one-off kubectl bandage.

```text
Root App → Child App (api) → Deployment/Service in git
         → Child App (worker)
CI: conftest/kyverno on PR  →  Argo sync only green desired state
```

### Worked example

App-of-apps child pointer (conceptual Argo CD Application):

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: mailguard-api
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.example.com/org/mailguard-deploy.git
    path: apps/api          # Why path-per-app: reviewable blast radius
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: mailguard
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
```

```yaml
apiVersion: mailguard.example.com/v1alpha1
kind: HoldQueueClaim
metadata:
  name: hold-queue
spec:
  compositionSelector:
    matchLabels: { type: sqs-hold }
  # Why a claim: app teams request infra like any other API object
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Self-heal means ignore bad merges.”** Self-heal restores *git* desired state — if git is wrong, the cluster stays wrong until you revert.
- **“Crossplane replaces Terraform forever.”** Both can compose cloud resources; Crossplane is another style in the Kubernetes control loop — awareness, not a rewrite mandate.
- **“One mega Application for all services.”** Flat trees become unreviewable; app-of-apps keeps ownership and blast radius clear ([Argo CD docs](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/)).
- **“Policy only at admission is enough.”** CI failure on the PR stops bad desired state earlier and leaves an audit trail in git.

# Reading — GitOps + policy

## Learning objectives

1. Diagram pull-based sync of manifests from git.
2. Fail CI on a policy violation (e.g. missing probes).
3. Keep claims proportional to what you automated.

**Why this matters.** Laptop `kubectl apply` does not scale and is hard to audit. Drift appears when someone “just fixed prod” outside git. Policy-as-code stops unsafe desired state (no probes, `:latest`, privileged pods) before it becomes the cluster’s reality. On the job, platform and security teams expect git as the source of truth for what runs mail/identity workloads — and CI gates that reject bad manifests.

**How it works.**

1. Treat git as the **desired state** for Deployments/Services (and related objects).
2. In **pull** mode, an in-cluster agent (Argo CD-class) watches the repo and reconciles drift.
3. In **push** mode, CI runs `kubectl`/`helm` from outside — simpler start, credentials live in CI.
4. Policy tools (Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper, Conftest) validate manifests in CI or at admission.
5. This module reuses Module 14 checks and adds a “bad manifest” fixture that must fail — keep claims proportional to what you automated.

```text
git commit (desired) → CI policy check → sync agent pulls → cluster matches git
                              ↓ fail
                         PR blocked (bad probes/tags/privileges)
```

Trade-off: pull GitOps needs an agent and RBAC in-cluster; push is simpler to start but credentials live in CI and drift is easier if people apply by hand.

### Worked example

Fail CI before sync (Conftest-class; Kyverno/OPA equivalent works the same idea). Good shape mirrors [`../fixtures/good_deployment.yaml`](../fixtures/good_deployment.yaml) (probes + pinned tag + requests):

```bash
# Why fail CI before sync: stop bad desired-state from rolling out
# Policies live in this module's policy/ (Rego for Conftest + a Kyverno sketch)
conftest test fixtures/bad_deployment.yaml -p policy/
# Expected: FAIL — missing readinessProbe / :latest
conftest test fixtures/good_deployment.yaml -p policy/
# Expected: PASS
# Sample CI shape: .github/workflows/policy-check.yml under this module (copy into your fork root)
```

```text
# Sync flow after green CI
PR merge → git desired state updated → agent detects drift → apply → Ready pods
```

Keep claims honest: if you only failed a fixture in CI, do not say “production GitOps” yet.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“GitOps means nobody reviews YAML.”** Git is the source of truth *and* the review surface — policy + humans still gate merges.
- **“Fix prod with kubectl, commit later.”** That is drift; the next sync may overwrite your hotfix — revert/fix in git and let the agent reconcile.
- **“Passing sync equals safe cluster.”** Without policy, privileged pods and missing probes sync “successfully.”
- **“Push and pull are the same risk.”** Push stores deploy credentials in CI; pull needs careful in-cluster RBAC — pick deliberately ([OpenGitOps Principles](https://opengitops.dev/)).

## Short intro

GitOps treats git as the desired state; a sync agent applies it. Policy-as-code stops unsafe manifests before they roll out. This module reuses Module 14 checks and adds a “bad manifest” fixture that must fail. GitOps + policy-as-code turn “hope the YAML is safe” into enforceable gates.

4. [Kubernetes Pod Security Standards](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/pod-security-standards/)

# Reading — Supply-chain security

## Learning objectives

1. Produce or consume an **SBOM** for an image/app you build.
2. **Pin** dependencies and enable automated update PRs (Dependabot-class).
3. Sketch **cosign** signature verify and **SLSA**-minded provenance claims honestly.

**Why this matters.** Compromised npm/PyPI packages and unsigned `:latest` images bypass otherwise careful app code. Without SBOMs, pinning, and signature checks, GitOps happily syncs poisoned desired state. On the job, platform and security reviews ask how you know what shipped and whether anyone signed it.

**How it works.**

1. Build an image/artifact in CI with a **locked** dependency file (`package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`, `go.sum`).
2. Generate an **SBOM** (CycloneDX/SPDX) and store it next to the artifact.
3. Enable **Dependabot** (or Renovate) so bumps are reviewable PRs — not silent `latest`.
4. Sign the image with **cosign** (keyless OIDC is common on GitHub Actions); verify before cluster sync.
5. Aim for **SLSA**-style provenance (who built what from which source) — claim only the level you actually automated.

```text
source → CI build (pinned deps) → SBOM + cosign signature → policy verify → GitOps sync
```

### Worked example

```bash
# Conceptual — pin + SBOM + sign (tool versions vary)
cosign sign --yes "$IMAGE_DIGEST"
cosign verify "$IMAGE_DIGEST"
# SBOM: syft / trivy image "$IMAGE" -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“SBOM alone blocks malware.”** It inventories; policy + updates + signatures act on the inventory.
- **“`:latest` is fine for demos.”** Untagged drift breaks forensics; pin digests for anything that matters.
- **“We are SLSA 4.”** Overclaiming fails audits — document the controls you actually run.
- **“Signing replaces vulnerability scanning.”** Signatures prove origin; scanners find known CVEs.

## Read these (verified)

1. [SLSA](https://slsa.dev/)
2. [Sigstore cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/system_config/installation/)
3. [GitHub Dependabot](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/dependabot)
4. [CycloneDX](https://cyclonedx.org/)

## Next step

Add a one-page note to your Module 16 assignment: what you pin, where the SBOM lives, and whether verify runs in CI or admission.

# Svelte primer

**Why this matters.** Optional Module 17 (Phish Lite) uses **Svelte / SvelteKit** for a small learning UI. You need just enough framework literacy to follow the assignment — and a hard ethical boundary: simulations never capture real credentials. On the job, security-awareness UIs fail when honesty and metrics are an afterthought; the framework is secondary to that boundary.

**How it works.**

1. Install/reuse **Node.js** + npm (same toolchain family as the Vue primer).
2. **Svelte** compiles components at build time (less runtime framework overhead than some SPA approaches).
3. **SvelteKit** adds routing and project structure for pages like consent → scenario → results.
4. In Module 17, label learning purpose clearly and never harvest credentials — the framework only hosts that UI.

```text
node/npm → scaffold Kit app → components + routes → build/dev server
```

This primer has no assignment, quiz, or download pack.

**Svelte** is a UI framework; **SvelteKit** is its full-stack application framework. Module 17’s language chip is Svelte — Vue was Module 08.

Teams pick Svelte for small, fast interactive apps and teaching demos. In security-awareness work, clear UI copy matters as much as the framework — honesty about simulation purpose is mandatory.

# Reading — Phish Lite

## Learning objectives

1. Build a small awareness quiz UI (Svelte preferred).
2. Label the experience as a learning simulation.
3. Prefer report-rate metrics over “gotcha” humiliation.

**Why this matters.** Phishing remains a top initial-access path into mail and identity systems. Awareness tools help — but badly designed simulations harvest passwords, shame clickers, or train people to distrust IT. Without clear learning labels and report-focused metrics, you optimize for “gotchas” instead of healthy reporting culture. On the job, security teams are judged on whether people **report** suspicious mail quickly, not only on raw click rates.

**How it works.**

1. Disclose purpose up front (consent / learning label) so participants know this is training.
2. Present labeled scenarios (quiz UI — Svelte preferred); score answers without collecting real passwords.
3. Offer a **report** action and compute **report rate** (and optionally time-to-report).
4. Debrief clearly; avoid public shame boards.
5. The graded kata scores quiz answers and computes a simple report-rate metric.

```text
Consent / disclosure → scenario quiz → optional “report” action
                    → score + report-rate (not public shame boards)
```

Trade-off: hyper-realistic login clones teach recognition but cross into credential-capture risk — this course forbids that pattern.

### Worked example

Report-rate metric (same idea as `score.js` in this module’s kata):

```text
report_rate = reported / (reported + clicked)
# Example: reportRate(3, 1) → 0.75  (three reports, one click-without-report)
# “clicked” here means non-report outcomes that still count toward the denom.
# Why prefer this over vanity click rates alone: rewards the behavior you want on real mail.
```

Ethics gate checklist:

```text
[ ] Consent / “SIMULATION” label visible before scenarios
[ ] No password / secret input fields
[ ] Results are private aggregates — not a public shame board
[ ] Debrief explains what “good” looks like (report quickly)
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Higher click rates mean better training.”** Click bait without reporting culture trains fear; report rate and time-to-report measure the job skill ([NIST SP 800-50](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/50/final)).
- **“Fake login pages that POST passwords are OK if labeled in fine print.”** Capturing credentials is out of scope and unethical here — do not build harvesters.
- **“Public leaderboards of who failed motivate people.”** Humiliation destroys trust in IT and suppresses future reporting.
- **“Awareness replaces SPF/DKIM/DMARC and hold rules.”** Training is one layer; mail authentication and outbound hold still matter.

## Short intro

Phishing awareness tools train people to spot risky messages. Keep ethics first: informed participants, no real password capture, clear debrief. The graded kata scores quiz answers and computes a simple report-rate metric.


## Videos (verified)

1. **[Svelte Tutorial for Beginners](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3TVy6GdtNuQ)**  
   Why it helps: UI stack for the awareness quiz.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Svelte tutorial](https://svelte.dev/tutorial)

3. [APWG — Phishing activity](https://apwg.org/) (industry context)

## On the job

When designing training for people who handle held mail or admin consoles, honesty and metrics beat cinematic fake login pages.

# Reading — Ethical phishing-training app

## Learning objectives

1. Design a **Svelte/SvelteKit**-shaped training UI with consent and **no credential capture**.
2. Prefer **report rate** and time-to-report over vanity click rates.
3. Keep simulations clearly labeled as training — never weaponize against unaware users.

**Why this matters.** A pixel-perfect fake login that POSTs passwords “for scoring” is not training — it is a credential harvester with a story. Organizations also get sued or lose trust when campaigns omit disclosure. Prefer metrics that reward reporting. On the job, usable-security work for mail/identity products sits next to awareness programs; both need the same honesty rule.

**How it works.**

1. Structure SvelteKit routes for consent → scenario → results.
2. Gate the experience on consent and a visible **SIMULATION** label.
3. Score with helpers such as `scoreAnswers` / `reportRate` / `timeToReportSeconds` (see `score.js`); lock ethics with `ethicalSimOk({ consent, capturesCredentials })`.
4. Keep aggregates private; never target real customer mailboxes without notice.
5. Tests (Vitest/Playwright-class) fail if credential capture is enabled or consent is missing.

```text
SvelteKit route: /train → consent banner → scenarios → results (private aggregates)
```

### Worked example

Ethics + metrics helpers (implementations live in the kata; contract shape):

```js
// Why no password fields: capturing secrets is out of scope and unethical here
ethicalSimOk({ consent: true, capturesCredentials: false })  // → true
ethicalSimOk({ consent: true, capturesCredentials: true })   // → false

// reportRate(reported, clicked) = reported / (reported + clicked)
reportRate(3, 1)  // → 0.75

// timeToReportSeconds(sentAt, reportedAt) — faster reporting is the job skill
```

```text
# Why label “SIMULATION”: users must distinguish training from real IdP pages
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“We’ll strip password fields after the demo.”** If the form can capture secrets, the ethics gate must fail in tests — do not ship a harvester “temporarily.”
- **“Consent once in a README is enough.”** The UI itself must disclose purpose before scenarios ([NIST SP 800-50](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-50/final)).
- **“Click-through rate is the KPI.”** Report rate and time-to-report align with how people should treat real suspicious mail.
- **“Weaponize against unaware coworkers for realism.”** Unannounced campaigns without policy/consent are out of scope for this course.

```bash
cd 17-phish-lite/starter && npm install && npm test
```
