# Reading — OSS contribution & security UX

## Learning objectives

1. Describe a respectful OSS contribution loop (read contributing guide → issue → minimal PR → respond to review).
2. List three qualities of a good **security warning** in an admin UI (clarity, action, no alarm fatigue).
3. Explain why phishing *simulations* need consent/honesty framing when used for learning.

**Why this matters.** Solo repos do not prove you can collaborate on security-sensitive code. Weak warning UX (scary modals users click through forever) creates alarm fatigue and missends still ship. Career-prep portfolios that show “I can collaborate beyond a solo repo” often include a small upstream contribution and evidence you care how humans meet security controls. On the job, mail/identity admin UIs live or die on clear hold/release warnings — not denser red banners.

**How it works.**

1. **OSS loop:** read `CONTRIBUTING` → find/create issue → minimal PR with test plan → respond to review.
2. **Security UX:** state the risk, the consequence, and the primary/secondary actions; avoid permanent one-click dismiss of critical warnings.
3. **Training honesty:** learning UIs disclose purpose; never harvest credentials (ties to Module 17).

```text
Read guide → reproduce → small PR → CI + review → merge
Hold UI: clear consequence → confirm release → audit log
```

Trade-off: more friction on release can prevent missend but slows legitimate ops — design confirmations that match severity.

### Worked example

Hold-release warning checklist item for an admin UI PR:

```text
PR checklist — security warning UX
[ ] Risk stated in plain language (who/what is affected)
[ ] Consequence explicit (e.g. “External recipients will receive this message”)
[ ] Primary action = safe default; destructive release requires confirm
[ ] No permanent “don’t show again” on critical release warnings
[ ] Screenshot or test plan so reviewers verify without guessing
```

```bash
# Why fork + branch: keep proposed changes reviewable and reversible
git checkout -b fix/hold-warning-copy
# Why tests/screenshots in the PR: reviewers verify without guessing
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Redder banners = safer product.”** Alarm fatigue trains operators to dismiss everything; clarity and action beat volume ([NN/g — Error Message Guidelines](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/error-message-guidelines/)).
- **“Forever-dismiss is a nice convenience.”** Critical hold/release warnings must not disappear permanently after one click-through.
- **“Huge first PRs impress maintainers.”** Minimal, documented changes with a test plan get review; kitchen-sink diffs stall ([Open Source Guides](https://opensource.guide/how-to-contribute/)).
- **“Phishing education UIs can borrow real login flows.”** Consent/honesty framing is mandatory — never train users into unsafe credential entry (Module 17).

## Short intro

Career-prep portfolios that show “I can collaborate beyond a solo repo” often include a small upstream contribution and evidence you care how humans meet security controls. MailGuard’s admin hold/release flow is a natural place to practice warning copy and confirmation UX.

## Videos (verified)

Prefer the written Open Source Guides + NN/g + Chromium enamel links below (contribution and warning-UX video IDs bitrot quickly).  
Optional: search YouTube for “usable security warnings” / “alarm fatigue security UX” from academic or browser-team talks and confirm the current title before watching.

Prefer written links if a video moves.

1. [GitHub — Open Source Guides: How to contribute](https://opensource.guide/how-to-contribute/) — practical contribution path (issue → PR → review).
2. [First Contributions](https://github.com/firstcontributions/first-contributions) — friendly first-PR practice (optional sandbox).
3. [NN/g — Error Message Guidelines](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/error-message-guidelines/) — clear, actionable messages (apply carefully to security warnings).
4. [Chromium — Permission UX / quiet UI notes](https://www.chromium.org/Home/chromium-security/enamel/) — browser-team thinking on interruptions (skim).
5. [OWASP — Authentication Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html) — only for “don’t train users into unsafe clicks” mindset when designing phishing *education* UIs.

# Capstone — small mail filter end-to-end

This module closes the course: ship a **coherent demo** of outbound message filtering (hold / allow / reject), prove it with tests, and self-grade against [`../../CAPSTONE-RUBRIC.md`](../../CAPSTONE-RUBRIC.md).

**Why this matters.** Separate labs (rules, API, worker, CI, IAM) do not prove you can tell one story. Hiring managers and portfolio reviewers look for a runnable thread: sample messages in → policy actions out → tests green → honest gaps. Without that integration, skills look like disconnected checklists. On the job, outbound missend prevention is exactly this shape — ordered rules, operator release path, and evidence you did not hard-code secrets.

**How it works.**

1. Define an ordered **rule list** (first-match-wins unless you document another order).
2. Actions: `hold`, `allow`, `reject` on sample fixtures (internal/external, risky recipients, keywords).
3. Prove behavior with **table-driven tests** that fail on empty stubs — why: green stubs would not prove your code.
4. Show an **operator path** (print held queue or approve/release helper).
5. Map each Must rubric row to a file/command; keep Stretch optional and honest.

```text
fixtures → rule engine → hold | allow | reject
                ↓
         pytest contract + short demo notes
```

### Worked example

Table-driven contract sketch (conceptual):

```python
# Why table-driven: one harness proves many edges; stubs must fail
CASES = [
    {"msg": {"to": ["ada@internal.example"], "subject": "hi"}, "want": "allow"},
    {"msg": {"to": ["ceo@partner.example"], "subject": "Q4"}, "want": "hold"},
    {"msg": {"to": ["evil@example.com"], "subject": "wire transfer"}, "want": "reject"},
]

def test_rules_first_match(engine):
    for case in CASES:
        assert engine.evaluate(case["msg"]) == case["want"]
```

Demo notes checklist item:

```text
[ ] Command to run tests (and why: proves non-stub behavior)
[ ] Command to feed one fixture and show hold|allow|reject
[ ] Path to rule list + operator release helper
[ ] Explicit gaps (no production SMTP, no cloud IAM claim, …)
```

The student implements the filter and fills the assignment.

Continue with the assignment from the downloads on this page. The quiz is **required**.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Green tests on empty stubs count.”** Contracts must fail until the engine is real — otherwise the demo is theater.
- **“Unordered rules are fine if ‘mostly right.’”** First-match order is policy; silent reorder changes allow/hold outcomes.
- **“Skip the operator path — automation is enough.”** Human-in-the-loop release is part of the MailGuard story and the rubric.
- **“Claim production gateway readiness.”** Capstone is a coherent demo with honest gaps — not a live MTA.

---

## What “done” looks like

A stranger can:

1. Read your short demo notes  
2. Run documented commands (annotate **why** each step exists)  
3. See a sample message held, allowed, or rejected by rules you wrote  
4. See tests pass on your implementation  

You are **not** claiming a production mail gateway.

---

## Suggested shape (keep it small)

| Piece | Role | Why that way |
|-------|------|--------------|
| Rule list | Ordered rules; first-match-wins (or document another order) | Predictable, reviewable policy |
| Actions | `hold`, `allow`, `reject` | Matches earlier MailGuard vocabulary |
| Sample messages | 3–5 fixtures covering internal/external, risky recipients, subject keywords | Proves edge cases, not one happy path |
| Tests | Table-driven cases that fail on empty stubs | Contract before implementation theater |
| Operator path | Print held queue *or* a tiny approve/release function | Shows human-in-the-loop, not fire-and-forget |

Reuse ideas from Challenge Gym hold rules, MailGuard API, and threat-model notes — do not paste vendor product claims.

---

## Evidence for the rubric

Map each Must row in `CAPSTONE-RUBRIC.md` to a file path or command in your assignment. Stretch rows are optional ceiling; pick at least two if you want “portfolio-ready” as defined there. **Why map explicitly:** self-grade stops optimistic checkboxes without proof.

---

# Reading — SCIM / JIT / directories

## Learning objectives

1. Describe SCIM 2.0 resources and filtering (RFC 7643/7644).
2. Contrast JIT vs SCIM vs directory sync (e.g. Entra Connect patterns).
3. Explain why **deprovisioning latency** often matters more than provisioning speed.

**Why this matters.** Joiner speed feels like a helpdesk win; **leaver lag** is a security incident waiting to happen — ex-employees who still reach hold queues, admin consoles, or mailbox forwards. System for Cross-domain Identity Management (**SCIM**) 2.0 standardizes create/update/deactivate across SaaS apps. Just-In-Time (**JIT**) provisioning creates users on first single sign-on (**SSO**) but may not tear them down promptly. On the job, identity engineers are measured on deprovision SLAs as much as onboarding UX.

**How it works.**

1. **[RFC 7643](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7643)** defines resources (User, Group) and schemas; **[RFC 7644](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644)** defines the HTTP protocol (`/Users`, filters, PATCH).
2. An Identity Provider (**IdP**) (or broker) POSTs/PATCHes users into the app’s SCIM endpoint; clients often **filter** first (`userName eq …`) to avoid duplicates.
3. **JIT:** account appears at first SSO — simple, but lifecycle depends on later hooks.
4. **Directory sync** (e.g. Entra Connect-class): continuous sync from on-prem/cloud directories — different operational model than app-level SCIM.
5. Deprovision: disable login **and** revoke app roles, tokens, forwarding, and group grants — incomplete disable leaves access paths.

```text
IdP lifecycle event → SCIM POST/PATCH/DELETE → app account state
                 ↘ JIT on first SSO (create only unless hooked)
```

Trade-off: SCIM needs a correct endpoint and filter support; JIT is faster to ship and weaker on leavers unless you add lifecycle jobs.

### Worked example

Filter-then-create (IdP-style) against a lab `/Users` endpoint:

```http
GET /Users?filter=userName%20eq%20%22ada@example.com%22
Authorization: Bearer <scim-token>
```

```http
POST /Users
Content-Type: application/scim+json

{
  "schemas": ["urn:ietf:params:scim:schemas:core:2.0:User"],
  "userName": "ada@example.com",
  "active": true,
  "emails": [{ "value": "ada@example.com", "primary": true }]
}
```

Why filter first: IdPs query before create/update to avoid duplicates ([RFC 7644](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644)). Why `active: false` on leave is not enough alone: revoke tokens, roles, and forwarding too.

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Fast join latency means identity is secure.”** Leaver lag (T+24h still active on hold queues) is the usual incident — measure deprovision SLAs.
- **“JIT replaces SCIM.”** JIT creates on first SSO; without lifecycle hooks it does not tear down promptly.
- **“Setting `active=false` closes all access.”** Sessions, API tokens, mailbox forwards, and group grants can outlive a disabled flag.
- **“Any filter string is fine.”** Incomplete filter support causes duplicate users or failed sync — support the subset IdPs actually send.

## Lab idea

Minimal FastAPI SCIM `/Users` endpoint passing a subset of filters; optionally validate against a vendor SCIM test harness.

## Read these (verified)

1. [RFC 7643 — SCIM core](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7643)
2. [RFC 7644 — SCIM protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7644)
3. [Microsoft Entra — SCIM overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/app-provisioning/use-scim-to-provision-users-and-groups)
4. [Google Workspace — Admin SDK Directory API](https://developers.google.com/admin-sdk/directory)

## On the job

Mail-security products inherit every account the IdP still believes is active. Ask “what happens at T+24h after termination?” before celebrating join latency.

## Next step

Assignments → katas → quiz.

# Reading — Global collaboration & privacy

## Learning objectives

1. Collaborate across timezones: async updates, explicit handoffs, inclusive meeting hygiene.
2. Compare major privacy laws at a literacy level: **GDPR**, **CCPA/CPRA**, **APPI**, **LGPD**, **PIPL**.
3. Connect privacy duties to MailGuard hold/release (minimization, access, retention, cross-border caution).

**Why this matters.** Hold queues can contain personal data (message bodies, recipients, attachments). A support engineer in another country asking for “just paste the held mail” can create a cross-border transfer problem. Global teams that only schedule meetings at one region’s afternoon quietly exclude others and slow incident response. On the job, email/identity SaaS work is multi-region by default — privacy literacy and async handoffs are operational skills, not soft extras.

**How it works.**

1. **Collaboration:** prefer written async handoffs with timezone stamps; rotate meeting hours or default to async; explicit owner for the next action.
2. **Privacy literacy:** General Data Protection Regulation (**GDPR**), California Consumer Privacy Act / California Privacy Rights Act (**CCPA/CPRA**), Japan’s Act on the Protection of Personal Information (**APPI**), Brazil’s Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (**LGPD**), China’s Personal Information Protection Law (**PIPL**) — different scopes and breach-notification expectations; cite primary sources, do not memorize every article.
3. **MailGuard link:** minimize what the hold store keeps, restrict who can release/read, define retention, and check transfer rules before foreign support access.

```text
Incident spanning TZ A/B → async handoff note → least-privilege access check
                         → privacy regime checklist → notify / refuse as needed
```

### Worked example

Cross-border support request checklist (literacy-level — verify against primary sources before compliance claims):

```text
Request: “Support in Region B needs the held message PDF for ticket 123.”
1. What data? (headers only vs body/attachments — minimize)
2. Who needs access? (named role, time-boxed — least privilege)
3. Transfer / lawful basis? (check GDPR / CPRA / APPI / LGPD / PIPL as applicable)
4. Retention? (delete export after ticket; do not leave in chat forever)
5. Handoff note (UTC timestamps + next owner) if IR spans timezones
→ If checks fail: refuse paste; escalate privacy/security — do not “just send the PDF”
```

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“Support overseas is the same as local admin access.”** Cross-border transfer and access rules may block casual paste of hold contents.
- **“Always-on meetings at one region’s 15:00 is inclusive.”** Fixed slots exclude others; rotate or default to async with explicit owners.
- **“Memorizing every article is the skill.”** Literacy + knowing where to cite ([GDPR.eu](https://gdpr.eu/), [CPPA](https://cppa.ca.gov/), [PPC](https://www.ppc.go.jp/en/), [ANPD](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br)) beats trivia.
- **“Hold queues are ‘just logs.’”** Bodies and attachments are personal data with retention and access duties.

## Keep in mind

No language-learning drills. No employer-specific culture decks. Focus on professional norms that travel: clarity, respect for local holidays/time, and privacy-by-design.

## Read these (verified)

1. [GDPR.eu overview](https://gdpr.eu/) (prefer EUR-Lex for normative text)
2. [California CPPA — CCPA/CPRA](https://cppa.ca.gov/)
3. [Japan PPC English](https://www.ppc.go.jp/en/)
4. [Brazil ANPD (LGPD)](https://www.gov.br/anpd/pt-br)
5. Optional PIPL overview from reputable legal summaries — verify against official PRC texts when making compliance claims.

## On the job

Interview scenarios often ask: “Support overseas needs hold contents — what do you check first?” Lawful basis / transfer / least privilege / retention beats “sure, here’s the PDF.”

## Next step

Assignments → kata → quiz.

# Reading — Git & code review

## Learning objectives

1. Open small, reviewable PRs with clear English descriptions.
2. Review for security: secrets, authz, input validation, dangerous defaults.
3. Use conventional commits, CODEOWNERS, and CI logs effectively.
4. Write a one-page design note / RFC-style proposal.

**Why this matters.** Large mixed PRs hide auth bugs; vague commits block bisect; approving a PEM in `config/` creates a breach. MailGuard-shaped changes (hold/release, identity, CI) need reviewers who ask **why** and **how**, not only “LGTM.” On the job, collaboration skills are how secure changes land without silent regressions.

**How it works.**

1. Branch → small commits with [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) subjects (`feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:` …).
2. Open a PR with intent, risk, and test plan; keep diff focused (split refactors from auth).
3. **CODEOWNERS** routes required reviewers by path ([GitHub — About code owners](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-code-owners)).
4. Reviewers check secrets, authz, validation, dangerous defaults; CI logs triage red jobs before merge.
5. For larger ideas, write a one-page design/RFC before coding — why: align threat model and UX before sunk cost.

```text
idea → short RFC → small PR → CI → security-minded review → merge
```

Trade-off: tiny PRs add merge overhead but cut review risk; mega-PRs feel faster and ship hidden footguns.

### Worked example

Security-minded PR review checklist item:

```text
PR review — MailGuard-shaped change
[ ] Intent / risk / test plan filled in (why this change, how verified)
[ ] No secrets (*.pem, API keys, long-lived cloud keys) in the diff
[ ] Authz: who can hold/release/read? defaults fail closed?
[ ] Input validation on new API fields
[ ] CI: read the failing job log before re-running blindly
[ ] Split: refactor commits separate from auth/policy commits
```

```bash
# Why conventional subject: changelog + bisect clarity
git commit -m "fix: require readinessProbe on api deployment"

# Why block *.pem in PRs: secrets in git outlive the PR tab
```

Do **not** rewrite course `main` history to “practice rebase games.”

### Common misconceptions / what goes wrong

- **“LGTM on a mega-PR is fine if CI is green.”** Auth bugs hide in large mixed diffs; split refactors from security-sensitive changes ([OWASP Code Review Guide](https://owasp.org/www-project-code-review-guide/)).
- **“Re-run CI without reading logs.”** Blind retries waste time; the failing contract usually names the file.
- **“CODEOWNERS is optional ceremony.”** Path-based owners are how teams force review on identity/mail/IAM paths.
- **“Force-pushing rewritten `main` teaches git.”** History rewrite on shared main is out of scope and harmful — practice on personal branches.

## Read these (verified)

1. [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
2. [GitHub — About code owners](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-code-owners)
3. [OWASP Code Review Guide](https://owasp.org/www-project-code-review-guide/)

## On the job

Security reviews of identity and mail features start with: secrets? authz? input validation? defaults? — then style.

## Next step

Assignment → kata → quiz. Practice repo optional.
